analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved experimental infections of three to five-day-old female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes divided into five groups (n = 200 per group) for simultaneous coinfection and four groups (n = 300 per group) for sequential coinfection. Mosquitoes were reared under standard insectary conditions and infected by membrane feeding.
analysis_en.methods: Mosquitoes were infected by membrane feeding using fresh blood from BALB/c mice. Viral RNA quantification was performed using RT-qPCR, and saliva samples were collected for transmission efficiency assessment. Statistical analyses included the Kruskal–Wallis test and Shapiro–Wilk test for normality.
analysis_en.main_results: At 7 dpi, DENV-1 infection rates and viral loads were significantly reduced in the CD1 group compared with monoinfections, while DENV-2 showed increased viral loads in saliva. No significant differences in viral loads were detected at any time point for sequential coinfections. CHIKV infection rates were significantly lower at 14 dpi in the monoinfected group compared to the DENV-1/CHIKV coinfection group.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that DENV-1 and DENV-2 exhibited different transmission dynamics when co-infected with CHIKV, with DENV-1 showing reduced infection rates and viral loads, and DENV-2 showing increased viral loads in saliva. This finding highlights the complex interactions between arboviruses in mosquitoes.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform surveillance strategies and risk assessments for dengue and chikungunya co-infections, as they demonstrate how viral interactions may affect transmission efficiency and vector competence in Aedes aegypti.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had three independent biological experiments, and inter-experiment variability was assessed, but no significant differences were detected, which may limit the confidence in the results. The evidence is moderate due to the controlled experimental setting and the use of statistical tests.

title_zh: 埃及伊蚊同时和相继同时感染 DENV-1、DENV-2 和 CHIKV 对 媒介 能力的影响
source_body_en: In this study, we investigated the effects of simultaneous coinfection with CHIKV and two DENV serotypes (DENV-1 and DENV-2) on the vector competence of Ae. Overall, our findings demonstrate that CHIKV–DENV coinfection in Ae. These results highlight the complexity of arboviral coinfections within this shared vector and emphasize the importance of considering different coinfection scenarios when evaluating vector competence and transmission risk in endemic settings.Keywords: Aedes aegypti, arbovirus coinfection, chikungunya virus, dengue virus serotypes, sequential infection, simultaneous infection, vector competence 2.Materials and methods2.1. aegypti (strain BH), maintained at the Laboratory of Medical Entomology, Fiocruz-Minas, Brazil, was used in this study. AbstractVector-borne diseases (VBD) caused by arboviruses represent a major public health threat in tropical regions. According to WHO’s Global Vector Control Response, more than 80% of the global population live in areas at risk for VBD. For instance, Aedes aegypti is the primary vector of dengue virus (DENV) and chikungunya virus (CHIKV), and its widespread distribution, particularly in Brazil, contributes to the occurrence of outbreaks. During these outbreaks, mosquitoes may acquire either monoinfections or coinfections, which can occur either simultaneously or sequentially, potentially influencing transmission dynamics. aegypti and described the characteristics of infection and transmission phenotypes following different orders of sequential arbovirus acquisition. Simultaneous coinfection resulted in serotype-dependent outcomes. At 7 days post-infection (dpi), DENV-1 infection rates and viral loads were significantly reduced compared with monoinfections, whereas DENV-2 showed increased viral loads in saliva....
abstract_zh: 在这项研究中,我们调查了寨卡病毒(媒介)与两种登革病毒血清型(DENV-1和DENV-2)同时感染对Ae. aegypti(BH株)的影响。总体而言,我们的研究结果表明,CHIKV–DENV共同感染在Ae. aegypti中表现出血清型依赖性结果。在感染后第7天(dpi),DENV-1的感染率和病毒载量显著低于单感染,而DENV-2在唾液中的病毒载量则有所增加。这些结果突显了在该共同宿主中,这种病毒共同感染的复杂性,并强调了在评估媒介能力及传播风险时,需要考虑不同的共同感染情况。关键词:Aedes aegypti,虫媒病毒共同感染,寨卡病毒,登革病毒血清型,顺序感染,同时感染,媒介能力。2.材料和方法2.1. 本研究中使用了Aedes aegypti(BH株),该蚊株由巴西Fiocruz-Minas的医学昆虫学实验室维持。摘要虫媒病毒引起的虫媒疾病(VBD)是热带地区的主要公共卫生威胁。根据世界卫生组织(WHO)的全球媒介控制响应,全球超过80%的人口生活在有VBD风险的地区。例如,Aedes aegypti是寨卡病毒(登革病毒)和登革病毒(DENV)的主要媒介,其在巴西的广泛分布促进了暴发的发生。在这些暴发期间,蚊虫可能获得单感染或共同感染,这些感染可能同时或顺序发生,可能影响传播动态。
summary_zh: 在这项研究中,我们调查了寨卡病毒(媒介)与两种登革病毒血清型(DENV-1和DENV-2)同时感染对Ae. aegypti(BH株)的影响。总体而言,我们的研究结果表明,CHIKV–DENV共同感染在Ae. aegypti中表现出血清型依赖性结果。在感染后第7天(dpi),DENV-1的感染率和病毒载量显著低于单感染,而DENV-2在唾液中的病毒载量则有所增加。这些结果突显了在该共同宿主中,这种病毒共同感染的复杂性,并强调了在评估媒介能力及传播风险时,需要考虑不同的共同感染情况。关键词:Aedes aegypti,虫媒病毒共同感染,寨卡病毒,登革病毒血清型,顺序感染,同时感染,媒介能力。2.材料和方法2.1. 本研究中使用了Aedes aegypti(BH株),该蚊株由巴西Fiocruz-Minas的医学昆虫学实验室维持。摘要虫媒病毒引起的虫媒疾病(VBD)是热带地区的主要公共卫生威胁。根据世界卫生组织(WHO)的全球媒介控制响应,全球超过80%的人口生活在有VBD风险的地区。例如,Aedes aegypti是寨卡病毒(登革病毒)和登革病毒(DENV)的主要媒介,其在巴西的广泛分布促进了暴发的发生。在这些暴发期间,蚊虫可能获得单感染或共同感染,这些感染可能同时或顺序发生,可能影响传播动态。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查同时感染 CHIKV 和两种 DENV 血清型(DENV-1 和 DENV-2)对埃及伊蚊 媒介 能力的影响,弥补关于同时感染如何影响热带地区病毒 媒介 动态的知识差距。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及 3 至 5 天大的雌性埃及伊蚊的实验感染,分为五组(每组 200 只)同时合并感染和四组(每组 300 只)顺序合并感染。蚊子在标准昆虫条件下饲养并通过膜饲感染。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用 BALB/c 小鼠的新鲜血液通过膜饲法感染蚊子。使用 RT-qPCR 进行病毒 RNA 定量,并收集唾液样本用于 传播 效率评估。统计分析包括 Kruskal-Wallis 检验和 Shapiro-Wilk 正态性检验。
analysis_zh.main_results: 7 dpi时,与单一感染相比,CD1组的DENV-1感染率和病毒载量显着降低,而DENV-2则显示唾液中的病毒载量增加。在连续共感染的任何时间点均未检测到病毒载量的显着差异。与 DENV-1/CHIKV 合并感染组相比,单一感染组在 14 dpi 时的 CHIKV 感染率显着降低。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,DENV-1和DENV-2在与CHIKV共同感染时表现出不同的传播动态,其中DENV-1显示感染率和病毒载量降低,而DENV-2显示唾液中病毒载量增加。这一发现凸显了蚊子中虫媒病毒之间复杂的相互作用。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可以为登革热和基孔肯雅热联合感染的 监测 策略和风险评估提供信息,因为它们证明了病毒相互作用如何影响埃及伊蚊的 监测 效率和 媒介 能力。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究进行了三个独立的生物学实验,并评估了实验间的变异性,但没有检测到显着差异,这可能会限制结果的可信度。由于受控的实验设置和统计测试的使用,证据是中等的。

title: A nationwide ecological time-series analysis found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025

source_records.title: A nationwide ecological time-series analysis found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025

full_text: Article summary The COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted the ecology and surveillance of infectious diseases, raising questions about potential interactions between dengue and COVID-19. This study found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025, indicating that COVID-19 dynamics do not enhance the prediction of dengue incidence. Abstract Using national surveillance records, we evaluated whether COVID-19 dynamics explain, anticipate, or improve prediction of weekly dengue surveillance-record burden in Mexico during 2020–2025. We analysed 1,085,869 dengue records and 20,632,470 COVID-19 records. Audit of daily symptom-onset coverage identified 10 incomplete dengue weeks clustered around year-end/source snapshot boundaries; these weeks were treated as missing rather than zero, leaving 8,695 state-week observations from 32 entities for inferential analyses. Primary weekly counts were transformed as log10(records + 1), with a population-standardized sensitivity analysis using fixed 2020 INEGI populations. We examined pooled, year-specific, pandemic/post-pandemic, state-specific seasonal, nonlinear time-adjusted and lagged associations, and performed a direct predictive ablation. The audited pooled association was inverse (Pearson r = -0.331, bootstrap 95% CI -0.349 to -0.312; Spearman rho = -0.311), but its direction and magnitude varied by year, from r = 0.096 in 2021 to r = -0.312 in 2023. Population standardization yielded r = -0.386, whereas removal of both state and calendar-week effects reduced the association to r = -0.049. After state-specific adjustment for year, cyclic epidemiological-week structure and nonlinear time, the pooled residual correlation was r = -0.055; after additional AR(4) prewhitening, the largest absolute lag correlation was 0.053. In the direct ablation, adding COVID-19 lags to dengue lags, seasonal week and state effects changed test RMSElog10 from 0.1753 to 0.1749 (delta = -0.0004; block-bootstrap 95% interval − 0.0019 to 0.0011). These findings support no stable direct temporal or predictive coupling between the two surveillance series; the pooled inverse association is primarily a feature of calendar-time and epidemic-regime structure. 1 Introduction The COVID-19 pandemic profoundly altered the ecology and surveillance of infectious diseases. Beyond the direct burden of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the pandemic modified human mobility, social behaviour, health-care seeking, diagnostic pathways, laboratory capacity, public-health staffing, and the continuity of routine notification systems. Non-pharmaceutical interventions were associated with marked changes in the incidence of several infectious diseases, although their effects varied by pathogen, region, and surveillance context [1,2,3,4]. For vector-borne diseases, these disruptions were particularly complex: reduced travel may have limited imported infections, whereas confinement, increased domestic exposure, altered water-storage practices, interruption of vector-control activities, clinical misclassification, and competing health-system priorities may have suppressed, amplified, or obscured transmission [5,6,7]. Dengue remains one of the most important arboviral diseases worldwide and a major public-health threat in the Americas. It is caused by four antigenically distinct dengue virus serotypes and is transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and, to a lesser extent, Aedes albopictus. Global estimates indicate a large annual burden, with substantial under-ascertainment because many infections are asymptomatic, mild, self-managed, or misclassified as other acute febrile illnesses [8, 9]. Dengue transmission is shaped by temperature, rainfall, humidity, urbanization, population density, water storage, human mobility, vector abundance, viral serotype circulation, population immunity, and the intensity of vector-control programmes [10,11,12,13]. Climate change, demographic expansion, urban growth, and global connectivity are expected to further increase the population at risk of Aedes-borne transmission [14, 15]. The post-pandemic resurgence of dengue has intensified the need to understand whether pandemic-era time series contain useful epidemiological information. The Americas experienced a historically large dengue epidemic in 2024, exceeding previous regional records and placing renewed pressure on surveillance and health-care systems. Global preparedness strategies have emphasized the need for integrated surveillance, early warning, vector control, clinical management, and cross-border coordination for dengue and other Aedes-borne arboviruses [16]. Mexico is a particularly relevant setting because dengue transmission is spatially heterogeneous across federal entities and influenced by climatic gradients, urban ecology, vector distribution, and local health-system capacity. Simultaneously, COVID-19 generated large national waves and substantial changes in health-care demand, while national open-data systems provide longitudinal surveillance records for vector-borne diseases [17]. The relationship between dengue and COVID-19 is biologically plausible but epidemiologically difficult to interpret. Both diseases may initially present with fever, headache, myalgia, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, and non-specific systemic manifestations, complicating differential diagnosis in dengue-endemic regions [18,19,20]. Reports of false-positive dengue serology among patients with confirmed COVID-19 raised concerns about diagnostic cross-reactivity and misclassification [21, 22]. Conversely, evidence on laboratory-confirmed co-infection and serological cross-reactivity remains heterogeneous, highlighting the need to distinguish syndromic overlap, serological interference, and true dual infection [20, 23,24,25]. Individual-level mechanisms such as immune crosstalk, antibody-dependent enhancement, or viral interference have been proposed [26, 27], but they cannot be evaluated using aggregated state-week surveillance data. Accordingly, the present study does not test or infer immunological interactions between dengue virus and SARS-CoV-2. At the population level, apparent dengue–COVID-19 correlations may reflect shared temporal structure rather than direct epidemiological coupling. A previous multi-country study proposed a neural-network “Correlation Model” linking dengue and COVID-19 while incorporating external variables such as climate, holidays, and temporal structure [28]. However, weekly ecological correlations can be misleading if they are not separated from seasonality, secular trends, geographic heterogeneity, reporting artefacts, and dengue’s own autoregressive behaviour. Two features are particularly important for the present question. Forecasting work in Mexico has shown that both short-term and seasonal dengue autocorrelation carry substantial predictive information, while municipality-level analyses have documented marked spatial heterogeneity in climatic and socioeconomic drivers of Aedes-borne disease [29, 30]. More generally, meteorological effects on SARS-CoV-2 transmission can be nonlinear and embedded within spatial and temporal structure, reinforcing the need to separate seasonal and long-term variation from any residual cross-disease association [31]. Previous work assessing COVID-19-related disruption of dengue used pre-2020 observations to establish expected seasonal and multi-year dengue dynamics before evaluating pandemic-era departures [4]. In this study, we extend this modelling logic to Mexico using individual-level surveillance records aggregated into a federal-entity–week panel across the pandemic and post-pandemic period. We evaluate contemporaneous correlations, year-specific and pandemic/post-pandemic associations, state-specific dengue-season relationships, lagged associations, peak concordance, and predictive performance. Our central question is whether any dengue–COVID-19 association is stable across years and dengue seasons, persists after state-specific seasonal and nonlinear temporal adjustment, and adds predictive information beyond dengue’s own recent history, seasonal week and state effects. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design and data sources We conducted a longitudinal ecological study using national surveillance records for dengue and COVID-19 in Mexico. The analytical unit was the federal-entity–week, constructed by aggregating individual-level records according to state of residence and symptom-onset week. Two final surveillance extracts were analysed. Symptom-onset dates ranged from 1 January 2020 to 24 May 2025 for dengue and from 1 January 2020 to 2 June 2025 for COVID-19. The primary analysis used calendar matching by state of residence and epidemiological week. Entity codes 1–32 were matchable across both datasets and were included in the paired dengue–COVID-19 panel. Dengue records with non-matchable entity codes were retained for descriptive summaries but excluded from paired analyses. Symptom-onset date was used as the temporal reference because it better approximates epidemic dynamics than registration or database-update dates. The study was ecological; therefore, results describe aggregated surveillance patterns and not individual-level risk. No pre-2020 dengue observations were present in the supplied analytical extract. We therefore did not construct a counterfactual pre-pandemic baseline by combining differently harmonized external series; instead, we performed year-specific and pandemic-versus-post-pandemic sensitivity analyses and treat the absence of a pre-2020 baseline as an interpretative limitation. 2.2 Data preprocessing and variable construction Dates were converted into ISO epidemiological weeks, with Monday as the first day of the week. For each disease and state-week, we computed record counts, hospitalization proportion, mean and median age, and proportions of available binary demographic or clinical variables, including sex, Indigenous status, pregnancy, diabetes and, for COVID-19, hypertension. Binary variables coded as “yes” and “no” were recoded as 1 and 0, whereas non-applicable, unknown or unspecified codes were treated as missing. Weekly surveillance-record counts were transformed as: where \(\:{n}_{d,s,t}\) denotes the number of surveillance records for disease \(\:d\), federal entity \(\:s\), and epidemiological week \(\:t\). This transformation stabilized variance, reduced the dominance of large COVID-19 waves, and approximated the analytical strategy used in the reference correlation-model framework [28]. For the population-standardized sensitivity analysis, weekly counts were divided by fixed 2020 state populations from the INEGI Population and Housing Census and expressed as surveillance records per 100,000 residents [32]; these rates were transformed as log10(rate + 1). Because the denominator was fixed and the numerators were surveillance records, these measures describe standardized reported burden rather than person-time incidence. For weeks with complete national date coverage, state-week combinations without reported records were retained as zero; incomplete national dengue weeks identified by the audit described below were treated as missing rather than zero. Before weekly completion and inferential analysis, we audited national daily symptom-onset coverage for each disease. A calendar week was classified as incomplete when one or more calendar days within the observed source date range were entirely absent from the national extract. Ten dengue weeks met this criterion: weeks beginning 2020-12-28, 2021-12-27, 2022-12-26, 2023-12-18, 2023-12-25, 2024-12-02, 2024-12-09, 2024-12-16, 2024-12-23, and 2024-12-30. These gaps clustered around year-end or source-snapshot boundaries; COVID-19 had no analogous internal missing national dates. The incomplete dengue weeks were excluded from correlation, lag, peak and predictive analyses and represented as gaps in time-series figures. Partial weeks at the actual study boundaries were retained for the days covered by the extract. The resulting audited paired panel contained 8,695 state-week observations. 2.3 Descriptive analysis We summarized both datasets using total record counts, age distribution, sex composition, hospitalization proportion, and available clinical or demographic characteristics. State-level distributions were calculated as both absolute counts and cumulative surveillance records per 100,000 residents to describe geographic heterogeneity and the effect of population size. National weekly epidemic curves were generated by summing state-level counts and were visualized both as raw counts and as log-transformed counts. 2.4 Correlation, lag and peak analyses Pearson and Spearman correlations between dengue and COVID-19 log-transformed counts were estimated in the audited matched state-week panel and separately by state. Pearson correlation quantified linear association on the transformed scale, while Spearman correlation assessed monotonic association. National uncertainty was quantified using bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for Pearson correlation, and state-specific p values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate procedure. Temporal heterogeneity was examined by estimating correlations within each epidemiological year and separately for the pandemic (2020–2022) and post-pandemic (2023–2025) periods; within-year state-adjusted correlations were obtained after removal of state fixed effects. To avoid imposing a single national dengue season, each entity’s high-transmission season was defined empirically as the shortest contiguous circular epidemiological-week window capturing at least 70% of its mean annual dengue burden after normalizing each observed year to its annual total, with a minimum window length of eight weeks. Associations were then summarized within and outside these state-specific high-transmission windows. Raw cross-correlations were estimated from − 12 to + 12 weeks using exact calendar-date matching, so incomplete weeks could not be bridged by row position. Positive lags indicate that COVID-19 precedes dengue, whereas negative lags indicate that the COVID-19 series is shifted after dengue. To separate lagged cross-disease association from seasonal and long-term temporal structure, dengue and COVID-19 were residualized separately within each state using categorical epidemiological year, a cyclic cubic spline for epidemiological week (6 degrees of freedom), and a cubic regression spline for continuous time (12 degrees of freedom). Lag profiles were repeated on these residuals and after AR(4) prewhitening of each residual series. This constitutes a seasonal time-series sensitivity analysis rather than a causal model. Temperature, rainfall and humidity were not integrated and may therefore contribute to residual seasonal/environmental forcing. Peak concordance was assessed using two definitions: relative peaks, defined as local maxima, and high-burden peaks, defined as weeks at or above the disease-specific and state-specific 90th percentile. Peak detection required adjacent calendar weeks, so an incomplete surveillance interval could not create an artificial local maximum across a gap. 2.5 Predictive modelling We evaluated the incremental predictive value of COVID-19 using a direct ablation in otherwise identical ElasticNetCV models with dengue log-transformed weekly counts as the outcome. The dengue-specific baseline included dengue lags from one to four weeks, categorical epidemiological week and state effects. The augmented model added contemporaneous COVID-19 burden and COVID-19 lags from one to 12 weeks while retaining the identical dengue, seasonal and state feature set. Lag variables were created by exact 7-day calendar matching so incomplete surveillance weeks did not create artificial lag chains. The final 20% of unique calendar weeks was held out as a temporal test block, and both ablation models were evaluated on the same complete test rows. A naive dengue(t-1) benchmark was retained as an additional autoregressive comparator. Performance was assessed using mean absolute error, root mean squared error and R2 on the log10 scale, with MAE and RMSE also calculated after back-transformation to reported-record counts. Uncertainty in the incremental COVID-19 contribution was quantified by paired block bootstrap resampling of test weeks (2,000 replicates), preserving all states within each sampled week. full_text_sections.full_text: Article summary The COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted the ecology and surveillance of infectious diseases, raising questions about potential interactions between dengue and COVID-19. This study found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025, indicating that COVID-19 dynamics do not enhance the prediction of dengue incidence. Abstract Using national surveillance records, we evaluated whether COVID-19 dynamics explain, anticipate, or improve prediction of weekly dengue surveillance-record burden in Mexico during 2020–2025. We analysed 1,085,869 dengue records and 20,632,470 COVID-19 records. Audit of daily symptom-onset coverage identified 10 incomplete dengue weeks clustered around year-end/source snapshot boundaries; these weeks were treated as missing rather than zero, leaving 8,695 state-week observations from 32 entities for inferential analyses. Primary weekly counts were transformed as log10(records + 1), with a population-standardized sensitivity analysis using fixed 2020 INEGI populations. We examined pooled, year-specific, pandemic/post-pandemic, state-specific seasonal, nonlinear time-adjusted and lagged associations, and performed a direct predictive ablation. The audited pooled association was inverse (Pearson r = -0.331, bootstrap 95% CI -0.349 to -0.312; Spearman rho = -0.311), but its direction and magnitude varied by year, from r = 0.096 in 2021 to r = -0.312 in 2023. Population standardization yielded r = -0.386, whereas removal of both state and calendar-week effects reduced the association to r = -0.049. After state-specific adjustment for year, cyclic epidemiological-week structure and nonlinear time, the pooled residual correlation was r = -0.055; after additional AR(4) prewhitening, the largest absolute lag correlation was 0.053. In the direct ablation, adding COVID-19 lags to dengue lags, seasonal week and state effects changed test RMSElog10 from 0.1753 to 0.1749 (delta = -0.0004; block-bootstrap 95% interval − 0.0019 to 0.0011). These findings support no stable direct temporal or predictive coupling between the two surveillance series; the pooled inverse association is primarily a feature of calendar-time and epidemic-regime structure. 1 Introduction The COVID-19 pandemic profoundly altered the ecology and surveillance of infectious diseases. Beyond the direct burden of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the pandemic modified human mobility, social behaviour, health-care seeking, diagnostic pathways, laboratory capacity, public-health staffing, and the continuity of routine notification systems. Non-pharmaceutical interventions were associated with marked changes in the incidence of several infectious diseases, although their effects varied by pathogen, region, and surveillance context [1,2,3,4]. For vector-borne diseases, these disruptions were particularly complex: reduced travel may have limited imported infections, whereas confinement, increased domestic exposure, altered water-storage practices, interruption of vector-control activities, clinical misclassification, and competing health-system priorities may have suppressed, amplified, or obscured transmission [5,6,7]. Dengue remains one of the most important arboviral diseases worldwide and a major public-health threat in the Americas. It is caused by four antigenically distinct dengue virus serotypes and is transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and, to a lesser extent, Aedes albopictus. Global estimates indicate a large annual burden, with substantial under-ascertainment because many infections are asymptomatic, mild, self-managed, or misclassified as other acute febrile illnesses [8, 9]. Dengue transmission is shaped by temperature, rainfall, humidity, urbanization, population density, water storage, human mobility, vector abundance, viral serotype circulation, population immunity, and the intensity of vector-control programmes [10,11,12,13]. Climate change, demographic expansion, urban growth, and global connectivity are expected to further increase the population at risk of Aedes-borne transmission [14, 15]. The post-pandemic resurgence of dengue has intensified the need to understand whether pandemic-era time series contain useful epidemiological information. The Americas experienced a historically large dengue epidemic in 2024, exceeding previous regional records and placing renewed pressure on surveillance and health-care systems. Global preparedness strategies have emphasized the need for integrated surveillance, early warning, vector control, clinical management, and cross-border coordination for dengue and other Aedes-borne arboviruses [16]. Mexico is a particularly relevant setting because dengue transmission is spatially heterogeneous across federal entities and influenced by climatic gradients, urban ecology, vector distribution, and local health-system capacity. Simultaneously, COVID-19 generated large national waves and substantial changes in health-care demand, while national open-data systems provide longitudinal surveillance records for vector-borne diseases [17]. The relationship between dengue and COVID-19 is biologically plausible but epidemiologically difficult to interpret. Both diseases may initially present with fever, headache, myalgia, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, and non-specific systemic manifestations, complicating differential diagnosis in dengue-endemic regions [18,19,20]. Reports of false-positive dengue serology among patients with confirmed COVID-19 raised concerns about diagnostic cross-reactivity and misclassification [21, 22]. Conversely, evidence on laboratory-confirmed co-infection and serological cross-reactivity remains heterogeneous, highlighting the need to distinguish syndromic overlap, serological interference, and true dual infection [20, 23,24,25]. Individual-level mechanisms such as immune crosstalk, antibody-dependent enhancement, or viral interference have been proposed [26, 27], but they cannot be evaluated using aggregated state-week surveillance data. Accordingly, the present study does not test or infer immunological interactions between dengue virus and SARS-CoV-2. At the population level, apparent dengue–COVID-19 correlations may reflect shared temporal structure rather than direct epidemiological coupling. A previous multi-country study proposed a neural-network “Correlation Model” linking dengue and COVID-19 while incorporating external variables such as climate, holidays, and temporal structure [28]. However, weekly ecological correlations can be misleading if they are not separated from seasonality, secular trends, geographic heterogeneity, reporting artefacts, and dengue’s own autoregressive behaviour. Two features are particularly important for the present question. Forecasting work in Mexico has shown that both short-term and seasonal dengue autocorrelation carry substantial predictive information, while municipality-level analyses have documented marked spatial heterogeneity in climatic and socioeconomic drivers of Aedes-borne disease [29, 30]. More generally, meteorological effects on SARS-CoV-2 transmission can be nonlinear and embedded within spatial and temporal structure, reinforcing the need to separate seasonal and long-term variation from any residual cross-disease association [31]. Previous work assessing COVID-19-related disruption of dengue used pre-2020 observations to establish expected seasonal and multi-year dengue dynamics before evaluating pandemic-era departures [4]. In this study, we extend this modelling logic to Mexico using individual-level surveillance records aggregated into a federal-entity–week panel across the pandemic and post-pandemic period. title_original: A nationwide ecological time-series analysis found no stable temporal or predictive relationship between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records in Mexico from 2020 to 2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate whether the dynamics of the COVID-19 pandemic could explain, anticipate, or improve the prediction of dengue incidence in Mexico during 2020–2025, given the potential ecological and surveillance interactions between these two diseases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A longitudinal ecological study was conducted using national surveillance records for dengue and COVID-19 in Mexico, covering the period from 2020 to 2025. Entity codes 1–32 were matchable across both datasets and were included in the paired dengue–COVID-19 panel.
analysis.methods: The study used national surveillance records and residualized dengue and COVID-19 separately within each state using categorical epidemiological year, a cyclic cubic spline for epidemiological week, and a cubic regression spline for continuous time. Weekly surveillance-record counts were transformed as log10(rate + 1) for population-standardized analyses, and lag variables were created by exact 7-day calendar matching to avoid artificial lag chains.
analysis.main_results: The study found an inverse Pearson correlation (r = -0.331, bootstrap 95% CI -0.349 to -0.312; Spearman rho = -0.311) between dengue and COVID-19 surveillance records, but the direction and magnitude of this association varied by year, from r = 0.096 in 2021 to r = -0.312 in 2023. Population standardization yielded r = -0.386, whereas removal of state and calendar-week effects reduced the association to r = -0.049.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the lack of a stable temporal or predictive relationship suggests that the dynamics of the pandemic do not enhance the prediction of dengue incidence, and they extended the modelling logic to Mexico using individual-level surveillance records aggregated into a federal-entity–week panel.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the surveillance systems for dengue and COVID-19 in Mexico do not provide a stable basis for predicting dengue incidence, which has implications for the integration of surveillance data in public health planning and the understanding of disease interactions during pandemics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges that weekly ecological correlations may be misleading due to seasonality, secular trends, geographic heterogeneity, reporting artefacts, and dengue’s own autoregressive behavior. The evidence is moderate, as the analysis was limited by the absence of a pre-2020 baseline and the use of aggregated data rather than individual-level risk.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether the dynamics of the COVID-19 pandemic could explain, anticipate, or improve the prediction of dengue incidence in Mexico from 2020 to 2025. Using national surveillance records, the researchers found an inverse correlation between dengue and COVID-19 records, but this relationship varied by year. The study highlights the complexity of ecological correlations and the limitations of using aggregated data for disease prediction. The findings suggest that the pandemic did not significantly enhance the predictability of dengue incidence, which has implications for public health surveillance and disease forecasting. However, the study's conclusions are limited by the absence of a pre-pandemic baseline and the potential for confounding factors such as seasonality and geographic heterogeneity.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估鉴于两种疾病之间潜在的生态和 监测 相互作用,COVID-19 大流行的动态是否可以解释、预测或改进 2020-2025 年墨西哥登革热 监测 的预测。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用墨西哥登革热和 COVID-19 的国家 监测 记录进行了一项纵向生态研究,涵盖 2020 年至 2025 年期间。实体代码 1-32 在两个数据集中都是匹配的,并包含在配对的登革热 - COVID-19 面板中。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用了国家 监测 记录,并使用分类流行病学年份、流行病学周的循环三次样条和连续时间的三次回归样条分别在每个州内残留登革热和 COVID-19。每周 监测 记录计数转换为 log10(率 + 1)以进行群体标准化分析,并通过精确的 7 天日历匹配创建滞后变量,以避免人为滞后链。
elements_zh.main_results: 该研究发现登革热和 COVID-19 监测 记录之间存在皮尔逊反相关性(r = -0.331,bootstrap 95% CI -0.349 至 -0.312;Spearman rho = -0.311),但这种关联的方向和幅度因年份而异,从 2021 年的 r = 0.096 到 2023 年的 r = -0.312。人口标准化得出 r = -0.386,而消除州和日历周效应则将关联性降低至 r = -0.049。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,缺乏稳定的时间或预测关系表明,大流行的动态不会增强登革热 监测 的预测,并且他们使用汇总到联邦实体周面板中的个人级 监测 记录将建模逻辑扩展到墨西哥。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,墨西哥的登革热和 COVID-19 的 监测 系统并未为预测登革热 监测 提供稳定的基础,这对于将 监测 数据整合到公共卫生规划中以及了解大流行期间疾病相互作用具有影响。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究承认,由于季节性、长期趋势、地理异质性、报告假象以及登革热自身的自回归行为,每周的生态相关性可能会产生误导。证据是中等的,因为分析因缺乏 2020 年之前的基线以及使用汇总数据而不是个人层面的风险而受到限制。

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用墨西哥登革热和 COVID-19 的国家 监测 记录进行了一项纵向生态研究,涵盖 2020 年至 2025 年期间。实体代码 1-32 在两个数据集中都是匹配的,并包含在配对的登革热 - COVID-19 面板中。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究使用了国家 监测 记录,并使用分类流行病学年份、流行病学周的循环三次样条和连续时间的三次回归样条分别在每个州内残留登革热和 COVID-19。每周 监测 记录计数转换为 log10(率 + 1)以进行群体标准化分析,并通过精确的 7 天日历匹配创建滞后变量,以避免人为滞后链。
analysis_zh.main_results: 该研究发现登革热和 COVID-19 监测 记录之间存在皮尔逊反相关性(r = -0.331,bootstrap 95% CI -0.349 至 -0.312;Spearman rho = -0.311),但这种关联的方向和幅度因年份而异,从 2021 年的 r = 0.096 到 2023 年的 r = -0.312。人口标准化得出 r = -0.386,而消除州和日历周效应则将关联性降低至 r = -0.049。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,缺乏稳定的时间或预测关系表明,大流行的动态不会增强登革热 监测 的预测,并且他们使用汇总到联邦实体周面板中的个人级 监测 记录将建模逻辑扩展到墨西哥。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,墨西哥的登革热和 COVID-19 的 监测 系统并未为预测登革热 监测 提供稳定的基础,这对于将 监测 数据整合到公共卫生规划中以及了解大流行期间疾病相互作用具有影响。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究承认,由于季节性、长期趋势、地理异质性、报告假象以及登革热自身的自回归行为,每周的生态相关性可能会产生误导。证据是中等的,因为分析因缺乏 2020 年之前的基线以及使用汇总数据而不是个人层面的风险而受到限制。

full_text: AbstractBackgroundDengue fever has become an epidemiological concern worldwide, with 531,617 cases reported in Argentina during the 2023–2024 season. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon has been linked to changes in dengue dynamics. This study assessed the relationships among ENSO, local climatic variables, and dengue outbreaks in Argentina from 2018 to 2024.MethodsA nationwide spatiotemporal analysis was conducted using dengue cases and monthly mean temperature, relative humidity, and rainfall. The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) was used as the ENSO indicator (El Niño phase ≤ −0.5, neutral phase = −0.5 to 0.5, and La Niña phase ≥ 0.5). We fitted Hierarchical Bayesian models with Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). A Negative Binomial distribution of dengue cases was used to account for overdispersion. Spatial dependence was modeled by using the Besag–York–Mollié 2 (BYM2) structure, adjusted for population.ResultsThe final model achieved a Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 of 0.537. Exposure-response curves of posterior probability and 95% credible intervals suggested that dengue risk increased when monthly mean temperatures were between 20° and 30° Celsius during the El Niño or neutral phase, with less consistent effects during the La Niña phase. Humidity >50% was associated with increased dengue risk during the La Niña phase, with less steep or absent associations during El Niño or neutral phases. Negative SOI scores were associated with an increased risk of dengue after controlling for the covariates.ConclusionDengue outbreaks in Argentina were independently associated with temperatures between 20 and 30 °C during the El Niño and neutral phases, humidity > 50% during the La Niña phase, and the El Niño phase of the ENSO. Incorporating ENSO indices into predictive models could enhance early warning systems and timely public health interventions in Argentina.Keywords: Aedes aegypti, Argentina, dengue fever, El Niño-Southern Oscillation, epidemic dynamics, SOI 2.Methods2.1.Data collectionWe conducted a nationwide analysis of dengue case distribution in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 at a monthly resolution. Argentina is in the southern part of South America, covers an area of 2,780,400 km2 of continental and insular territory, and has a population of just over 46 million inhabitants. Argentina stretches over 3,700 km from north to south, which explains why it spans a remarkable variety of climates, from subtropical in the north to subpolar in the far south (15). This great length also gives rise to diverse biomes, including rainforests, grasslands, deserts, and Patagonian tundra. The country is divided into 525 departments and an autonomous city, Buenos Aires (hereinafter referred to as departments). Data on dengue incidence were obtained from the National Ministry of Health Surveillance System 2.0, accessed through https://datos.salud.gob.ar/dataset/vigilancia-de-dengue-y-zika (Date of Accession: 2025-02-01). A dengue case was defined as any confirmed or probable dengue infection reported through the national health surveillance system. For each department, monthly dengue incidence was calculated as the number of cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Population and population density data for each department were sourced from the 2022 National Census conducted by the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC, https://www.indec.gob.ar/, Date of Accession: 2025-02-01).Climatic data were obtained from NASA’s POWER Project (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) (16). For each department and month, we used the monthly mean of daily values for temperature (measured in degrees Celsius, °C) and relative humidity (measured in %), both at 2 meters above ground, as well as the monthly accumulated rainfall (measured in millimeters, mm). The spatial resolution of the satellite data is 0.5° latitude × 0.625° longitude (approximately 50 km). Daily values were extracted for each centroid within each administrative department and subsequently averaged to obtain monthly means; for rainfall, daily values were summed to derive monthly totals.The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) was also considered as a measure of ENSO (17, 18). This index reflects differences in atmospheric pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia, and is used to characterize the El Niño and La Niña phases. SOI scores were used in the analyses as a measure of the magnitude and direction of ENSO variability, which facilitates the climatological interpretation of exposure–response relationships. SOI scores above 0.5 indicated the La Niña phase; scores below −0.5 indicated the El Niño phase, with values between −0.5 and 0.5 characterizing a neutral phase, following the threshold criteria used in previous ENSO dengue studies (14).2.2.Statistical analysisWe fitted hierarchical Bayesian models using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) framework in R 4.5 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria; R-INLA package).The response variable was the monthly number of dengue cases, and we assumed a Negative Binomial likelihood to account for overdispersion.The general model fitted was:Yit∼NegBin(μit,φ)log(μit)=log(Eit)+f1(Temperaturelag)+f2(Humiditylag)+f3(Rainfalllag)+f4(SOIlag)+fn(SOI−categorizedlag∗climate_variableslag)+β1log(pop.densityi)+ui+vi+γyear(t)+smonth(t)Where Yit denotes the number of dengue cases observed in department i during month t, assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution. The term log(Eit) denotes the logarithm of the population size and is used as an offset. Nonlinear effects of temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, and SOI, as well as their interactions, were modeled using second-order random walks (RW2), which impose smoothness by penalizing second differences between adjacent latent effects. The RW2 terms were fitted using the default INLA penalized complexity priors for the precision parameter. For the RW2 components, climate parameters and SOI were centered and transformed into ordered indices representing adjacent exposure levels. Temperature and relative humidity were rounded to the nearest integer and converted to sequential indices, rainfall was rounded to the nearest 5-mm interval and converted to sequential indices, and SOI anomalies were rounded to the nearest integer and indexed similarly. These indices were then used as the covariates in the RW2 smooth terms, allowing estimation of nonlinear exposure–response relationships across the observed range of values. Population density was log-transformed and standardized before being included as a linear fixed effect.Interactions between the ENSO phase and climatic variables were implemented using the replicate argument in INLA. Specifically, separate RW2 smooth functions were estimated for temperature and relative humidity within each SOI category (El Niño, Neutral, and La Niña), while sharing a common smoothing prior structure. The terms ui and vi represent the structured and unstructured spatial random effects, respectively, modeled using the Besag–York–Mollié 2 specification. Departmental neighborhood relationships were defined using a first-order contiguity adjacency matrix derived from the departmental polygon shapefile, in which two departments were considered neighbors if they shared a common boundary. This adjacency matrix was supplied to INLA through the BYM2 specification. The BYM2 spatial effect was fitted using the default penalized complexity (PC) priors implemented in R-INLA.Temporal dependence was modeled through a 12-month cyclic seasonal effect to account for recurrent intra-annual patterns, together with an independent random effect for year to capture interannual variability in dengue transmission.We explored the best-fitting lags for SOI and climate parameters by computing and comparing the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) and the Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) between the models. Candidate lags from 0 to 11 months were evaluated independently for each climatic variable and SOI. The lag yielding the lowest DIC and WAIC values was retained in the final model.The interactions between the SOI and the climatic variables at their best-fitting lags were explored by categorizing SOI values, as established in the literature into El Niño (<−0.5), Neutral (−0.5 to 0.5), and La Niña (>0.5) phases (14). Models were fitted, and DIC and WAIC were used to select the best model.The final model adequacy was assessed through posterior predictive checks, including the randomized Probability Integral Transform (PIT) histogram, Q–Q plots of the randomized PIT values, and simulation-based residual diagnostics using the DHARMa package. DHARMa diagnostics included quantile residual Q–Q plots and residual-versus-predicted value assessments to evaluate potential deviations from distributional assumptions, overdispersion, and residual structure. To assess model performance, we calculated a pseudo-R2 using Nagelkerke’s method, based on the deviance values from the fitted and null models. Final inferences are presented as posterior means and 95% credible intervals from the INLA posterior summaries. Exposure-response curves were then obtained. When interactions with SOI were present, exposure–response curves had three curves, one for each SOI category. 3.ResultsThe total number of dengue cases reported from 2018 to 2024 was 1,559, 2,754, 52,027, 3,852, 793, 139,525, and 492,287, respectively (Figure 1A). No major differences in mean temperature or relative humidity were observed between 2018 and 2024 (Figures 1B,C). In contrast, the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) exhibited marked temporal variability, with predominantly negative values between 2018 and 2020, followed by positive values from 2020 to 2023, and a decline thereafter.Figure 1Temporal patterns of dengue incidence and environmental variables in Argentina (2018–2024). Shaded areas represent the maximum and minimum values for climate parameters across the country.Five-panel time series graphic from 2018 to 2025: Panel A shows reported cases peaking twice in 2023 and 2024; Panel B depicts annual cyclical temperature fluctuations; Panel C represents steady relative humidity; Panel D presents variable rainfall with sporadic spikes; Panel E tracks fluctuating SOI anomalies.Table 1 shows the fit of models involving different lags for the climatic and SOI variables. The best-fitting lag for temperature and humidity was 2 months, for rainfall was 3 months, and for SOI, 5 months. The final model included the variables at the best-fitting lags. Table 2 compares the fit of the different models tested. The introduction of SOI-climate parameter interaction terms reduced DIC and WAIC values and increased Nagelkerke R2. When the SOI*temperature and SOI*humidity terms were considered together, the fitting measures improved. Conversely, when the SOI*precipitation term was added, WAIC increased considerably. Therefore, the model retained contained SOI*temperature and SOI*humidity interaction terms plus the main effect terms for all other variables.Table 1Identification of the best lags in climatic and SOI variables included in the model.Lag (months)TemperatureHumidityRainfallSOI056,566/56,73356,568/56,73456,568/56,73556,565/56,731156,321/56,50256,480/56,65356,562/56,73456,332/56,5092 56,138/56,332 56,265/56,483 56,368/56,55156,624/56,794356,427/56,63956,496/56,682 56,366/56,548 56,281/56,540456,326/56,54556,546/56,76356,425/56,61056,215/56,393556,369/56,54056,666/56,87356,540/56,705 55,929/56,182 656,279/56,45356,636/56,79856,520/56,70056,621/56,796756,349/56,53256,576/56,75456,431/56,61456,251/56,457856,263/56,50056,444/56,61256,455/56,63356,593/56,774956,197/56,42256,206/56,40656,493/56,66456,653/56,8181056,202/56,41256,278/56,59856,435/56,60356,766/56,9481156,208/56,42956,290/56,49456,388/56,56756,761/56,930DIC/WAIC values are shown for each variable at each lag. A complete summary of the final model specification is provided in Table 3. The final model equation is:u,,,log(μit)=log(Eit)+f1(Temperaturelag2)+f2(Humiditylag2)+f3(Rainfalllag3)+f4(SOIlag5)+f5(SOI−categorizedlag5∗Temperaturelag2)+f6(SOI−categorizedlag5∗Humiditylag2)+β1log(pop.densityi)+ui+vi+γyear(t)+smonth(t)Table 3Summary of the final Bayesian spatiotemporal model.Model componentSpecificationSignificanceLikelihoodNegative binomialCompensation for overdispersed countsResponseMonthly dengue countsStudy outcomeSpatial effectBYM2Spatial structured and unstructured heterogeneityTemporal effectSeasonal (month) + IID yearControls for seasonality and year-to-year variation.TemperatureRW2, lag 2Nonlinear main effectHumidityRW2, lag 2Nonlinear main effectRainfallRW2, lag 3Nonlinear main effectSOI scoreRW2, lag 5Nonlinear main effectTemperature × SOI-categoricalRW2 replicated by ENSO phaseNonlinear interaction termHumidity × SOI-categoricalRW2 replicated by ENSO phaseNonlinear interaction termPopulation densityLinear standardized effectLinear main effectOffsetlog(population)Incidence adjustmentBYM2, Besag–York–Mollié 2 structure; ENSO, El Niño–Southern Oscillation; SOI, Southern Oscillation Index; RW2, second-order random walk; AR1, first-order autoregressive process.Exposure-response curves for posterior estimates of dengue relative risk across the predictors, along with the corresponding 95% credible intervals, are shown in Figure 2. Temperature (Figure 2A) was a risk factor when the monthly means were between 20 and 30 °C for the El Niño and neutral phases. During the El Niño phase, a monthly mean temperature of 25 °C was associated with an estimated RR of 2.92 (95% CrI, 1.69–4.23). Above 30 °C, the estimated risk declined markedly. Positive residual spatial effects were concentrated in north-eastern departments, indicating higher dengue risk than expected based on the variables included in the model, whereas many central regions showed lower-than-expected risk. SOI scores above 0.5 indicated the La Niña phase; scores below −0.5 indicated the El Niño phase, with values between −0.5 and 0.5 characterizing a neutral phase, following the threshold criteria used in previous ENSO dengue studies (14).2.2.Statistical analysisWe fitted hierarchical Bayesian models using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) framework in R 4.5 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria; R-INLA package).The response variable was the monthly number of dengue cases, and we assumed a Negative Binomial likelihood to account for overdispersion.The general model fitted was:Yit∼NegBin(μit,φ)log(μit)=log(Eit)+f1(Temperaturelag)+f2(Humiditylag)+f3(Rainfalllag)+f4(SOIlag)+fn(SOI−categorizedlag∗climate_variableslag)+β1log(pop.densityi)+ui+vi+γyear(t)+smonth(t)Where Yit denotes the number of dengue cases observed in department i during month t, assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution. The term log(Eit) denotes the logarithm of the population size and is used as an offset. Nonlinear effects of temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, and SOI, as well as their interactions, were modeled using second-order random walks (RW2), which impose smoothness by penalizing second differences between adjacent latent effects. The RW2 terms were fitted using the default INLA penalized complexity priors for the precision parameter. For the RW2 components, climate parameters and SOI were centered and transformed into ordered indices representing adjacent exposure levels. Temperature and relative humidity were rounded to the nearest integer and converted to sequential indices, rainfall was rounded to the nearest 5-mm interval and converted to sequential indices, and SOI anomalies were rounded to the nearest integer and indexed similarly. These indices were then used as the covariates in the RW2 smooth terms, allowing estimation of nonlinear exposure–response relationships across the observed range of values. Population density was log-transformed and standardized before being included as a linear fixed effect.Interactions between the ENSO phase and climatic variables were implemented using the replicate argument in INLA. Specifically, separate RW2 smooth functions were estimated for temperature and relative humidity within each SOI category (El Niño, Neutral, and La Niña), while sharing a common smoothing prior structure. The terms ui and vi represent the structured and unstructured spatial random effects, respectively, modeled using the Besag–York–Mollié 2 specification. Departmental neighborhood relationships were defined using a first-order contiguity adjacency matrix derived from the departmental polygon shapefile, in which two departments were considered neighbors if they shared a common boundary. This adjacency matrix was supplied to INLA through the BYM2 specification. The BYM2 spatial effect was fitted using the default penalized complexity (PC) priors implemented in R-INLA.Temporal dependence was modeled through a 12-month cyclic seasonal effect to account for recurrent intra-annual patterns, together with an independent random effect for year to capture interannual variability in dengue transmission.We explored the best-fitting lags for SOI and climate parameters by computing and comparing the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) and the Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) between the models. Candidate lags from 0 to 11 months were evaluated independently for each climatic variable and SOI. The lag yielding the lowest DIC and WAIC values was retained in the final model.The interactions between the SOI and the climatic variables at their best-fitting lags were explored by categorizing SOI values, as established in the literature into El Niño (<−0.5), Neutral (−0.5 to 0.5), and La Niña (>0.5) phases (14). Models were fitted, and DIC and WAIC were used to select the best model.The final model adequacy was assessed through posterior predictive checks, including the randomized Probability Integral Transform (PIT) histogram, Q–Q plots of the randomized PIT values, and simulation-based residual diagnostics using the DHARMa package. DHARMa diagnostics included quantile residual Q–Q plots and residual-versus-predicted value assessments to evaluate potential deviations from distributional assumptions, overdispersion, and residual structure. To assess model performance, we calculated a pseudo-R2 using Nagelkerke’s method, based on the deviance values from the fitted and null models. Final inferences are presented as posterior means and 95% credible intervals from the INLA posterior summaries. Exposure-response curves were then obtained. When interactions with SOI were present, exposure–response curves had three curves, one for each SOI category.

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionOur results suggest a close relationship between dengue outbreaks in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 and the El Niño phenomenon. Such a relationship has been observed in other parts of the world. In Asia, a study conducted in Thailand between 1996 and 2005 examined the impact of ENSO on dengue outbreaks in two geographically contrasting regions: a tropical coastal region in the south and a mountainous region in the north (17). Using autoregressive Poisson models adjusted for seasonality and population density, a statistically significant association was identified between negative ENSO phases and dengue outbreaks, with time lags of up to 11 months (17). The best correlations were observed when ENSO Indices were lagged by 4–6 months. Consistent with these findings, the best lag for SOI in our study was 5 months. On average, ENSO accounted for up to 22% of the monthly variability of cases in the northern provinces and 15% in the southern provinces (17). In our study, the models incorporating SOI and climate parameters accounted for 53.7% of the variance in the data.A longitudinal study integrating data from Puerto Rico, Mexico, and Thailand evaluated the association between ENSO, local climatic variables, and dengue incidence through time-frequency domain coherence analysis (wavelet analysis) (19). In Puerto Rico, a transient relationship was identified among ENSO, temperature, and dengue incidence; however, on multi-year scales, only rainfall was significantly correlated with reported cases. However, the El Niño phenomenon, which generates droughts and higher temperatures in this country, is an important predictor of arbovirus disease outbreaks up to a year in advance (20). In Thailand, both temperature and precipitation were associated with ENSO; however, the link between precipitation and dengue cases was non-stationary (19). In contrast, in Mexico, no significant associations were found between ENSO, climate, and dengue on a multi-year scale. A study in Brazil, using a hierarchical spatio-temporal model grounded on a Bayesian framework, explored the relationship between ENSO, seasonal weather fluctuations, and the larval index, while adjusting for population density and wealth inequalities (14). El Niño events, higher seasonal rainfall, and temperatures above 23.3 °C were all strongly associated with increases in the Aedes aegypti larval index. Mosquito proliferation was especially pronounced in socially vulnerable municipalities, highlighting the role of environmental and social factors in vector abundance. A similar study was conducted in Peru, adopting a Bayesian hierarchical modeling approach to address spatial correlation and B-splines with four knots per year to address temporal correlation, to analyze ENSO and climate parameters (21). Temperature and ENSO significantly increased the risk of dengue outbreaks, especially in summer and in some regions. Rainfall showed no strong independent effect. These findings suggest that local climatic conditions, urbanization patterns, and other contextual factors may modulate ENSO’s influence on dengue epidemiology. A study mapped the spatial association between ENSO activity (SOI) and dengue fever incidence across the Americas from 1995 to 2004, including the major 1997–1998 El Niño event (22). The authors analyzed standardized SOI and annual dengue incidence using regression and spatial interpolation to identify geographic patterns. Results show stronger ENSO–dengue coupling in Mexico, Central America, the northern Caribbean, and northern South America, with epidemic centers shifting southward and several countries exhibiting higher dengue incidence during El Niño phases. Our results extend these findings to Argentina. Recent findings indicate that the intensity of the El Niño phenomenon is likely to increase as climate change progresses (23), underscoring the need to better characterize its impact on dengue and other mosquito-borne infectious diseases.Higher temperatures, associated with El Niño events, have been shown to increase the incidence of dengue, possibly by favoring viral replication and vector behavior (4). Similar results have been observed in a study in 14 island nations in the South Pacific (24). In line with these findings, we observed a higher dengue risk at temperatures between approximately 20 °C and 30 °C during the El Niño and neutral phases, with less consistent effects during the La Niña phase (Figure 2A). Above 30 °C, dengue risk dropped significantly, which may be related to lower mosquito survival in high-temperature regions (25). Studies in Paraguay have also observed a similar U-shaped relationship (26). Humidity, which is also a significant factor in boosting mosquito survival (25), exhibited different patterns across ENSO phases. During the La Niña (dry, cold) phase, humidity was a strong conditioner of dengue risk. During neutral and El Niño phases, the effect was less marked. Rainfall was not associated with dengue risk, in concordance with previous observations (21).Recent evidence suggests that non-climatic mechanisms may also contribute to dengue outbreaks. While our results do not permit mechanistic inferences, it is worth reviewing some of these non-climatic mechanisms, as they might help explain some findings. Prolonged ENSO events can affect drinking water availability and the deterioration of sanitation infrastructure, which can force vulnerable communities to store water under precarious conditions, thereby contributing to the proliferation of Aedes aegypti breeding sites (27). This mechanism could potentially contribute to the residual SOI effect observed after controlling for climatic covariates; however, water-storage practices and sanitation conditions were not evaluated in our study. Therefore, this interpretation should be regarded as an untested hypothesis that warrants investigation in future studies.Population displacement might also be a relevant factor. A study of the South Pacific islands detected synchrony in dengue outbreaks between neighboring countries, even in the absence of direct local climate correlations (27). The authors hypothesized that the virus could spread between islands via flows of infected people, facilitated by regional maritime and air transport networks. In urban areas with high territorial connectivity, such as many cities in Argentina, movement between provinces and/or borders could accelerate the introduction of the virus and/or vector into new areas, even without substantial changes in the local climate. However, population mobility and viral circulation were not included in our models, and their potential contribution to the observed spatial patterns remains hypothetical. Future studies incorporating mobility and viral genomic data could help determine whether these mechanisms contribute to dengue dissemination across Argentina.Transfrontier population movements may also help explain the results of our spatial analysis, which revealed a residual higher incidence of dengue in the northern states that border Paraguay and Brazil (26, 28). Brazil, facing the worst dengue fever situation globally, reported over 3 million cases in 2023 and over 1 million cases in the first part of 2024 (28). Dengue has been endemic in Paraguay since 2009, with all four dengue virus serotypes circulating since 2011 (26). Conversely, the high residual risk in Argentina’s southern provinces is harder to explain. These are cold, dry regions where the common Aedes aegypti mosquito is not expected to survive. However, acclimated A. aegypti (29) and cold-resistant strains of A. albopictus (30) may be responsible for dengue outbreaks in these regions. It must be noted that these considerations have not been directly addressed in our models. Therefore, they are purely speculative. More research is needed to test these hypotheses.The findings presented herein must be interpreted within the framework of the limitations inherent in the methodol…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionIn this ecological study covering the period from 2018 to 2024, we found associations between ENSO, local climatic conditions, and dengue outbreaks in Argentina. Negative SOI scores, associated with the El Niño phase, were associated with higher dengue risk after adjustment for climatic and sociodemographic covariates. Monthly temperatures between 20 °C and 30 °C were associated with higher dengue risk during the El Niño and neutral phases, whereas humidity >50% was associated with higher risk during the La Niña phase. Population density was also positively associated with dengue risk. Our results further suggest that unmeasured factors may contribute to the observed spatial and temporal patterns. These findings support the potential value of considering ENSO indicators, alongside local climatic and epidemiological information, in dengue outbreak modeling. Further research is needed to determine whether incorporating ENSO measures improves the performance of early-warning systems for dengue outbreaks.
full_text_sections.other: HighlightsThis study linked the El Niño phenomenon to dengue fever outbreaks in Argentina.Other predictors of increased risk were monthly mean temperatures between 20° and 30° Celsius during the El Niño and neutral phases, and humidity > 50% during the La Niña phase.There was a high degree of spatial residual variance, not accounted for by the factors considered in the model, in dengue risk, which was increased in some northern and southern provinces of Argentina. 1.IntroductionDengue is a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes, mainly Aedes aegypti (1, 2). The causative agent is the dengue virus, which belongs to the Flaviviridae family and has four different serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4) (2). Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, with higher incidence during rainy seasons, when mosquito populations increase (2). Approximately 380 million cases and 22,000 deaths occur each year. In Argentina, 531,617 cases were registered during the 2023–2024 season with 419 deaths (3). The most affected regions were the northern provinces.Several studies in tropical and subtropical regions of Latin America have demonstrated a significant correlation between dengue incidence and climatic variables, with temperature, humidity, and, to a lesser extent, rainfall as the primary factors (4, 5). There has been a significant increase in Earth’s temperature of about 1.16 Celsius degrees since 1951 (6), which may have contributed to the acceleration of the dengue burden (5).Higher temperatures accelerate dengue virus transmission by reducing the vector incubation period, increasing the contagion rate, and causing an exponential increase in cases (7). Rainfall and ambient humidity improve vector survival rates by promoting the accumulation of stagnant water, which supports mosquito development (4, 8).The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a recurring climate pattern that results from variations in ocean temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, coupled with changes in atmospheric pressure patterns across the tropical Pacific (9–11). ENSO has two main phases: El Niño (the warm phase) and La Niña (the cool phase), as well as a neutral phase (12). During El Niño events, abnormally warm sea surface temperatures develop in the eastern Pacific, disrupting typical weather patterns and leading to increased rainfall and humidity in some regions, while causing droughts in others (13) Conversely, La Niña events are characterized by cooler-than-average sea surface temperatures in the same region, which strengthens the trade winds and often results in opposite weather anomalies-drier conditions in some areas and increased rainfall in others. In Argentina, the El Niños phase is associated with increased ambient humidity, and the La Niña phase with dry conditions.Several studies suggest a relationship between ENSO and dengue outbreaks. A recent study found that El Niño was positively correlated with the global risk of dengue outbreaks, with a correlation coefficient of 0.52 (13). These results have been replicated in some regions of Brazil. A study conducted across 645 municipalities in the state of São Paulo (Brazil) linked El Niño events to increases in the mosquito larval index, a measure of mosquito proliferation (14).Despite growing evidence linking ENSO variability to dengue transmission in tropical and subtropical regions, its influence on dengue dynamics in Argentina remains poorly characterized. In particular, it is unclear whether the association between local climatic conditions and dengue risk varies across ENSO phases and whether ENSO contributes to dengue risk beyond the effects of local temperature, humidity, and precipitation. Addressing these relationships is particularly relevant in Argentina, where dengue transmission is spatially heterogeneous and occurs across regions with markedly different climatic conditions. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to model the influence of ENSO on dengue outbreaks across Argentina while accounting for local climatic conditions and the spatial and temporal structure of dengue transmission. 2.1.Data collectionWe conducted a nationwide analysis of dengue case distribution in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 at a monthly resolution. Argentina is in the southern part of South America, covers an area of 2,780,400 km2 of continental and insular territory, and has a population of just over 46 million inhabitants. Argentina stretches over 3,700 km from north to south, which explains why it spans a remarkable variety of climates, from subtropical in the north to subpolar in the far south (15). This great length also gives rise to diverse biomes, including rainforests, grasslands, deserts, and Patagonian tundra. The country is divided into 525 departments and an autonomous city, Buenos Aires (hereinafter referred to as departments). For each department, monthly dengue incidence was calculated as the number of cases per 100,000 inhabitants. title_original: Modeling the impact of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation on the dynamics of dengue outbreaks in Argentina between 2018 and 2024

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand how the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influences dengue outbreaks in Argentina, as dengue fever has become a significant epidemiological concern with 531,617 cases reported during the 2023–2024 season.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nationwide analysis of dengue case distribution in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 was conducted at a monthly resolution, incorporating climate parameters and the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) across all departments.
analysis.methods: The study used monthly mean temperature and humidity data, along with accumulated rainfall, and applied a Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial model with nonlinear effects and lags. Model selection was based on DIC and WAIC, and posterior predictive checks were used to assess model adequacy.
analysis.main_results: Dengue risk increased with temperatures between 20° and 30° Celsius during El Niño or neutral phases, while humidity >50% was linked to higher risk during La Niña. Negative SOI scores were associated with increased dengue risk after controlling for covariates. The final model included SOI interactions with temperature and humidity, with temperature and humidity modeled as nonlinear effects with a 2-month lag.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that dengue outbreaks in Argentina are independently associated with temperature, humidity, and SOI anomalies, highlighting the importance of ENSO indices in understanding outbreak dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that integrating ENSO indices into predictive models could improve early warning systems and public health interventions for dengue in Argentina.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is moderate, as it relies on observational data and does not establish causality. The model's generalizability may be limited due to the focus on Argentina and the use of a single dataset.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the impact of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on dengue outbreaks in Argentina from 2018 to 2024. It finds that dengue risk increases with temperatures between 20° and 30° Celsius during El Niño or neutral phases and with humidity >50% during La Niña. Negative Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) scores are also linked to higher dengue risk. The authors suggest that incorporating ENSO indices into predictive models could enhance early warning systems and public health interventions. The study uses a Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial model with nonlinear effects and lags, and the results are supported by posterior predictive checks. However, the evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and potential limitations in generalizability.

full_text: AbstractDengue remains a major public health concern in Latin America and the Caribbean, where vaccination has emerged as a key strategy to reduce severe disease. However, its successful implementation depends on population knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP). This study aimed to synthesize available evidence on KAP related to dengue vaccination in the region. A scoping review was conducted following JBI guidelines. Searches were performed in international and regional databases, including MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, SciELO, and the Virtual Health Library. Original studies were included without language or date restrictions. Study selection and data extraction were conducted independently and in duplicate. Sixteen studies were included. Most studies reported limited knowledge regarding vaccine availability, safety, and mechanisms of action. In contrast, attitudes were generally favorable, with high acceptance and willingness to pay, estimated at approximately USD 23 for a three-dose regimen. However, willingness to participate in clinical trials remained low due to safety and trust concerns. Evidence from a study conducted in Puerto Rico indicated that the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with increased intention to receive the dengue vaccine. Practices were less studied, and findings showed low completion of vaccination schedules, indicating a gap between attitudes and uptake. Despite generally favorable attitudes, important knowledge gaps and implementation challenges persist. Strengthening educational strategies and promoting qualified communication between healthcare professionals and the population - particularly during the introduction of new vaccines and in the context of adverse events - may support informed decision-making and improve dengue vaccine uptake.Keywords: Dengue; Vaccines; Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice MethodsThis scoping review followed the methodological framework established by the JBI 19 and the rationale of Arksey & O’Malley 20 . The review process included five key steps: identifying the research question; identifying relevant studies; selecting studies; charting data; and collating, summarizing, and reporting results. Prior to initiating the review, a protocol was drafted and published in the Open Science Framework 21 . The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist was used to guide the reporting of this manuscript 22 .Eligibility criteriaEligibility criteria were based on the Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework recommended by the JBI.The population included all individuals residing in Latin America and the Caribbean, with no restrictions on sex, age, education level, or occupation.The central concept was the evaluation of KAP regarding dengue vaccination.In this review, “knowledge” referred to factual understanding of dengue vaccination, including availability, effectiveness, safety, indications, and mechanisms of action. “Attitudes” encompassed perceptions, beliefs, concerns, and intentions toward vaccination, whether favorable or unfavorable. “Practices” included observable or self-reported behaviors, such as vaccine uptake, refusal, and adherence to recommendations. These definitions were applied consistently throughout the manuscript to ensure conceptual coherence.The context focused on original scientific studies - such as clinical trials and observational research - conducted within the Latin American and Caribbean region.To ensure explicit alignment with the PCC framework, the search strategy incorporated descriptors corresponding to each component: Population (P): populations from Latin America and the Caribbean; Concept (C): KAP regarding dengue vaccination; and Context (C): community and healthcare service settings located in countries of Latin America and the Caribbean.No limitations were applied regarding language or date of publication.Bibliographic searchAn exhaustive search was conducted across nine databases: PubMed, Scopus, SciELO, Embase, Google Scholar, Web of Science, the Virtual Health Library (VHL), LILACS, and Redalyc. Controlled vocabulary terms (e.g., Medical Subject Headings - MeSH) were combined with free-text keywords and adapted to each database; full strategies are detailed in Supplementary Material (https://cadernos.ensp.fiocruz.br/ojs/index.php/csp/article/view/12107/21105).In Redalyc, three searches were performed using “dengue” AND “vacuna”, “vacina”, and “vaccine”, screening the first 100 results from each query based on relevance (up to 300 records before duplicate removal). Additionally, reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were manually screened. The last search date was March 15, 2026.The search strategy was developed by the research team under the supervision of a senior author with formal training and experience in systematic reviews. Although no information specialist participated, the strategy was internally reviewed and refined to ensure methodological rigor and reproducibility.Selection of studiesAfter retrieval, records were grouped, classified, and imported into Rayyan (https://www.rayyan.ai/), where duplicates were manually removed. Two independent reviewers (D.G.V. and N.R.) screened titles and abstracts in a blinded manner based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria.Full-text articles were subsequently assessed independently and in duplicate by paired reviewers from the research team (R.G.V., J.I.M., R.A.R.S., R.A.N., and M.R.A.N.), following the same criteria. After unblinding, discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus, with involvement of a senior author when necessary. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented. The study selection process is illustrated in Figure 1.Figure 1Flow diagram summarizing the study search and selection process.Data extractionAfter organizing the selected studies in an Excel spreadsheet (https://products.office.com/), a pilot test was conducted with five articles to ensure consistency and accuracy in data extraction, with no discrepancies identified. The extracted data included author, study type, publication year, study characteristics (e.g., location and setting), and population characteristics (e.g., age, gender, and KAP-related variables regarding dengue vaccination).Data extraction was performed independently and in duplicate by paired reviewers (R.G.V., J.I.M., R.A.R.S., R.A.N., and M.R.A.N.). After unblinding, extracted data were compared, and disagreements were resolved by consensus, with consultation of a senior author (N.R. or D.G.V.) when necessary. No attempts were made to contact study authors for additional information, given the exploratory nature of this scoping review.Synthesis of resultsThe collected data were summarized in tables describing the characteristics of the included studies, complemented by a narrative synthesis of the main findings related to the research question. A scoping review approach was adopted to map the available evidence, categorize studies, and analyze the conceptual focus of the literature, in line with Arksey & O’Malley 20 .
