As of August 2026, Dengvaxia (Sanofi Pasteur, https://www.sanofi.us), Qdenga TAK-003 (Takeda, https://www.takeda.com), and Butantan-DV (Instituto Butantan, https://en.butantan.gov.br) are 3 licensed vaccines to prevent dengue; however, Dengvaxia use remains limited because of safety concerns (6,7). Brazil remains one of the most affected countries by dengue and has annual epidemics, widespread vector distribution, and co-circulation of all 4 DENV serotypes (8). We integrate epidemiologic and genomic methods to investigate DENV transmission dynamics during 2010–2025 in Ceará, a hyperendemic state in Brazil. We retroactively obtained national epidemiologic data on laboratory-confirmed dengue cases during January 2010–January 2025 from Brazil’s Ministry of Health. We obtained additional epidemiologic data from the Central Laboratory of Public Health of Ceará for dengue cases reported during July 2014–June 2025. We used the MiSeq platform (Illumina, https://www.illumina.com) to sequence residual quantitative reverse transcription PCR–positive DENV serum samples collected from case-patients with DENV-1–3 serotypes during February 2024–July 2025. We assigned DENV lineages by using the DENV typing tool (9), followed by phylogenetic reconstruction. We also performed time-series, spatial mapping, and demographic analyses (Appendix). During January 3, 2010–January 25, 2025, Brazil reported 1,657,046 laboratory-confirmed dengue cases across 98.9% (5,509/5,570) of municipalities in all 26 states and the Federal District. We identified 13 major epidemic waves at the national level; annual incidence varied from 4.0 to 190.4 cases/100,000 inhabitants, and the largest epidemic occurred in 2024 (Figure 1, panel A). National DENV testing positivity rate ranged from 18.2% (19,460/106,901 inhabitants) to 57.1% (146,649/256,981 inhabitants) during those 15 years (Figure 1, panel B). In Ceará, a total of 131,961 laboratory-confirmed cases were reported, corresponding to a cumulative incidence of 1,500 cases/100,000 inhabitants. Ceará epidemic peaks coincided with national trends but frequently reached higher incidence and positivity rates (Figure 1). By 2026, dengue had been reported in all 184 municipalities in Ceará; cumulative incidences range from 41.4 to 8,566 cases/100,000 inhabitants (Appendix). Nationally, dengue epidemics occurred mainly during February–June and peaked during March–April (peak monthly incidence mean 10.4 cases/100,000 inhabitants). In contrast, in Ceará, epidemics occurred during March–August, typically peaking in May (incidence mean 18.4 cases/100,000 inhabitants) (Appendix). Sex- and age-stratified analyses revealed a female-to-male ratio of 1.6 and higher incidence among female persons nationally (2-way ANOVA test, p<0.05) and in Ceará (p<0.01) (Appendix). The cumulative incidence in Ceará was higher in persons 10–39 years of age than in persons >70 years of age (p<0.05) (Appendix). We investigated the circulation of DENV serotypes in Ceará during July 2014–June 2025. DENV-1 was the predominant DENV serotype during 2014–2019 and again during 2023–2025 (Figures 2, 3). Fortaleza, the capital and most populous city in Ceará, reported co-circulation of DENV-1, DENV-3, and DENV-4 in 2015. DENV-2 reemerged in 2019, leading to its near-complete replacement of other DENV serotypes in 2021 and 2022 (Figures 2, 3). To assess current genetic diversity in Ceará, we sequenced 243 DENV genomes from cases reported during February 2024–July 2025 across 45 municipalities (Figure 4; Appendix). Cycle threshold values ranged from 10.6 to 33.0. We recovered complete or partial DENV genomes for 218 of the 243 samples (coverage 14.4%–99.2%; mean depth 16–9,877 per nucleotide) (Appendix). Among those genomes, we classified 82.6% (180/218) with >70% coverage into the following genotypes: DENV-1 V_D1.1 (n = 1), DENV-1 V_E1 (n = 111), DENV-2 II_F1.1.2 (n = 61), DENV-2 II_F1.1.5 (n = 2), DENV-2 III_C1.1 (n = 2), and DENV-3 III_B3.2 (n = 3) (9). We included those newly generated DENV genome sequences in maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analyses along with global DENV genome references (Appendix). Phylogenetic analysis showed that the recent epidemic in Ceará (2024–2025) was mainly caused by DENV-1 lineage V_E1 (61.6% [n = 111 cases]). DENV lineages identified in Ceará were distributed across multiple well-supported subclades with genomes from southeast (São Paulo), central-west (Federal District, Goiás, and Mato Grosso do Sul), and northeast (Alagoas) of Brazil and from Florida (USA) and Uruguay. Lineage II_F1.1.2 (94%) predominated among DENV-2 cases, and clustered with DENV genomes from southeast and northeast Brazil and the United States (10). Conversely, DENV-2 II_F1.1.5 genomes grouped with sequences from France (2023–2024) and the Dominican Republic (2024), suggesting a recent international introduction. Detection of DENV-3 genomes from Ceará was consistent with a reintroduction because no local detections have occurred since 2015. Those genomes belonged to lineage III_B3.2 and formed a well-supported clade (bootstrap 100%) with sequences from São Paulo (2024–2025) and Florida (2023) within a lineage widely circulating across the Americas, including in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, French Guiana, and Peru (Figure 4). This study provides a 15-year overview of dengue transmission in Ceará, a dengue hyperendemic state. Our epidemiologic analyses demonstrate that dengue occurred in all 184 municipalities of Ceará and that multiple DENV epidemics reached higher incidence and testing positivity rates than national trends. Epidemic peaks typically occurred ≈1 month later and lasted longer in Ceará than the national average, which might be explained by extended periods of high temperature and humidity (11), supporting near year-round vector abundance and sustained DENV transmission (3). We identified heterogeneous circulation of all 4 DENV serotypes and identified 6 distinct viral lineages across 3 serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, and DENV-3) sustained by multiple national and international introductions. We also documented the reintroduction of DENV-3, confirmed by its detection in July 2025, which could increase the risk for severe outcomes in the coming years through sequential infections and antibody-dependent enhancement after a decade of co-circulation of DENV-1 and DENV-2 (12). Moreover, our phylogenetic analyses showed that DENV-3 lineage III_B3.2 genomes clustered with DENV sequences detected during 2024–2025 in São Paulo State. full_text: AbstractArboviruses remain an important global health concern because of their expanding distribution, diverse transmission patterns, and the challenges associated with accurate and timely diagnosis. This review is centered on Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) as a representative model, focusing on diagnostic strategies across different stages of infection and the key diagnostic pitfalls that affect CHIKV detection in co-circulation settings. In this review, we summarize current laboratory-based approaches for CHIKV detection and differential diagnosis, including virus isolation, antigen detection, nucleic acid amplification and serological assays, with discussion of their applications, strengths and limitations. Particular attention is given to persistent issues affecting diagnostic accuracy and practical implementation, including serological cross-reactivity among co-circulating arboviruses and the challenges of translating advanced technologies into accessible tools for field and resource-limited settings. The samples are homogenized by grinding and clarified by filtration to remove debris, obtaining a final homogenate suitable for inoculation, as shown in Figure 1 (virus isolation and culture). The resulting homogenate is then subjected to viral culture. The successful cultivation of arboviruses depends critically on the use of permissive cell lines that enable robust viral replication and amplification. Two widely adopted systems for this purpose are the C6/36 cell line (derived from Aedes albopictus larvae) and the BHK-21 line (established from Syrian hamster kidney tissue). These cell lines demonstrate pronounced susceptibility to diverse arboviruses, a trait attributable to intrinsic genomic features that promote efficient viral entry and sustained replication. After introduction into permissive cells, the virus first attaches to and enters through specific surface receptors, then releases its RNA to redirect the host's cellular machinery for replication (Miller et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2020). The viral titer is determined by a plaque assay, a method based on the principle of localized infection. Following the addition of virus to a susceptible cell monolayer, a semi-solid overlay restricts infection to adjacent cells. Each infectious virus particle then produces a distinct plaque-a visible zone of cell lysis-through repeated cycles of infection and cell death. The number of these plaques is directly proportional to the concentration of infectious virus in the original sample (Carneiro et al., 2022; Takumi-Tanimukai et al., 2022; Waturangi, 2024). The plaque assay enables direct measurement of replication-competent infectious virus and accurate viral titration, making it a widely used reference method for infectious virus quantification. However, the assay places stringent demands on both technical execution and cell culture conditions. Its performance depends critically on the quality and confluency of the host-cell monolayer, as variations in cell condition and density can affect plaque formation and compromise the reproducibility and reliability of viral titration (Shurtleff et al., 2012; Baer and Kehn-Hall, 2014; Mendoza et al., 2020).3.3.2.Antigen detectionAntigen detection techniques rely on highly specific antibodies to recognize viral proteins, including structural and non-structural components. For infections caused by various viruses transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, such as DENV, ZIKV, and CHIKV, antigen detection is particularly suitable for early screening during the acute phase (Sekaran et al., 2022). However, for CHIKV, antigen detection remains constrained by the extent of validation across settings and by limited uptake of standardized assays in routine clinical practice. As seen from the structural modules of the aforementioned viruses (Figure 3B), this open reading frames (ORF) is translated and cleaved into structural proteins. However, the expression of these antigens during the viral infection process shows a clear time-dependent pattern: the viremia of CHIKV typically lasts for a short duration (usually declining rapidly within a few days post-infection), resulting in a narrow window for detecting the antigens in bodily fluids. This, in turn, may limit the clinical sensitivity of antigen detection (Choudhary et al., 2021). This variability further complicates the consistency of antibody recognition (Cho et al., 2024; Thannickal et al., 2024). In addition, this article also highlights the potential issue of “cross-reactivity-like” interference in antigen detection. Despite differences in their viral families and antigenic structures, CHIKV, DENV, and ZIKV continue to present substantial challenges for differential diagnosis. IgG antibodies are produced at later stages of the immune response and are considered indicators of past exposure or secondary infection (Marfía et al., 2025). By using enzyme-labeled antigens or antibodies, ELISA generates a detectable signal, such as a colorimetric change, through enzyme-catalyzed substrate reactions, allowing qualitative or quantitative detection of target antigens or antibodies. Over the past decade, rapid urbanization, altered land‐use patterns, and ecological shifts in vector habitats have catalyzed the reemergence and expansion of ST across diverse Indian states, affecting both rural and periurban populations [3,4].Despite its rising incidence, ST remains a neglected tropical disease, with limited awareness among frontline healthcare workers and public health authorities [4]. Its early clinical presentation is nonspecific, typically manifesting as acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) without pathognomonic features. Consequently, ST is frequently misdiagnosed as other coendemic tropical fevers such as dengue, malaria, typhoid, or leptospirosis [5,6]. This diagnostic ambiguity delays appropriate antimicrobial therapy, increasing the risk of progression to severe complications including multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (MODS), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury (AKI), myocarditis, hepatic dysfunction, and central nervous system (CNS) involvement such as acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) and meningoencephalitis [6-8].The public health threat posed by O. tsutsugamushi is further compounded by its immense biological heterogeneity. Genetic variation in the 56‐kDa type‐specific antigen (TSA) has given rise to distinct strain groups, including Karp, Gilliam, Kato, and Ikeda variants [1,3]. This diversity has severely hindered vaccine development, leaving no commercially available vaccine to date [4]. As a result, disease management relies entirely on early clinical suspicion, accurate laboratory triage, and vector control measures, imposing a disproportionate socioeconomic burden on vulnerable rural and agricultural populations [2,4].India has witnessed multiple ST outbreaks and rising case counts since 2010, with marked heterogeneity in clinical features, diagnostic modalities, and reported mortality rates across regions [3]. A major barrier to effective national control strategies is the reliance on low‐sensitivity rapid diagnostic tests, such as immunochromatographic tests (ICTs), and outdated serological assays, such as the Weil‐Felix agglutination test, which introduce diagnostic bias and systematically underestimate the true disease burden in high‐transmission zones [8,9]. Furthermore, while localized institutional outbreaks are frequently reported, nationwide syntheses linking diagnostic assay performance, regional transmission gradients, and predictors of inpatient mortality remain sparse [3,4].While several systematic reviews and meta-analyses published over the past decade have documented the re-emergence of O. tsutsugamushi in India, existing literature exhibits critical methodological vulnerabilities. Previous national syntheses frequently pooled highly heterogeneous screening denominators, indiscriminately blending baseline AUFI triage pools with preselected organ-failure registries (such as isolated AES or AKI cohorts) and secondary suspicion filtering series. This mixing introduces substantial selection bias, artificially inflates pooled prevalence estimates, and distorts true baseline clinical risk. Furthermore, prior reviews relied on raw proportion pooling without variance stabilization and failed to model the critical interaction between diagnostic assay stringency and regional transmission intensity.To overcome limitations in existing literature and provide an evidence‐based roadmap for clinical triage and public health policy, we conducted a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)‐compliant systematic review and meta‐analysis (SRMA) prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). ReviewMethodsSearch Strategy and Eligibility CriteriaThis SRMA was designed and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines (see Appendix A1) [10,11]. The study protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO under registration number CRD420261421341 [12]. The search was restricted to publications between January 2015 and June 2026 and included studies reporting observational data collected as early as 2012. This approach ensured the inclusion of both recent outbreak reports and hospital-based cohort data, thereby capturing a broad temporal spectrum of disease burden and enhancing the contextual relevance of findings.The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings, Emtree terms, and free-text keywords, structured with Boolean operators to ensure reproducibility (see Appendix A2). The matrix was designed around four conceptual blocks: target pathogen or disease, syndromic presentation, epidemiological outcomes, and geographic setting, combined through logical operators. No language restrictions were applied, and duplicate records were removed before two independent reviewers conducted title and abstract screening followed by full-text evaluation. To enhance sensitivity, reference lists of included articles and related reviews were hand‐searched. Duplicate records were removed, and two independent reviewers performed title and abstract screening followed by full‐text assessment to ensure methodological rigor.Inclusion and Exclusion CriteriaEligibility criteria were enforced to minimize heterogeneity and ensure methodological rigor. Studies were included if they were peer-reviewed observational designs, either prospective or retrospective, including cross-sectional investigations or tertiary care screening series conducted within India. The target population was restricted to hospitalized or outpatient cohorts presenting explicitly with AUFI, defined as an acute febrile syndrome lacking recognizable localizing signs, focal infection, or organ-specific etiology at the time of baseline triage. Laboratory confirmation of O. tsutsugamushi infection was required, using validated diagnostic modalities such as immunoglobulin M (IgM) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), polymerase chain reaction (PCR), indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA), or ICT. Eligible studies were also required to report extractable and verified quantitative metrics, including denominators representing the total AUFI patients screened and numerators representing confirmed ST cases, along with clinical features or survival outcomes.Exclusion criteria were applied systematically to eliminate bias and preserve the integrity of pooled estimates. Case reports, small series with fewer than 10 patients, narrative reviews, editorials, protocols, letters, and conference abstracts lacking complete methodological frameworks were excluded. Studies evaluating generalized acute febrile illness (AFI) without an undifferentiated classification, or those meeting the prolonged criteria for pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO), were removed to avoid dilution of the AUFI spectrum. Similarly, studies restricted to localized or organ-specific syndromes at baseline triage, such as AES, meningoencephalitis, or AKI cohorts, were excluded because they bypass the AUFI framework. Institutional datasets that applied secondary clinical-suspicion filters prior to enrollment, such as restricting the denominator to febrile patients already exhibiting highly suggestive features like rashes, eschars, or organ failure, were excluded to prevent artificial inflation of prevalence estimates. Community-based seroprevalence surveys in asymptomatic populations and household contact-tracing clusters were also excluded because they did not reflect the active clinical triage burden. The scale assesses quality across three core domains: selection of study participants (maximum five stars), comparability of study groups (maximum two stars), and ascertainment of outcome/exposure (maximum three stars), yielding a cumulative maximum score of 10 stars. Studies scoring 8-10 stars were categorized as high quality, five to seven stars as moderate quality, and zero to four stars as low quality. full_text: Pregnancy is a unique physiological state characterised by altered immune responses that may predispose women to severe manifestations of infection. Vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue pose significant risks to pregnant women and their foetuses, including miscarriage, preterm labour, placental abruption, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Co-infection with multiple vector-borne pathogens is extremely rare but can exacerbate maternal morbidity and complicate foetal outcomes. This case report aims to describe the clinical presentation, diagnosis, management, and maternal and foetal outcomes of a rare triple vector-borne co-infection during pregnancy.A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 21 weeks of gestation presented with a triple vector-borne infection involving Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium falciparum, and dengue virus. Prompt diagnosis was achieved through rapid diagnostic testing for dengue and malarial parasites, followed by antimalarial therapy and symptomatic supportive treatment. The patient showed complete clinical and laboratory recovery, evidenced by improvement in haemoglobin and platelet counts, normalization of liver function parameters, and clearance of parasitaemia.This case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges associated with multiple vector-borne infections during pregnancy and illustrates the potential value of early recognition, appropriate diagnostic evaluation, multidisciplinary management, and close maternal and foetal monitoring in achieving a favourable clinical outcome. DiscussionTriple vector-borne co-infection involving P. falciparum, P. vivax, and dengue virus in pregnancy is exceedingly rare, with only isolated case reports documented in the literature. The present case adds to the limited body of evidence and highlights the importance of early diagnosis and prompt multidisciplinary management to achieve favourable maternal and foetal outcomes. The overlap in the geographic distribution of these pathogens, especially in endemic regions, creates the potential for simultaneous transmission; however, the clinical documentation of such triple infections remains limited [1,6].Malaria and dengue are independently associated with significant maternal and foetal morbidity. P. falciparum is known for its ability to cause placental sequestration, contributing to IUGR, stillbirth, and preterm labour. Although P. vivax is considered less virulent, it can still lead to severe anaemia, a major contributor to maternal morbidity and mortality during pregnancy [2]. Dengue virus infection can result in plasma leakage, thrombocytopenia, and haemorrhagic complications, which are particularly hazardous in the obstetric context [7].In the present case, the coexistence of these three infections may have had a synergistic effect. Co-infection may exacerbate systemic inflammation through heightened cytokine responses, contributing to endothelial dysfunction, maternal haemodynamic instability, and foetal hypoxia [8]. The resulting complications, including severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and GI bleeding, require intensive monitoring and supportive therapy, including packed RBC and platelet transfusions when clinically indicated.The diagnosis of co-infections is particularly challenging because of overlapping clinical features, such as fever, myalgia, and thrombocytopenia. In this case, early identification relied on rapid diagnostic testing, followed by peripheral blood smear microscopy for confirmation of the diagnosis. However, in many settings, delayed or missed diagnoses occur because of the limited availability of additional diagnostic modalities, such as PCR or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), for the detection of dengue and malaria [5, 9]. The need for improved access to integrated serological and molecular diagnostic tools is critical, especially in resource-limited, high-burden regions [7].The management of co-infections during pregnancy requires a careful balance between efficacy and foetal safety. Antimalarial therapy with quinine and clindamycin was chosen because of its relative safety in the second trimester, although the patient experienced quinine-induced hypoglycaemia and tinnitus. Dengue management is supportive, focusing on careful fluid management and transfusion when clinically indicated to address bleeding and haemorrhagic risk. Close multidisciplinary care, including foetal surveillance, contributed to favourable short-term maternal and foetal outcomes.This case highlights important public health implications. Historically, dengue cases in the UAE have been largely imported. However, since 2023, locally transmitted cases with no travel history have been reported, likely driven by climate change and increasingly favourable conditions for vector proliferation. This evolving epidemiological landscape emphasises the need for enhanced vector surveillance, preventive strategies, and heightened clinical suspicion in pregnant patients with febrile illnesses who have recently travelled to endemic regions [1,6,10]. Second, the period of direct clinical observation was limited to the seven-day hospitalization. A detailed travel and exposure history, together with timely malaria testing, peripheral blood smear examination, and dengue-specific testing, can facilitate the recognition of co-infection when clinical manifestations overlap. A tailored multidisciplinary approach is essential to minimise maternal and foetal risks. Increased awareness of co-infections in patients travelling from endemic areas is crucial for improving outcomes. Appropriate diagnostic and treatment protocols should be followed. This case also highlights the need for public health interventions to minimise vector exposure during outbreaks. IntroductionVector-borne diseases remain a substantial global health concern, accounting for over 17% of infectious diseases and causing more than 700,000 deaths annually [1]. Malaria and dengue, among the most prevalent vector-borne diseases, are independently associated with significant maternal and foetal complications during pregnancy, including anaemia, miscarriage, preterm labour, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and stillbirth [1]. Pregnancy is a unique physiological state characterised by immunological and physiological adaptations that may increase susceptibility to severe manifestations of infection [2].During pregnancy, maternal immunity undergoes changes that have traditionally been described as a shift from predominantly T-helper 1 (Th1)-mediated cellular immunity towards a T-helper 2 (Th2)-predominant response [3]. This shift has been particularly described during the second trimester and contributes to maternal tolerance of the foetus; however, it may also increase susceptibility to certain intracellular pathogens and favour parasite persistence [3]. These immunological adaptations may contribute to the increased susceptibility to malaria observed during pregnancy [3].When malaria and dengue occur concurrently in the same individual, the severity and duration of one or both infections may increase [4]. Malaria has a complex pathophysiology involving direct RBC destruction, as well as inflammatory and immune responses, with anaemia being an important clinical manifestation [4]. Dengue similarly involves complex interactions between the virus and the host immune response and is frequently associated with thrombocytopenia [4]. Consequently, concurrent infection may result in overlapping and potentially more severe clinical manifestations than either infection alone, making early recognition and appropriate management particularly important [4].Although malaria-dengue co-infection has been reported, concurrent infection with P. falciparum, P. vivax, and dengue virus during pregnancy remains rare and poorly documented. Physiological changes during pregnancy, including altered immune responses and increased plasma volume, may further complicate the clinical presentation and management of these infections [5].This report aims to describe the clinical presentation, diagnostic challenges, management, and short-term maternal and foetal outcomes of a rare triple vector-borne co-infection with P. falciparum, P. vivax, and dengue virus in a pregnant patient at 21 weeks of gestation. The case also highlights the importance of considering concurrent vector-borne infections in febrile pregnant patients with recent travel to endemic regions. Case presentationThis single-patient case report describes a rare triple vector-borne co-infection during pregnancy and is presented for its educational value in illustrating the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges associated with simultaneous multi-pathogen infections in pregnancy.Clinical presentationA 32-year-old primigravida at 21 weeks of gestation presented to our hospital in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with a two-day history of fever, fatigue, and episodes of coffee-ground vomiting, along with one episode of syncope. She had recently returned from Ethiopia, where she had stayed for approximately 25 days, and had arrived back in the UAE five days before presentation. During her stay in Ethiopia, she reported exposure to mosquitoes and had not received antimalarial prophylaxis before or during travel.On admission, her blood pressure was 90/50 mmHg, pulse rate was 95 beats/min, oxygen saturation was 99% on room air, and body temperature was 36.3°C. On examination, she was icteric. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were otherwise unremarkable.On abdominal examination, the abdomen was soft with generalized tenderness, which was more pronounced in the right upper quadrant. Obstetric examination revealed a gravid uterus corresponding to approximately 20-21 weeks of gestation, and foetal heart sounds were detected.Diagnostic assessmentInitial laboratory investigations demonstrated severe anaemia, with a haemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dL; thrombocytopenia, with a platelet count of 29,000/μL; hypokalaemia; hypocalcaemia; elevated liver enzymes; and hyperbilirubinaemia. Peripheral blood smear microscopy demonstrated P. falciparum rings, P. vivax rings, and P. vivax gametocytes, confirming mixed malarial infection. Obstetric USG demonstrated a single live intrauterine foetus corresponding to 21 weeks of gestation, as shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Obstetric ultrasound findings consistent with a single intrauterine fetus at 21 weeks of gestation.(A) Fetal heart rate of 158 bpm. (B) Biparietal diameter corresponding to 21 weeks of gestation. (C) Abdominal circumference corresponding to 21 weeks of gestation. (D) Femur length corresponding to 20 weeks of gestation.The patient was admitted to the ICU because of severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and concurrent infection with P. falciparum, P. vivax, and dengue virus.Therapeutic interventionManagement involved a multidisciplinary team comprising internal medicine physicians, infectious disease specialists, obstetricians, cardiologists, and general surgeons. The patient was placed on continuous cardiac monitoring. Supportive treatment included IV fluids, high-flow nasal oxygen, antipyretics, proton pump inhibitor therapy, and foetal monitoring. Fluid input and output were closely monitored, with urine output maintained above 60 mL/hour.Electrocardiography demonstrated a prolonged corrected QT (QTc) interval of 493 ms (Figure 2). On admission, the serum calcium level was 6.9 mg/dL (reference range: 8.9-10.2 mg/dL), indicating hypocalcaemia, while the serum magnesium level was 1.98 mg/dL (reference range: 1.6-2.6 mg/dL), which was within the normal range. Cardiology consultation was obtained before initiating IV quinine because of the potential risk of ventricular arrhythmias. The patient was maintained on continuous cardiac monitoring, medications associated with QTc prolongation were avoided, and electrolyte levels were closely monitored and corrected as required.Figure 2Electrocardiogram showing a prolonged QTc interval.Specific antimalarial treatment consisted of IV quinine 600 mg infused over four hours every eight hours and IV clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours for seven days. The patient was maintained on continuous cardiac monitoring because of the prolonged QTc interval and the potential for quinine-associated cardiac adverse effects. The clinical course was complicated by quinine-associated hypoglycaemia and tinnitus. Hypoglycaemia was managed with a 10% dextrose infusion. The patient received four units of packed red blood cells and three units of platelets in the context of severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and suspected gastrointestinal bleeding, as indicated by coffee-ground vomiting. The general surgery team was consulted to evaluate other potential causes of suspected gastrointestinal bleeding. Tranexamic acid was administered intravenously at a dose of 1 g three times daily.Complete blood count, coagulation profile, liver function tests, blood glucose, electrolytes, and parasitaemia were monitored during treatment. Electrocardiography was repeated every 24-48 hours to monitor for arrhythmias. Potassium was supplemented intravenously and maintained above 4 mmol/L. Magnesium and calcium levels were monitored and supplemented as required. The patient was also monitored closely for bleeding manifestations.A dietitian was consulted, and a high-iron diet and nutritional supplementation with Fortisip 125 mL were prescribed.Follow-up and outcomesThe patient demonstrated progressive clinical and haematological improvement during treatment. Haemoglobin increased from 6.2 g/dL on admission to 8.4 g/dL by day 4, while the platelet count increased from 29,000/μL to 91,000/μL. Bilirubin decreased from 3.03 mg/dL on admission to 1.93 mg/dL by day 4, and inflammatory markers also showed a downward trend.Parasitaemia decreased during antimalarial treatment, reaching <0.1% by day 4, as illustrated in Figure 3. The patient was transferred from the ICU to the general ward on day 5, completed seven days of antimalarial therapy, and was discharged in stable condition after a total hospital stay of seven days. Follow-up was arranged for continued monitoring of maternal and foetal well-being throughout the remainder of the pregnancy.Figure 3Line graph showing the decline in parasitaemia (%) from admission to day 4 following antimalarial treatment. Day 4 parasitaemia was estimated at <0.1%.

full_text: ABSTRACTBackground: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections. This study investigated arboviruses in Aedes spp. larvae collected from a hospital area in Brasília, Federal District, Brazil. Methods: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks. Hatched Aedes spp. larvae were pooled weekly, and viral detection was performed by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR. Results: Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, Zika virus, and Chikungunya virus were identified, with an overall positivity rate of 30.76%. Conclusion: The surveillance strategy effectively detected arboviral RNA in a hospital setting, suggesting local arboviral circulation associated with the transmission triad.Keywords: Ovitrap, RT-qPCR, One Health, Epidemiological monitoring, Entomo-virological surveillance SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIALSupplementary Material Table 1 Supplementary MaterialsSupplementary Material Table 1 ACKNOWLEDGMENTSWe offer our deepest thanks to the Armed Forces Hospital that provided technical support for the development and implementation of this study. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTBackground: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections. This study investigated arboviruses in Aedes spp. larvae collected from a hospital area in Brasília, Federal District, Brazil. Methods: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks. Hatched Aedes spp. larvae were pooled weekly, and viral detection was performed by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR. Results: Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, Zika virus, and Chikungunya virus were identified, with an overall positivity rate of 30.76%. Conclusion: The surveillance strategy effectively detected arboviral RNA in a hospital setting, suggesting local arboviral circulation associated with the transmission triad.Keywords: Ovitrap, RT-qPCR, One Health, Epidemiological monitoring, Entomo-virological surveillance

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the presence of dengue virus and other arboviruses in Aedes larvae collected from a hospital environment in Brasília, Brazil. Over 26 weeks, 18 ovitraps were used to gather larvae, which were pooled weekly and tested by RT‐qPCR. Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, along with Zika and Chikungunya viruses, were detected, yielding a 30.76% overall positivity rate. The authors concluded that entomo‐virological surveillance can reveal arboviral circulation in healthcare settings, underscoring the potential for nosocomial transmission. They highlighted that combining larval surveillance with serological surveys of symptomatic patients can pinpoint early transmission hotspots, informing targeted public‐health interventions. No limitations were reported in the available evidence.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks to collect Aedes spp. larvae in a hospital area of Brasília, Federal District, Brazil.
elements_en.methods: Larvae were pooled weekly and viral detection was performed by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR.
elements_en.main_results: Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, Zika virus, and Chikungunya virus were identified, with an overall positivity rate of 30.76%.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The surveillance strategy effectively detected arboviral RNA in a hospital setting, suggesting local arboviral circulation associated with the transmission triad.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Entomo-virological surveillance followed by serological active survey of symptomatic individuals is helpful to identify hotspots of early arbovirus transmission.

full_text: AbstractSuccessful pandemic preparedness and sustainable healthcare security increasingly rely on One Health—linking humans, animals, and the environment. Novel real-time geolocated data sources from social media, the web, digital traces, and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, combined with traditional surveillance data, are increasingly used to power AI models and enhance environmental sensing that is essential for preparedness and response in the One Health context. Despite the abundance of data streams and sensing data, the potential of AI and IoT environmental monitoring for One Health remains unfulfilled. The OHSEW (One Health Surveillance and Early Warning) framework architecture fills this gap by defining a human-centric architecture for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental sensing, designed in particular for monitoring vector-borne diseases, zoonoses, and other environmental reservoirs of infectious diseases where the risk of spillover to human populations is high. In the OHSEW framework, we identify a rich spectrum of multiple heterogeneous data sources and a pipeline for improved surveillance, data visualisation, and training predictive AI models. These include open-source population and socioeconomic data, land use, satellite sensing, and weather forecasts, enriched by IoT environmental sensing (providing microclimate data streams) and traditional routine surveillance data reported by public health and environmental health experts. These models generate real-time data and actionable evidence for public health managers and policymakers, visualised through customisable dashboards, and provide early warning signals enabling rapid response and effective risk communication with the public. In this article, we outline the framework architecture, individual components, data pipeline, and configurable and localisable setup. To demonstrate the feasibility of the architecture, components of the OHSEW framework were piloted in real-world deployments of mosquito surveillance systems at two sites, Madeira, Portugal, and Cabedelo, Brazil. The architectures and results of these real-world deployments are presented to illustrate the feasibility of the OHSEW framework, with directions for further research outlined.Keywords: AI modelling, architecture framework, Internet of Things, One Health, vector-borne disease 4.Discussion and Future WorkIn this section, we will discuss the strengths of the framework to consider when implementing OHSEW, the key challenges to address, and opportunities for scale-up.4.1.StrengthsThe main strengths are interdisciplinarity, privacy, transparency, data standardisation and interoperability, and generalisability. Interdisciplinary The architecture will be driven by and used by public health and One Health experts, while the details of analysis, bias, and AI model training will be led by public health experts and ecologists rather than AI engineers. Through the process of adoption and localisation of the framework for their specific needs, users might prefer to tune the architecture for impact and environmental plausibility or opt for simple yet tailored solutions rather than fully generic ones with the best precision and recall. Privacy Data privacy and responsible data sharing are recommended to be built into the system and protected through open data frameworks, as defined in Layer 2, rather than treated as an afterthought (63). This is an essential matter of public trust in technology, which was severely dented after COVID-19 with the arrival of Big Tech in healthcare and governments (64). Data standardisation and interoperability Well-defined standards need to be defined and implemented in Layers 1 and 2: One Health Data and Data Integration through a Federated Architecture. Generalisability While the pilot was implemented for mosquito-borne disease surveillance, the framework and associated tools are generalisable to routine data collection for other vectors—we are currently exploring the adaptation of the digital tools for tick surveillance.Engagement with public health stakeholders builds on the collaboration from the mosquito surveillance networks. Implementing OHSEW for human disease surveillance, such as influenza or influenza-like illness (ILI), will require engagement of public health agencies, access to and sharing of reported data, and use of data provided by participatory surveillance apps such as InfluenzaNet2 (popular due to the high prevalence of the disease in the community, which was not the case for VBDs). However, the components and pipeline of the OHSEW framework will remain the same.4.2.Challenges and LimitationsIn this section, we outline key challenges to address when building AI predictive systems using the OHSEW framework, aligned with generic principles of responsible AI (39). While a detailed discussion of these principles is beyond the scope of this study, we outline a suitable governance framework and key studies to follow. Explainability AI-generated models used in the framework cannot be non-reproducible black boxes (65); they need to be sufficiently transparent and interpretable to be trusted to support scientific learning and decision-making (42). Surveillance ethics and data abuse Ethical challenges for AI in public health surveillance have been well understood (39). These include concerns over the access to and use of citizens’ private data, such as phone mobility data (e.g., COVID-19 proximity tracking), due to the danger of disproportionate surveillance, policy measures for enforcement of compliance, unfair false positives, and documented data misuse (39, 66). However, data ownership and data access in public health (67) are societal challenges that we are currently grappling with, rather than being exclusive to One Health (68). Noise and misinformation Noise from digital data sources, fake accounts, and trolls on social media can exacerbate misinformation, making the extraction of meaningful information increasingly challenging (69). Prudence with incorporating social media (especially X) is recommended. Methods for filtering low-quality, biased news and misinformation are also recommended, as shown by an analysis of Twitter during COVID-19 (70) and around HPV vaccine misinformation (71, 72). These studies demonstrated that misinformation often originates from a small number of accounts and sources. Another major challenge for public health agencies when relying on data collected by IT providers and AI companies, rather than the bespoke tools recommended by OHSEW, is the poorly regulated role of Big Tech in health, with these companies dominating social media platforms with unprecedented political influence, gatekeeping public narratives, and having private access to healthcare systems data such as that of the NHS. OHSEW recommends building bespoke apps and tools for data collection to avoid challenges associated with open and public data sources.These issues lead to the need for data and AI Sovereignty for Europe and other nations to reduce the overreliance on the US tech sector—for data control, AI governance, and ownership. As Europe is emerging as an important player, principles have been proposed for responsible One Health systems (73). Bias Bias in data used for training AI models is well described. This is of particular importance in One Health systems, where inequitable data collection is an inevitable outcome of the lack of resources and access in less-resourced parts of the world (74). Equitable Data Partnerships across the Global North and South are of intrinsic importance—between public health and animal health experts, ecologists, and those affected—humans, animals, farmers, and environmentalists—as well as international stakeholders. These principles are essential for interoperability in OHSEW systems integrating veterinary, medical, and environmental systems through federated architectures.In general, more robust ethical governance for AI models is required, relying on clarifying core ethical principles from the outset of development while empowering citizens and stakeholders to participate in collaborative governance frameworks supporting ethics-by-design methodologies for systems using AI to be equitable and safe beyond One Health (75).4.3.Effective Deployment and Future WorkIn order to effectively deploy the OHSEW architecture in any context, national investment in infrastructure, routine surveillance, and capacity building is essential.Furthermore, safe data-sharing platforms are required. In Europe, the open health data paradigm is supported through the European Health Data Space (EHDS) (76). EHDS establishes common standards for health data quality, interoperability, and cross-border access, and, as a result, should enable AI model training on diverse data from European populations, improving fairness. EHDS also includes provisions for secondary data use in research while maintaining strong safeguards. EHDS provides a new opportunity for One Health systems.In terms of AI responsibility and safety, the use of AI models developed and trained for specific diseases by researchers at the national level might be the natural choice. If industry models are considered by national governments, their governance might be a challenge, as the recent WHO report highlighted (77). Even in the European region, only 8% of MSs have an AI vision and health strategy; AI literacy is lagging behind technological developments, and EHDS readiness remains low (only 30% have guidance on the secondary use of health data and cross-border sharing) (78).Another challenge lies in the intrinsically collaborative nature of public health and One Health and the need for the implementation of data standards and interoperability, as highlighted in OHSEW Layer 2: Data Integration through a Federated Architecture. This is much more challenging in public health and One Health settings than in primary and clinical care, which is a national responsibility and where data standards are normally well regulated (79). One Health relies on multiple international organisations to work together and agree on standards, data sharing, model training, and coordinating response.Our current efforts and future research include further recommenders on the selection of One Health data streams for various diseases (Layer 1), standards and protocols (Layer 2), selection of models (Layer 3), and definitions of components for the dashboard (Layer 4). 5.ConclusionPandemic preparedness and global health security rely on One Health—the interaction among humans, animals, and the environment. However, leveraging the abundance of real-time, geolocated data sources and developing bespoke apps and digital tools for AI predictive modelling and IoT environmental monitoring, trained and calibrated by routine surveillance data for One Health needs, remain unfulfilled.In this study, we presented the OHSEW framework—a human-centric architecture for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response leveraging heterogeneous data sources for AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring, championing the development and deployment of bespoke mobile tools and IoT sensor sets to fill the gap in missing fine-grained, real-time, GPS-enabled surveillance datasets, particularly much-needed ones in LMICs. The architecture consists of six layers implementing the data pipeline—One Health Data Sources, Data Integration through a Federated Architecture, Spatiotemporal and AI Modelling for Early Warning, Component-based Configurable Dashboards for decision-makers, Interventions and Control Measures, and Public Risk Communication and Community Engagement.We have demonstrated the feasibility of the framework through a real-word pilot for mosquito surveillance deployed with users in Brazil and Madeira over 2 years, demonstrating the potential of the framework in real-world settings. 1.BackgroundIn this section, we introduce the concept of One Health, disease surveillance, and early warning systems, as well as the related concept of antibiotic resistance (AMR), advances in AI modelling and Internet of Things (IoT) environmental sensing, and the unprecedented role of digital technology in addressing this global challenge (1).1.1.One HealthThe core of the One Health paradigm—linking humans, animals, and the environment—recognises the essential connections among animals, humans, plants, and ecosystems, as well as planetary health. One Health is the driving approach for detecting outbreaks of existing communicable diseases and potential spillovers (cross-species outbreaks) and for identifying settings of human-to-human transmission–the most likely onset of the next pandemic.According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 60% of emerging infectious diseases reported globally come from animals, both wild and domestic. Furthermore, over 30 new human pathogens have been detected in the last three decades, 75% of which have originated in animals (2).One of the highest threats is posed by vector-borne diseases (VBDs)—such as dengue, Zika, West Nile virus, and Lyme disease—as they account for more than 17% of all infectious diseases, causing more than 700,000 deaths annually, according to the WHO (3). They are further exacerbated by climate change, urbanisation, and global travel. VBDs transmitted specifically by mosquitoes in tropical parts of the world amount to an estimated 219 million cases globally and result in more than 400,000 deaths every year. From this perspective, mosquitoes are among the deadliest killers.Health threats, vectors, and viruses do not respect borders. Only through intersectoral international collaboration, data and results sharing, and coordinated action can future outbreaks and epidemics be prevented and effectively controlled, early warnings of spillovers of new viruses from zoonotic diseases to humans expedited, and rapid response and effective management of diseases at local, national, and international levels enabled (4).In order to achieve this ambitious goal, two major international activities have recently been established—the Quadripartite collaboration of UN agencies—Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), WHO, and World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) (5). In Europe, the five European Union One Health agencies agreed on a similar strategic cooperation—including the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), European Chemicals Agency, European Environment Agency, and European Medicines Agency (6).In order to effectively advance the One Health agenda, monitoring of human and environmental systems needs to better analyse social interactions in society and interactions between humans and animals that might drive transmission of infectious agents from animals to humans and could result in a virus spillover. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractSuccessful pandemic preparedness and sustainable healthcare security increasingly rely on One Health—linking humans, animals, and the environment. Novel real-time geolocated data sources from social media, the web, digital traces, and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, combined with traditional surveillance data, are increasingly used to power AI models and enhance environmental sensing that is essential for preparedness and response in the One Health context. Despite the abundance of data streams and sensing data, the potential of AI and IoT environmental monitoring for One Health remains unfulfilled. The OHSEW (One Health Surveillance and Early Warning) framework architecture fills this gap by defining a human-centric architecture for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental sensing, designed in particular for monitoring vector-borne diseases, zoonoses, and other environmental reservoirs of infectious diseases where the risk of spillover to human populations is high. In the OHSEW framework, we identify a rich spectrum of multiple heterogeneous data sources and a pipeline for improved surveillance, data visualisation, and training predictive AI models. These include open-source population and socioeconomic data, land use, satellite sensing, and weather forecasts, enriched by IoT environmental sensing (providing microclimate data streams) and traditional routine surveillance data reported by public health and environmental health experts. These models generate real-time data and actionable evidence for public health managers and policymakers, visualised through customisable dashboards, and provide early warning signals enabling rapid response and effective risk communication with the public. In this article, we outline the framework architecture, individual components, data pipeline, and configurable and localisable setup. To demonstrate the feasibility of the architecture, components of the OHSEW framework were piloted in real-world deployments of mosquito surveillance systems at two sites, Madeira, Portugal, and Cabedelo, Brazil. The architectures and results of these real-world deployments are presented to illustrate the feasibility of the OHSEW framework, with directions for further research outlined.Keywords: AI modelling, architecture framework, Internet of Things, One Health, vector-borne disease
full_text_sections.discussion: 4.Discussion and Future WorkIn this section, we will discuss the strengths of the framework to consider when implementing OHSEW, the key challenges to address, and opportunities for scale-up.4.1.StrengthsThe main strengths are interdisciplinarity, privacy, transparency, data standardisation and interoperability, and generalisability. Interdisciplinary The architecture will be driven by and used by public health and One Health experts, while the details of analysis, bias, and AI model training will be led by public health experts and ecologists rather than AI engineers. Through the process of adoption and localisation of the framework for their specific needs, users might prefer to tune the architecture for impact and environmental plausibility or opt for simple yet tailored solutions rather than fully generic ones with the best precision and recall. Privacy Data privacy and responsible data sharing are recommended to be built into the system and protected through open data frameworks, as defined in Layer 2, rather than treated as an afterthought (63). This is an essential matter of public trust in technology, which was severely dented after COVID-19 with the arrival of Big Tech in healthcare and governments (64). Data standardisation and interoperability Well-defined standards need to be defined and implemented in Layers 1 and 2: One Health Data and Data Integration through a Federated Architecture. Generalisability While the pilot was implemented for mosquito-borne disease surveillance, the framework and associated tools are generalisable to routine data collection for other vectors—we are currently exploring the adaptation of the digital tools for tick surveillance.Engagement with public health stakeholders builds on the collaboration from the mosquito surveillance networks. Implementing OHSEW for human disease surveillance, such as influenza or influenza-like illness (ILI), will require engagement of public health agencies, access to and sharing of reported data, and use of data provided by participatory surveillance apps such as InfluenzaNet2 (popular due to the high prevalence of the disease in the community, which was not the case for VBDs). However, the components and pipeline of the OHSEW framework will remain the same.4.2.Challenges and LimitationsIn this section, we outline key challenges to address when building AI predictive systems using the OHSEW framework, aligned with generic principles of responsible AI (39). While a detailed discussion of these principles is beyond the scope of this study, we outline a suitable governance framework and key studies to follow. Explainability AI-generated models used in the framework cannot be non-reproducible black boxes (65); they need to be sufficiently transparent and interpretable to be trusted to support scientific learning and decision-making (42). Surveillance ethics and data abuse Ethical challenges for AI in public health surveillance have been well understood (39). These include concerns over the access to and use of citizens’ private data, such as phone mobility data (e.g., COVID-19 proximity tracking), due to the danger of disproportionate surveillance, policy measures for enforcement of compliance, unfair false positives, and documented data misuse (39, 66). However, data ownership and data access in public health (67) are societal challenges that we are currently grappling with, rather than being exclusive to One Health (68). Noise and misinformation Noise from digital data sources, fake accounts, and trolls on social media can exacerbate misinformation, making the extraction of meaningful information increasingly challenging (69). Prudence with incorporating social media (especially X) is recommended. Methods for filtering low-quality, biased news and misinformation are also recommended, as shown by an analysis of Twitter during COVID-19 (70) and around HPV vaccine misinformation (71, 72). These studies demonstrated that misinformation often originates from a small number of accounts and sources. Another major challenge for public health agencies when relying on data collected by IT providers and AI companies, rather than the bespoke tools recommended by OHSEW, is the poorly regulated role of Big Tech in health, with these companies dominating social media platforms with unprecedented political influence, gatekeeping public narratives, and having private access to healthcare systems data such as that of the NHS. OHSEW recommends building bespoke apps and tools for data collection to avoid challenges associated with open and public data sources.These issues lead to the need for data and AI Sovereignty for Europe and other nations to reduce the overreliance on the US tech sector—for data control, AI governance, and ownership. As Europe is emerging as an important player, principles have been proposed for responsible One Health systems (73). Bias Bias in data used for training AI models is well described. This is of particular importance in One Health systems, where inequitable data collection is an inevitable outcome of the lack of resources and access in less-resourced parts of the world (74). Equitable Data Partnerships across the Global North and South are of intrinsic importance—between public health and animal health experts, ecologists, and those affected—humans, animals, farmers, and environmentalists—as well as international stakeholders. These principles are essential for interoperability in OHSEW systems integrating veterinary, medical, and environmental systems through federated architectures.In general, more robust ethical governance for AI models is required, relying on clarifying core ethical principles from the outset of development while empowering citizens and stakeholders to participate in collaborative governance frameworks supporting ethics-by-design methodologies for systems using AI to be equitable and safe beyond One Health (75).4.3.Effective Deployment and Future WorkIn order to effectively deploy the OHSEW architecture in any context, national investment in infrastructure, routine surveillance, and capacity building is essential.Furthermore, safe data-sharing platforms are required. In Europe, the open health data paradigm is supported through the European Health Data Space (EHDS) (76). EHDS establishes common standards for health data quality, interoperability, and cross-border access, and, as a result, should enable AI model training on diverse data from European populations, improving fairness. EHDS also includes provisions for secondary data use in research while maintaining strong safeguards. EHDS provides a new opportunity for One Health systems.In terms of AI responsibility and safety, the use of AI models developed and trained for specific diseases by researchers at the national level might be the natural choice. If industry models are considered by national governments, their governance might be a challenge, as the recent WHO report highlighted (77). Even in the European region, only 8% of MSs have an AI vision and health strategy; AI literacy is lagging behind technological developments, and EHDS readiness remains low (only 30% have guidance on the secondary use of health data and cross-border sharing) (78).Another challenge lies in the intrinsically collaborative nature of public health and One Health and the need for the implementation of data standards and interoperability, as highlighted in OHSEW Layer 2: Data Integration through a Federated Architecture. This is much more challenging in public health and One Health settings than in primary and clinical care, which is a national responsibility and where data standards are normally well regulated (79). One Health relies on multiple international organisations to work together and agree on standards, data sharing, model training, and coordinating response.Our current efforts and future research include further recommenders on the selection of One Health data streams for various diseases (Layer 1), s…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionPandemic preparedness and global health security rely on One Health—the interaction among humans, animals, and the environment. However, leveraging the abundance of real-time, geolocated data sources and developing bespoke apps and digital tools for AI predictive modelling and IoT environmental monitoring, trained and calibrated by routine surveillance data for One Health needs, remain unfulfilled.In this study, we presented the OHSEW framework—a human-centric architecture for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response leveraging heterogeneous data sources for AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring, championing the development and deployment of bespoke mobile tools and IoT sensor sets to fill the gap in missing fine-grained, real-time, GPS-enabled surveillance datasets, particularly much-needed ones in LMICs. The architecture consists of six layers implementing the data pipeline—One Health Data Sources, Data Integration through a Federated Architecture, Spatiotemporal and AI Modelling for Early Warning, Component-based Configurable Dashboards for decision-makers, Interventions and Control Measures, and Public Risk Communication and Community Engagement.We have demonstrated the feasibility of the framework through a real-word pilot for mosquito surveillance deployed with users in Brazil and Madeira over 2 years, demonstrating the potential of the framework in real-world settings.

They are further exacerbated by climate change, urbanisation, and global travel. VBDs transmitted specifically by mosquitoes in tropical parts of the world amount to an estimated 219 million cases globally and result in more than 400,000 deaths every year. From this perspective, mosquitoes are among the deadliest killers.Health threats, vectors, and viruses do not respect borders. Climate change has accelerated the emergence of pathogens and the resurgence of VBDs, in particular arboviruses, that are causing significant threats to both national and global health security (8). Changing rainfall patterns and increasing temperatures have recently contributed to public health outbreaks of dengue, Zika, Oropouche, and yellow fever in endemic areas and in new geographic territories that were previously not affected in Asia, Africa, and the Americas (9, 10), as well as increasing the risk of spillovers in a number of geographic regions (11, 12).In the United Kingdom, the 2023 report on Health Effects of Climate Change (13) specifically addressed the impact of climate change on VBDs. Owing to climate change, these vectors may soon become established in traditionally mild climates across Europe and Asia, leading to local transmission.1.3.One Health and Antimicrobial ResistanceAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global challenge, often called a “slow pandemic,” that society faces because antibiotics are no longer effective against common infections. According to the 2019 study “Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019: a systematic analysis” (15), it is estimated that drug-resistant infections contribute to nearly 5 million deaths every year, and AMR remains a major challenge in high-income countries such as Europe (16) as well as in LMIC countries (17).AI models analysing genomic data from humans, animals, and environmental sources, such as wastewater, have demonstrated the potential for early warning and strengthening antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) (18). Furthermore, predicting resistance phenotypes from genomic data using supervised learning has also demonstrated potential to strengthen AMS (19).1.4.Data in Disease Surveillance and Early WarningDisease surveillance is a routine public health process that collects indicator-based data from clinical and primary care, microbiological laboratories, and the community to assess the burden of disease, support early warning and rapid response, and implement effective public health interventions. Heterogeneous data sources in combination with indicator-based reported data are essential for driving an effective EWS (21). analysis.summary_en: This study presents an interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring. The framework's feasibility was demonstrated through a real-world pilot for mosquito-borne disease surveillance in Brazil and Madeira over two years, showing increased dengue, chikungunya, and malaria cases. analysis_en.main_results: Imported dengue cases increased from 631 in 2023 to 904 in 2024, while chikungunya and malaria cases also increased. AI models analysing genomic data from humans, animals, and environmental sources, such as wastewater, have demonstrated the potential for early warning and strengthening antimicrobial stewardship (AMS).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The architectures and results of these real-world deployments are presented to illustrate the feasibility of the OHSEW framework, with directions for further research outlined. One Health is the driving approach for detecting outbreaks of existing communicable diseases and potential spillovers (cross-species outbreaks) and for identifying settings of human-to-human transmission–the most likely onset of the next pandemic.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Implementing OHSEW for human disease surveillance, such as influenza or influenza-like illness (ILI), will require engagement of public health agencies, access to and sharing of reported data, and use of data provided by participatory surveillance apps such as InfluenzaNet2.
