title: Nursing actions indicative of autonomy and authority compatible with Advanced Nursing Practice in Brazil*

source_records.title: Nursing actions indicative of autonomy and authority compatible with Advanced Nursing Practice in Brazil*

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: AbstractObjective: this study analyzed representative actions indicating autonomy and clinical authority among nurses in primary health care, compatible with Advanced Nursing Practice in Brazil. Method: the ecological study used secondary data from 2023 from the Brazilian Ministry of Health’s information system, covering all 26 states and the Federal District. Indicators related to consultations, medication prescriptions, diagnostic tests, and clinical referrals were examined. Results: the results reveal a wide range of activities performed by nurses in areas characteristic of Advanced Nursing Practice, while also showing significant geographical inequality, predominantly in the Southeast and South regions. Conclusion: the analysis reveals the effective exercise of advanced competencies, even without specific regulations, and highlights the need for public policies that promote specialized training, regulatory standardization, and the legal recognition of Advanced Nursing Practice to improve the quality and equity of health care.Descriptors: Primary Health Care, Professional Autonomy, Nursing, Ecological Study, Advanced Nursing Practice, Health Policies Highlights: (1) The results show that Advanced Nursing Practice is already being implemented in routine health services. (2) 52 million nursing consultations; 37,000 medication prescriptions. (3) 9.5 million diagnostic tests prescribed and 83 million clinical referrals. (4) Effective performance of advanced practices, even without specific regulations. (5) Fertile ground for establishing Professional Master’s programs in Advanced Nursing Practice, aligned with SUS and ICN. ResumoObjetivo: este estudo analisou ações representativas de autonomia e autoridade clínica de enfermeiros na Atenção Primária à Saúde compatíveis com a Prática Avançada de Enfermagem no Brasil. Método: a pesquisa ecológica utilizou dados secundários de 2023 provenientes do sistema de informação do Ministério da Saúde do Brasil, considerando os 26 estados e o Distrito Federal. Foram examinados indicadores de consultas, prescrições de medicamentos e testes diagnósticos, além de encaminhamentos clínicos. Resultados: os resultados revelam uma ampla atuação dos enfermeiros em domínios característicos de Prática Avançada de Enfermagem expressando, no entanto, desigualdade geográfica expressiva predominante nas regiões Sudeste e Sul. Conclusão: a análise revela o exercício efetivo de competências avançadas, mesmo sem regulamentação específica, e destaca a necessidade de políticas públicas que promovam formação especializada, padronização normativa e reconhecimento legal da Prática Avançada de Enfermagem, visando à qualificação e equidade dos cuidados em saúde.Descritores: Atenção Primária à Saúde, Autonomia Profissional, Enfermagem, Estudo Ecológico, Prática Avançada de Enfermagem, Políticas de Saúde Destaques: (1) O resultado sustenta que a Prática Avançada da Enfermagem já se concretiza no cotidiano dos serviços. (2) 52 milhões de consultas de Enfermagem; 37 mil prescrições de medicamentos. (3) 9,5 milhões de testes diagnósticos prescritos e 83 milhões de encaminhamentos clínicos. (4) Exercício efetivo de ações avançadas, mesmo sem regulamentação específica. (5) Terreno fértil para instituir Mestrados Profissionais em Prática Avançada da Enfermagem, alinhados ao SUS e ao ICN. ResumenObjetivo: este estudio analizó acciones representativas de la autonomía y la autoridad clínica de los enfermeros en la atención primaria de salud, compatibles con la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada en Brasil. Método: estudio ecológico con datos secundarios de 2023 del sistema de información del Ministerio de Salud de Brasil, considerando los 26 estados y el Distrito Federal. Se examinaron indicadores de consultas, prescripciones de medicamentos, pruebas diagnósticas y derivaciones clínicas. Resultados: se evidenció una amplia actuación de los enfermeros en ámbitos característicos de la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada, aunque con marcada desigualdad geográfica, predominante en el Sudeste y Sur. Conclusión: el análisis revela el ejercicio de competencias avanzadas, incluso sin regulación específica, y destaca la necesidad de políticas que promuevan la formación especializada, la estandarización normativa y el reconocimiento legal de la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada, con el objetivo de mejorar la calidad y equidad de la atención en salud.Descriptores: Atención Primaria de Salud, Autonomía Profesional, Enfermería, Estudio Ecológico, Práctica Avanzada de Enfermería, Políticas de Salud Destacados: (1) El resultado sostiene que la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada ya se concreta en el día a día de los servicios. (2) 52 millones de consultas de enfermería; 37.000 prescripciones de medicamentos. (3) 9,5 millones de pruebas diagnósticas prescritas y 83 millones de derivaciones clínicas. (4) Ejercicio efectivo de acciones avanzadas, incluso sin regulación específica. (5) Terreno fértil para la institución de maestrías profesionales en la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada, alineadas con el SUS y el ICN. MethodStudy designThis is an ecological study 15 , with an aggregated analysis unit comprising the Brazilian territory and its subdivision into 26 states and the Federal District of Brazil, in 2023.Secondary data sources and variablesSecondary public databases were used, extracted from the following national platforms: the Health Information System for Primary Care (SISAB, as per its acronym in Portuguese) 16 and the National Registry of Health Facilities (CNES/Professionals) 17 . From these two databases, four indicators (14, 15, 16, and 17) related to ANP competencies were classified, and the selection, extraction, and organization of data followed a previously structured conceptual matrix derived from a previous study 18 , which establishes a relationship between the competencies of ANP, as proposed by the ICN 8 and the PNAB 12 . The conceptual framework used in the study allowed establishing a correspondence between internationally recognized clinical competencies and the duties assigned to nurses by the law governing professional practice and by the PNAB 12 , which, through municipal protocols and regulations, authorize the conduct of consultations, the request of diagnostic tests, the prescription of medications, and referrals. For analytical purposes, concise operational definitions were adopted: clinical autonomy as the nurse’s ability to conduct consultations and perform diagnostic assessments; and clinical authority as the prerogative to prescribe, request tests, and refer users as per current regulatory frameworks. Based on these definitions, the indicators were classified according to their clinical nature: indicator 14 (consultations), representing clinical autonomy in the different areas covered by SISAB 16 , such as prenatal care, childcare, postpartum care, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, smoking, use of alcohol and other drugs, monitoring of communicable diseases, and screening activities; indicator 15 (test request), expressing diagnostic authority; indicator 16 (medication prescription), reflecting therapeutic authority; and indicator 17 (referrals), indicating expanded clinical authority in directing users to other points in the health care network. The four indicators represent advanced clinical dimensions, as detailed in Figure 1.Figure 1Filters used for data extraction in the Health Information System for Primary Care-2023Geographic unitBrazilPeriod January to December 2023Report column Indicator 14 = type of production: individual care; problem/condition assessed: prenatal care, childcare, postpartum care (up to 42 days), sexual and reproductive health, smoking, alcohol use, other drug use, mental health, communicable diseases: dengue fever; STDs; leprosy, tuberculosis; breast cancer screening, cervical cancer screening, cardiovascular risk screeningIndicator 15 = type of production: individual care; problem/condition assessed: same as indicator 14; ICPC/ICD: ICPC (50) medication/prescription/renewal/injection, ICD (Z760) repeat prescription and issuanceIndicator 16 = type of production: procedure; procedure: test. proteinuria rapid test, HIV rapid test, pregnancy rapid test, hepatitis C rapid test, syphilis rapid test, and ophthalmologic screeningIndicator 17 = type of production: individual care; problem/condition assessed: same as indicator 14; conduct: scheduling for NASF*, scheduling for groups, discharge from episode, internal referral on the same day, intersectoral referral, referral to CAPS, referral for hospital admission, referral for home care service, referral for specialized care, referral for emergency care, return for continued/scheduled care, return for scheduled consultationType of careScheduled appointment. Prog/cont. care, scheduled appointment, initial/orientation request, same-day appointment request, urgent care requestProfessional categoryNurseCare sectorBHU, Mobile unit, Street, Home, School/daycare center, Others, Health center, Institution/shelter, Prison or similar facility, Socio-educational facilityType of healthcare team Family Health Team (ESF), Community Health Agent Team (EACS), NASF*/eMulti, Primary Care Team (EAB), Street Clinic Team (ECR), Oral Health Team (SB), Prison Primary Care Team (EABp), Primary Care Team - eAP*NASF = Family Health Support Center, as per its acronym in PortugueseIt is recognized that these indicators correspond to administrative production records rather than details on the clinical complexity of each action. Nevertheless, they represent the structural dimensions of the legal and regulatory scope of nursing practice in PHC, allowing for the analysis of the territorial distribution of these activities and their alignment with competencies described in international references. Collection proceduresThe extraction of SISAB data was carried out between November 3 and 5, 2024, through an automated, parameterized process that applied a single standardized filter across all states, team modalities, and care units, according to the system’s structural options. Records for the 12 months of 2023 were selected, restricted to professionals in the nursing category and covering the different modalities authorized in PHC [Family Health Team (ESF), Primary Care Team (eAP), Street Clinic Team (eCR), and other recognized teams], according to the standardized codes and parameters of the Management System for the Table of Procedures, Medications, and Orthoses, Prostheses, and Special Materials (SIGTAP) of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), as described in Figure 1. This procedure ensured uniformity in selection and reduced heterogeneity caused by coding differences across regions and team types.After extraction, the database underwent double validation, conducted by a statistician and a second researcher responsible for checking and manipulating the database, ensuring the integrity, consistency, and applicability of the records. As the data were aggregated by type of care, date, and procedure, according to the official SISAB parameters, no duplicates were found within the established criteria. Incomplete, invalid records or those incompatible with PHC were automatically excluded by the filter applied during extraction.In addition, geospatial data (maps and geographic coordinates) were obtained from the website of the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE, as per its acronym in Portuguese) 19 , using geographic projection. Information related to the general population size for each state and the total Brazilian population (census year) was compiled. Digital maps and their respective geodetic coordinates (files in *.shp, *.shx, and *.prj formats) of the national territory and its subdivision into states (reference year 2017) were obtained from http:downloads.ibge.gov.br/downloads_geociencias.htm. Files with the .shp extension assume the SIRGAS_2000 geographic projection, datum[“d_SIRGAS_2000”, spheroid[“grs_1980”,6378137,298.257222101], primem[“Greenwich”,0], unit[“degree”, 0.017453292519943295]].Data analysisThis stage was divided into two phases.Phase 1 - Descriptive analysisThe absolute frequencies of activities associated with the selected indicators were quantified by state. This phase allowed us to estimate the volume of actions performed by nurses in the PHC setting, classified by advanced practice domain (Figure 2). We also used the nursing workforce linked to PHC registered in the National Register of Health Facilities - CNES/Professionals 17 ) as a reference. The extraction was performed using data available for July 2023, totaling 100,614 nurses working in PHC across the country. Method: the ecological study used secondary data from 2023 from the Brazilian Ministry of Health’s information system, covering all 26 states and the Federal District. Indicators related to consultations, medication prescriptions, diagnostic tests, and clinical referrals were examined. Results: the results reveal a wide range of activities performed by nurses in areas characteristic of Advanced Nursing Practice, while also showing significant geographical inequality, predominantly in the Southeast and South regions. Conclusion: the analysis reveals the effective exercise of advanced competencies, even without specific regulations, and highlights the need for public policies that promote specialized training, regulatory standardization, and the legal recognition of Advanced Nursing Practice to improve the quality and equity of health care.Descriptors: Primary Health Care, Professional Autonomy, Nursing, Ecological Study, Advanced Nursing Practice, Health Policies Highlights: (1) The results show that Advanced Nursing Practice is already being implemented in routine health services. (2) 52 million nursing consultations; 37,000 medication prescriptions. (3) 9.5 million diagnostic tests prescribed and 83 million clinical referrals. (4) Effective performance of advanced practices, even without specific regulations. (5) Fertile ground for establishing Professional Master’s programs in Advanced Nursing Practice, aligned with SUS and ICN. ResumoObjetivo: este estudo analisou ações representativas de autonomia e autoridade clínica de enfermeiros na Atenção Primária à Saúde compatíveis com a Prática Avançada de Enfermagem no Brasil. Método: a pesquisa ecológica utilizou dados secundários de 2023 provenientes do sistema de informação do Ministério da Saúde do Brasil, considerando os 26 estados e o Distrito Federal. Foram examinados indicadores de consultas, prescrições de medicamentos e testes diagnósticos, além de encaminhamentos clínicos. Resultados: os resultados revelam uma ampla atuação dos enfermeiros em domínios característicos de Prática Avançada de Enfermagem expressando, no entanto, desigualdade geográfica expressiva predominante nas regiões Sudeste e Sul. Conclusão: a análise revela o exercício efetivo de competências avançadas, mesmo sem regulamentação específica, e destaca a necessidade de políticas públicas que promovam formação especializada, padronização normativa e reconhecimento legal da Prática Avançada de Enfermagem, visando à qualificação e equidade dos cuidados em saúde.Descritores: Atenção Primária à Saúde, Autonomia Profissional, Enfermagem, Estudo Ecológico, Prática Avançada de Enfermagem, Políticas de Saúde Destaques: (1) O resultado sustenta que a Prática Avançada da Enfermagem já se concretiza no cotidiano dos serviços. (2) 52 milhões de consultas de Enfermagem; 37 mil prescrições de medicamentos. (3) 9,5 milhões de testes diagnósticos prescritos e 83 milhões de encaminhamentos clínicos. (4) Exercício efetivo de ações avançadas, mesmo sem regulamentação específica. (5) Terreno fértil para instituir Mestrados Profissionais em Prática Avançada da Enfermagem, alinhados ao SUS e ao ICN. ResumenObjetivo: este estudio analizó acciones representativas de la autonomía y la autoridad clínica de los enfermeros en la atención primaria de salud, compatibles con la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada en Brasil. Método: estudio ecológico con datos secundarios de 2023 del sistema de información del Ministerio de Salud de Brasil, considerando los 26 estados y el Distrito Federal. Se examinaron indicadores de consultas, prescripciones de medicamentos, pruebas diagnósticas y derivaciones clínicas. Resultados: se evidenció una amplia actuación de los enfermeros en ámbitos característicos de la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada, aunque con marcada desigualdad geográfica, predominante en el Sudeste y Sur. Conclusión: el análisis revela el ejercicio de competencias avanzadas, incluso sin regulación específica, y destaca la necesidad de políticas que promuevan la formación especializada, la estandarización normativa y el reconocimiento legal de la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada, con el objetivo de mejorar la calidad y equidad de la atención en salud.Descriptores: Atención Primaria de Salud, Autonomía Profesional, Enfermería, Estudio Ecológico, Práctica Avanzada de Enfermería, Políticas de Salud Destacados: (1) El resultado sostiene que la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada ya se concreta en el día a día de los servicios. (2) 52 millones de consultas de enfermería; 37.000 prescripciones de medicamentos. (3) 9,5 millones de pruebas diagnósticas prescritas y 83 millones de derivaciones clínicas. (4) Ejercicio efectivo de acciones avanzadas, incluso sin regulación específica. (5) Terreno fértil para la institución de maestrías profesionales en la Enfermería de Práctica Avanzada, alineadas con el SUS y el ICN.
full_text_sections.methods: MethodStudy designThis is an ecological study 15 , with an aggregated analysis unit comprising the Brazilian territory and its subdivision into 26 states and the Federal District of Brazil, in 2023.Secondary data sources and variablesSecondary public databases were used, extracted from the following national platforms: the Health Information System for Primary Care (SISAB, as per its acronym in Portuguese) 16 and the National Registry of Health Facilities (CNES/Professionals) 17 . From these two databases, four indicators (14, 15, 16, and 17) related to ANP competencies were classified, and the selection, extraction, and organization of data followed a previously structured conceptual matrix derived from a previous study 18 , which establishes a relationship between the competencies of ANP, as proposed by the ICN 8 and the PNAB 12 . The conceptual framework used in the study allowed establishing a correspondence between internationally recognized clinical competencies and the duties assigned to nurses by the law governing professional practice and by the PNAB 12 , which, through municipal protocols and regulations, authorize the conduct of consultations, the request of diagnostic tests, the prescription of medications, and referrals. For analytical purposes, concise operational definitions were adopted: clinical autonomy as the nurse’s ability to conduct consultations and perform diagnostic assessments; and clinical authority as the prerogative to prescribe, request tests, and refer users as per current regulatory frameworks. Based on these definitions, the indicators were classified according to their clinical nature: indicator 14 (consultations), representing clinical autonomy in the different areas covered by SISAB 16 , such as prenatal care, childcare, postpartum care, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, smoking, use of alcohol and other drugs, monitoring of communicable diseases, and screening activities; indicator 15 (test request), expressing diagnostic authority; indicator 16 (medication prescription), reflecting therapeutic authority; and indicator 17 (referrals), indicating expanded clinical authority in directing users to other points in the health care network. The four indicators represent advanced clinical dimensions, as detailed in Figure 1.Figure 1Filters used for data extraction in the Health Information System for Primary Care-2023Geographic unitBrazilPeriod January to December 2023Report column Indicator 14 = type of production: individual care; problem/condition assessed: prenatal care, childcare, postpartum care (up to 42 days), sexual and reproductive health, smoking, alcohol use, other drug use, mental health, communicable diseases: dengue fever; STDs; leprosy, tuberculosis; breast cancer screening, cervical cancer screening, cardiovascular risk screeningIndicator 15 = type of production: individual care; problem/condition assessed: same as indicator 14; ICPC/ICD: ICPC (50) medication/prescription/renewal/injection, ICD (Z760) repeat prescription and issuanceIndicator 16 = type of production: procedure; procedure: test. proteinuria rapid test, HIV rapid test, pregnancy rapid test, hepatitis C rapid test, syphilis rapid test, and ophthalmologic screeningIndicator 17 = type of production: individual care; problem/condition assessed: same as indicator 14; conduct: scheduling for NASF*, scheduling for groups, discharge from episode, internal referral on the same day, intersectoral referral, referral to CAPS, referral for hospital admission, referral for home care service, referral for specialized care, referral for emergency care, return for continued/scheduled care, return for scheduled consultationType of careScheduled appointment. Prog/cont. care, scheduled appointment, initial/orientation request, same-day appointment request, urgent care requestProfessional categoryNurseCare sectorBHU, Mobile unit, Street, Home, School/daycare center, Others, Health center, Institution/shelter, Prison or similar facility, Socio-educational facilityType of healthcare team Family Health Team (ESF), Community Health Agent Team (EACS), NASF*/eMulti, Primary Care Team (EAB), Street Clinic Team (ECR), Oral Health Team (SB), Prison Primary Care Team (EABp), Primary Care Team - eAP*NASF = Family Health Support Center, as per its acronym in PortugueseIt is recognized that these indicators correspond to administrative production records rather than details on the clinical complexity of each action. Nevertheless, they represent the structural dimensions of the legal and regulatory scope of nursing practice in PHC, allowing for the analysis of the territorial distribution of these activities and their alignment with competencies described in international references. Collection proceduresThe extraction of SISAB data was carried out between November 3 and 5, 2024, through an automated, parameterized process that applied a single standardized filter across all states, team modalities, and care units, according to the system’s structural options. Records for the 12 months of 2023 were selected, restricted to professionals in the nursing category and covering the different modalities authorized in PHC [Family Health Team (ESF), Primary Care Team (eAP), Street Clinic Team (eCR), and other recognized teams], according to the standardized codes and parameters of the Management System for the Table of Procedures, Medications, and Orthoses, Prostheses, and Special Materials (SIGTAP) of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), as described in Figure 1. This procedure ensured uniformity in selection and reduced heterogeneity caused by coding differences across regions and team types.After extraction, the database underwent double validation, conducted by a statistician and a second researcher responsible for checking and manipulating the database, ensuring the integrity, consistency, and applicability of the records. As the data were aggregated by type of care, date, and procedure, according to the official SISAB parameters, no duplicates were found within the established criteria. Incomplete, invalid records or those incompatible with PHC were automatically excluded by the filter applied during extraction.In addition, geospatial data (maps and geographic coordinates) were obtained from the website of the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE, as per its acronym in Portuguese) 19 , using geographic projection. Information related to the general population size for each state and the total Brazilian population (census year) was compiled. Digital maps and their respective geodetic coordinates (files in *.shp, *.shx, and *.prj formats) of the national territory and its subdivision into states (reference year 2017) were obtained from http:downloads.ibge.gov.br/downloads_geociencias.htm. Files with the .shp extension assume the SIRGAS_2000 geographic projection, datum[“d_SIRGAS_2000”, spheroid[“grs_1980”,6378137,298.257222101], primem[“Greenwich”,0], unit[“degree”, 0.017453292519943295]].Data analysisThis stage was divided into two phases.Phase 1 - Descriptive analysisThe absolute frequencies of activities associated with the selected indicators were quantified by state. This phase allowed us to estimate the volume of actions performed by nurses in the PHC setting, classified by advanced practice domain (Figure 2). We also used the nursing workforce linked to PHC registered in the National Register of Health Facilities - CNES/Professionals 17 ) as a reference. The extraction was performed using data available for July 2023, totaling 100,614 nurses working in PHC across the country. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe actions performed by nurses in PHC are aligned with the guidelines established by the ICN 8 for advanced nursing practice. This study focused on analyzing actions that reflect nurses’ clinical authority and autonomy: conducting consultations, clinical referrals, requesting diagnostic tests, and prescribing medications in the context of PHC.The distribution of these four sets of actions, in terms of volume of records, occurred in the following order: nursing consultation, referral of users to other health professionals and/or services, request of diagnostic tests, and, finally, prescription of medications. In an ecological study, inferences refer to collective units rather than the individual performance of professionals. The possibility of biases related to the quality of records and the structural heterogeneity of services must be considered, despite the adoption of standardization measures. Figure 3 is central to understanding the geographic pattern of implementation of the four types of action aligned with ANP in Brazil. The image shows a concentration of the four indicators in the South-Southeast axis, suggesting greater institutionalization of advanced practices in these territories. On the other hand, states in the North and Northeast regions, such as Acre, Roraima, Piauí, and Amapá, are in the lower quartiles, indicating a lower density of clinical actions compatible with ANP, which may reflect structural limitations, a scarcity of local protocols, or underreporting. This gradient shows that, although the actions developed by nurses in PHC in Brazil align with the assumptions of ANP, significant regional inequalities persist across states. Thus, the expansion of ANP seems to depend on investments in professional training, local regulation, and public financing.The significant number of nursing consultations recorded (52,128,446) demonstrated the wide range of clinical activities performed by nurses, especially in conditions that require greater diagnostic autonomy, such as women’s health, mental health, communicable diseases, and cancer screening. Although this practice is already consolidated in some territories, it is unevenly distributed among the states, with São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, Paraná, Bahia, and Rio Grande do Sul standing out, as shown in Figure 3 (upper quartile of the spatial analysis). These findings reinforce the existence of contexts more favorable to the consolidation of ANP in these states.National studies corroborate this scenario by highlighting the positive perception of nurse autonomy in PHC 14 ),( 22 )-( 24 , and showing that, when supported by regulations and scientific evidence, these professionals take on a leading role in clinical care, especially in sensitive areas such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and women’s health care 25 . Thus, the results presented in this study do not correspond to a formally recognized model of Advanced Nursing Practice in Brazil, given that this function lacks specific regulation, but they highlight dimensions of nurses’ clinical practice that align with competencies described in international frameworks and point to potential for development. These actions, performed by generalist nurses within the expanded scope permitted by Brazilian legislation, reveal patterns of clinical maturity and leadership that can support the development of training and regulatory frameworks aligned with international ANP guidelines. The results demonstrate a significant set of practices that engage with advanced domains, providing an empirical basis for guiding future debates and proposals.In addition, 83,025,882 referral records were identified, highlighting the role of nurses as care coordinators and facilitators of care flows. Quartile analysis showed a higher concentration of these records in the states of Ceará, Bahia, Minas Gerais, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Rio Grande do Sul, as shown in Figure 3. This concentration may be related to the greater institutionalization of municipal clinical protocols that support nurses’ clinical decisions. The literature 26 corroborates this finding by highlighting the role of the “liaison nurse” as a key element in the effective coordination of healthcare networks, especially in referral and counter-referral processes.Regarding the prescription of diagnostic tests and therapeutic treatments (n=9,512,794), the results indicated greater expression in the states of Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul, suggesting better structural and organizational conditions, such as greater coverage of the Family Health Strategy (ESF, as per its acronym in Portuguese) and technical training capacity. On the other hand, the results regarding the prescription of medications by nurses (n=37,212) were relatively low compared to the volume of consultations and referrals. Although the PNAB authorizes nurses to prescribe, the implementation of this competency depends on local protocols, leading to disparities between states. Figure 3 shows a higher incidence of prescriptions in the states of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo, Minas Gerais, Goiás, and Paraná. Previous studies 9 ),( 14 ),( 27 indicate that nurses feel prepared and recognize prescribing as an advance in professional autonomy, provided it is supported by technical regulations. Therefore, the low national figures for nurse prescribing may be related to the absence or outdated nature of municipal protocols, legal uncertainty, and institutional barriers. It should be noted that prescribing medications in the context of Advanced Nursing Practice in PHC represents an advance in line with the principles of comprehensive and effective care 9 ),( 14 . In this context, the ICN recommends the inclusion of drug prescription within the scope of action of ANP, at a global level, provided that it is accompanied by specific training and regulation, as well as institutional support 8 . In Europe, the implementation of ANP varies greatly, with only 11 of the 35 countries in the pan-European region having formal legislation on the subject 28 . There is still considerable variability in the definition of ANP, especially regarding nomenclature, scope of action, regulation, educational requirements for exercising the function, and financing strategies 28 , which compromises its implementation. In countries such as France, for example, the ambiguity of roles, combined with uncertainty regarding the financing model and institutional support, hinders the development of ANP, a scenario also seen in countries such as England, where the practice is widely established 29 )-( 30 . In Nordic and Oceanic countries, such as Australia, Finland, and Norway, there is greater standardization in the training, regulation, and recognition of ANP as strategic for health systems 31 . A European study highlights the importance of combating professional isolation through networking and mentoring as essential strategies for promoting the sustainability of the advanced practice nursing workforce 32 . In the region of the Americas, 64% of countries have implemented advanced nursing functions 33 . However, Latin American countries should increase investment in this strategy 14 ),( 34 , valuing dialogue between stakeholders 35 .In contexts where discussion about ANP is still incipient, although they consider it a promising initiative 36 )-( 37 , it is essential to strengthen the educational, political, and institutional foundations of nursing to ensure the sustainable and effective introduction of advanced practice 38 . Additionally, continuing education was considered a key factor in fostering confidence in the performance of advanced practice nursing, as demonstrated in studies that analyzed the type of educational intervention over the course of implementation 39 . In the Brazilian case, it is precisely the educational base that should become the focus of strategic actio…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionThis ecological study provides a national overview of the distribution and intensity of nursing clinical actions in primary health care. Although it does not allow for inferring the complexity of clinical reasoning or for characterizing advanced competencies as defined by the ICN, the patterns observed reveal a robust field of practice in which nursing plays a central role in care and accumulates experience that can support structural advances.The identified territorial heterogeneity indicates the influence of organizational capacities, infrastructure, and the availability of professionals, highlighting areas that require strengthening and capacity building. In addition, the presence of more than 100,000 nurses working in PHC, associated with a solid educational structure and a consolidated critical mass at the academic and professional postgraduate levels, constitutes a strategic scenario for the development of advanced training programs, including Professional Master’s programs oriented toward expanded clinical practice and aligned with the needs of the SUS.The findings point to concrete ways to improve nursing clinical practice in Brazil, including improving health information recording systems, standardizing coding, harmonizing protocols, and conducting qualitative and mixed-methods studies to deepen understanding of the decision-making processes and conditions that shape professional autonomy in PHC. By offering empirical evidence on the clinical work of nurses on a national scale, this study contributes to strategic debates on strengthening and expanding the clinical scope, reinforcing the relevance of measures that advance toward the regulation and recognition of nursing autonomy and clinical authority, which are central elements for the effectiveness and sustainability of primary health care in Brazil.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionThe reconfiguration of the health workforce has intensified amid service overload, insufficient resources, a shortage of professionals, and increased demand driven by an aging population, the growth of chronic diseases, and recent pandemics. Progress toward Universal Health Coverage requires not only the strengthening of health systems, but also the mobilization of a skilled workforce capable of responding to the complex needs of the population 1 )-( 2 .Nurses have been playing an increasingly strategic role, especially at the primary levels of health care, where comprehensive and longitudinal care is essential 3 .The strengthening of the profession through investment in training, regulation, and the expansion of the scope of practice has been identified by international organizations as essential to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and health equity. The World Health Organization (WHO) report State of the World’s Nursing 2025 highlights the strategic importance of nursing in achieving universal health coverage and recommends, among other measures, strengthening professional training and adopting Advanced Nursing Practice (ANP) to respond to the growing demands of health systems 1 . In this regard, evidence shows that advanced practice nurses can achieve clinical outcomes comparable to those of physicians, with high levels of patient satisfaction, especially in primary health care (PHC) 4 .Although ANP originated in the United States in the 1960s, the concept developed and gained relevance in countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia in the late 20th century, and has more recently spread to low- and middle-income countries. Its international adoption has been gradual and uneven across countries and regions, marked by persistent challenges such as role ambiguity, legal barriers, and institutional resistance 5 )-( 6 .Internationally, reviews indicate that the transition of nurses to advanced roles in PHC is influenced by factors such as clarity of scope, stakeholder support, and the quality of interprofessional relationships 7 )-( 8 . Furthermore, considered a promising model for expanding access to and improving the effectiveness of health services, initially conceived for areas with a shortage of physicians and high demand for ongoing care, the authority to prescribe medications occupies a central place, as it represents both an expansion of the clinical scope and a symbolic milestone of professional recognition 8 , among other competencies that characterize the work of advanced practice nurses.The International Council of Nurses (ICN) 8 defines ANP as an expanded level of practice characterized by advanced clinical skills, more complex diagnostic judgment, autonomous decision-making, and authority to prescribe, order tests, and make referrals 8 )-( 9 . Associated with the legal framework governing professional practice and regulations issued by the professional council 13 , these duties constitute an expanded clinical scope, which has concrete intersections with the competencies described by the ICN 8 , even though it lacks formal certification in advanced practice and a specific regulatory framework for this professional category 14 .Actions representing nurses’ autonomy and authority, compatible with the practice of ANP, have been little explored in the Brazilian literature 14 . Considering the potential of ANP to strengthen health systems and the growing demand from nurses for greater clinical autonomy, it is essential to analyze how this practice has manifested in specific contexts, such as Brazil. Thus, autonomy is discussed in light of the legal and ethical foundations that should guide the scope of advanced nursing practices in Brazil. Therefore, investigating key aspects, such as diagnostic authority and prescriptive responsibilities in the context of PHC, can help identify which clinical competencies nurses most frequently exercise, even in the absence of specific regulations for ANP. These data may be fundamental to support, among other developments, the updating of the National Curriculum Guidelines for undergraduate nursing programs, as well as to improve graduate programs and align professional training with the real demands of PHC. In addition, this analysis can strengthen the evidence base necessary for the consolidation of ANP in Brazil, promoting greater recognition, appreciation, and autonomy for nursing.This study aimed to analyze representative actions of autonomy and clinical authority of nurses in primary health care, compatible with Advanced Nursing Practice in Brazil. The conceptual framework used in the study allowed establishing a correspondence between internationally recognized clinical competencies and the duties assigned to nurses by the law governing professional practice and by the PNAB 12 , which, through municipal protocols and regulations, authorize the conduct of consultations, the request of diagnostic tests, the prescription of medications, and referrals. full_text_excerpt: AbstractObjective: this study analyzed representative actions indicating autonomy and clinical authority among nurses in primary health care, compatible with Advanced Nursing Practice in Brazil. Method: the ecological study used secondary data from 2023 from the Brazilian Ministry of Health’s information system, covering all 26 states and the Federal District. Results: the results reveal a wide range of activities performed by nurses in areas characteristic of Advanced Nursing Practice, while also showing significant geographical inequality, predominantly in the Southeast and South regions. Conclusion: the analysis reveals the effective exercise of advanced competencies, even without specific regulations, and highlights the need for public policies that promote specialized training, regulatory standardization, and the legal recognition of Advanced Nursing Practice to improve the quality and equity of health care.Descriptors: Primary Health Care, Professional Autonomy, Nursing, Ecological Study, Advanced Nursing Practice, Health Policies Highlights: (1) The results show that Advanced Nursing Practice is already being implemented in routine health services. Indicators related to consultations, medication prescriptions, diagnostic tests, and clinical referrals were examined. (2) 52 million nursing consultations; 37,000 medication prescriptions. (3) 9.5 million diagnostic tests prescribed and 83 million clinical referrals. (4) Effective performance of advanced practices, even without specific regulations. (5) Fertile ground for establishing Professional Master’s programs in Advanced Nursing Practice, aligned with SUS and ICN. full_text: BACKGROUND Aedes vittatus, an emerging invasive species and arboviral vector with high ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity, is expanding in the Caribbean, being detected in the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Jamaica and recently in Yucatán, Mexico.OBJECTIVESThis study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti.METHODSLarval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti. Specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding.FINDINGSWe report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Ae. (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico. Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Culex garciai and Culex interrogator in Haiti.MAIN CONCLUSIONSGiven its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study area - The survey was conducted in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti, restricted to the extensive, low-elevation coastal zones of both regions. Following the 2010 earthquake that struck the Port-au-Prince area, the North department experienced the arrival of more than 2.3 million people, resulting in rapid and largely unplanned urban expansion, increasing the suitable area for urban mosquitoes.( 6 ) This department is therefore densely populated (500 inhabitants/km2), in contrast to the Northeast, where population density is approximately 240 inhabitants/km2. The climate varies from tropical monsoon (North Department) to tropical savanna (Northeast Department), with mean annual temperatures of 24 to 28oC and seasonal rainfall (April to November), averaging between 1,000 and 1,500 mm per year, with a decreasing gradient from the coast toward the interior.The study area, located mainly within the coastal plains surrounding the departmental capital, Cap-Haïtien, extends from Limbé (19o42’N, 72o24’W) in the west to Ouanaminthe (19o29’N, 71o46’W), located on the Dominican border, 75 km east of Limbé, following the coastal fringe and reaching up to 20 km inland. It is characterised by moderately low relief, with most of the coastline and its surroundings lying at elevations generally below 100 m in urban and peri-urban zones. Mosquito sampling - Between October 7 and October 31, 2025, during the latter part of the rainy season, surveys were conducted in urban, peri-urban and rural areas across both departments. A total of 23 larval habitats were collected in 18 localities within 12 communes (seven in the North and five in the Northeast) (Fig. 1). Sampling time did not exceed 3 h per commune. Mosquito larvae were collected from peridomestic and public spaces. For each sample site, some collected larvae were mounted on slides, while others were reared to the adult stage, and both types of specimens were deposited in the ARIM-IRD collection.( 7 ) Geographical coordinates and data were uploaded to the GBIF platform.Fig. 1:location of the sampling sites. (A) Situation map of Haiti within Caribbean countries with presence (green area) and location of capture points (red dots) of Aedes vittatus in neighbouring countries; (B) Delimitation of study area in Haiti (blue rectangle) and location capture (red dots) of Ae. vittatus in Haiti and the Dominican Republic; (C) Location of the breeding site of Ae. vittatus in the study area (red dots) and other collection sites negative to Ae. vittatus (grey dots) (Table). Ethics statement - This study was conducted with authorisation from the Haitian Ministry of Environment, and the importation of mosquitoes from Haiti to France was approved by the Departmental Directorate for Population Protection (DDPP). Morphological and molecular identification - The invasive species Ae. vittatus was identified using European,( 8 ) African( 9 ) and Sahelian( 10 ) taxonomic keys, and confirmed with the species redescription of Huang.( 11 ) Five samples from the localities Quartier Morin (two adults: QUA003-Haiti06 and 07) and Lory, Milot (two adults: MIL001-Haiti08 and 09 and one larvae: MIL004LAV-10) were used for molecular identification. Mosquito DNA was extracted with the Qiagen Blood&tissue kit (Qiagen, Valencia, USA). Mosquitoes were individually homogenised with three metal beads in a Qiagen TissueLyserII at 30 Hz for 3 min. The remainder of the protocol followed the manufacturer’s instructions. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed in duplicate for each sample to validate the species identification through a universal invertebrate-specific primer pair LCO1490 (5′-GGT CAA CAA ATC ATA AAG ATA TTG G-3′) and HCO2198 (5′-TAA ACT TCA GGG TGA CCA AAA AAT CA-3′) to amplify a 658-bp fragment of the mitochondrial gene cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI).( 12 ) PCR reactions were performed in a total volume of 35 μL, containing 17.5 μL Invitrogen TM PlatinumTM Hot Start PCR 2X Master Mix, 0.35 μL of each primer, 9.8 μL of biology grade water, and 7 μL of DNA. PCR amplification products were sent to Macrogen (Macrogen Europe, Amsterdam, the Netherlands) for Sanger sequencing. A Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) analysis was conducted in the National Centre for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank database to explore species identification based on the amplified and sequenced molecular product.( 13 ) Sequence assembly, alignment and phylogenetic analyses - Forward and reverse reads of four samples, as one of the five samples (MIL004LAV-10) did not amplify, were assembled and edited to generate consensus sequences using CodonCode Aligner v12.0.4 (https://www.codoncode.com/aligner). Sequence alignments were performed with MAFFT v7 via the online server (https://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/server/) using default parameters.( 14 ) The resulting alignments were visually inspected and manually edited in AliView v1.28.( 15 ) The best-fit nucleotide substitution model was determined using jModelTest2 through the CIPRES Science Gateway (https://www.phylo.org/) under default settings.( 16 ) Mitochondrial sequences, including COI marker sequences of Aedes spp., were retrieved from GenBank (accession numbers provided in the phylogenetic tree). The dataset comprised sequences from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Caribbean, and a recently generated sequence from Mexico.Phylogenetic relationships among Ae. vittatus sequences were inferred using BEAST v1.10.5, applying a General Time Reversible substitution model+r returned by jModelTest2, a strict molecular clock, and a coalescent constant size tree prior. Psorophora ferox was designated as the outgroup.( 17 ) Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses were run for 10 million generations, with trees sampled every 100 generations. Effective sample sizes (ESS) were assessed using Tracer v 1.7.2,( 18 ) with values > 200 considered adequate. Convergence and stationarity were assessed by examining parameter traces, and the first 25% of samples were discarded as burn-in prior to summarising posterior probabilities. The final phylogenetic tree was visualised and edited using FigTree v1.4.4.( 19 ) Network analysis - Analyses at the intraspecific level were performed on datasets that encompassed only Ae. vittatus sequences. The genetic differentiation between specimens belonging to the major phylogroups inferred by the phylogenetic analyses of the combined dataset was assessed for each COI gene using DnaSP v.6.12.03.( 20 ) Haplotype networks were constructed using the median-joining method,( 21 ) which has the ability to deal with missing data as well as to infer ancestral haplotypes. This method also performs well against or outperforms other network approaches.( 22 ) It was implemented using the software PopART v1.7,( 23 ) with epsilon value set to 0 in order to minimise alternative median networks. The resulting networks were visualised and edited in Inkscape v1.2.2 (https://inkscape.org/). RESULTSDuring the sampling period, Ae. vittatus was detected in eight of the 23 sites (34.7%) across six municipalities in northern Haiti: Cap-Haïtien, Quartier Morin, Milot, Limbé, Trou du Nord, and Terrier Rouge (Table). The species was found alone in three of these sites and co-occurred with Ae. albopictus (three sites) and Ae. aegypti (two sites). Breeding habitats included diverse peridomestic and public environments across urban, peri-urban, and rural settings, such as water storage containers, groundwater accumulations, poultry waterers, wastewater channels, puddles, and tree root cavities. These habitats were generally devoid of vegetation and varied in water volume and organic content. Eight additional mosquito species were recorded, including Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex garciai, Culex interrogator, Culex nigripalpus, Psorophora confinnis and Psorophora pygmaea. diagnostic characters for the principal life stages for Ae. vittatus are summarised as follows (Fig. 2).Fig. 2: Aedes vittatus: morphological characteristics of the larval stage. (A) Detail of abdominal segments VIII-X (the long anal papillae are missing); (B) head showing single setae 5-C and 6-C (arrows); (C) mentum; (D) comb VIII with eight spines; (E) detail of the pecten teeth with two or three denticles; (F) atypical pecten with the rare presence of two teeth (instead of one, arrows) inserted distal to the 1-S setae. Female - Head with a dark proboscis with a median scattering of pale yellowish scales. Thorax: scutum with acrostichal setae; three pairs of distinct, small, white spots of narrow scales on the anterior two-thirds of the scutum; scutellum with broad white scales on all three lobes; lower mesepimeral setae present. Legs: tibia with a median white ring, tarsomeres III-1-4 with large basal white bands, tarsomere III-5 entirely white. Abdomen: tergite I with a large median white spot. Male genitalia - Gonocoxite elongated, without basal and apical lobes. The gonostyle has a very characteristic shape, strongly enlarged and globose at its tip, with a long, strongly curved apical spine located at the base of the globose part. The claspette is large, with a narrow base, and distinctly swollen from its middle. Larva (Fig. 2) - Head: setae 5-C single or sometimes double, 6-C single. Abdomen: setae 6-I-IV usually with two long branches; pecten with 19-25 very closely spaced spines, with 3-4 basal denticles; only the most distal spine (rarely two) more widely spaced and implanted beyond seta 1-S; comb of eight (6-10) scales in a single irregular row; saddle incomplete without marginal spicules; 1-X single, 2-X with 5 branches; four precratal setae; anal papillae long, about four times as long as saddle, slender and tapered. Molecular identification - Morphological identification was confirmed with COI-based DNA barcoding. The Ae. vittatus specimens (Haiti_06, Haiti_07, Haiti_08, Haiti_09) clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico).( 3 , 5 (24-27) In the haplotype network, they share closely related haplotypes separated by only a small number of mutations, suggesting a high level of genetic similarity within this group, particularly with Mexican populations( 5 ) (Fig. 3). This Caribbean/American cluster appeared distinct from African haplotypes and from most Asian haplotypes, which form separate groups within the network. The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction. The COI-based DNA barcoding confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Cx. garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study. Sequences of Ae. vittatus were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers PZ344144, PZ344145, PZ344146 and PZ344147. Sequences of Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Cx. garciai, Cx. interrogator, Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ps. pygmaea have been deposited under accession numbers PZ878903, PZ878904, PZ878905, PZ878906, PZ878907, PZ878908, PZ878909, PZ878910, PZ878911.Fig. 3:haplotype network and phylogenetic tree resulting from the analysis of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI) dataset. The haplotype network reconstruction considers missing data and gap. Values between parentheses on nodes indicate the inferred number of mutation steps between haplotypes or ancestral haplotypes (symbolised by a black node). The phylogenetic tree corresponds to the results of a Bayesian inference analysis (see text for details). DISCUSSIONSpecies identification was confirmed morphologically and by COI-based DNA barcoding. Haitian Ae. vittatus specimens clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, Dominican Republic, and Mexico) and were clearly distinct from African and most Asian lineages (Fig. 3). This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.Its absence from earlier surveys in 2013,( 6 ) combined with its detection in the Dominican Republic in 2019,( 3 ) is consistent with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Passive transport via water holding containers and other goods may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown. Passive transport via water-holding goods is a well-documented pathway for mosquito invasions, and the species’ desiccation-resistant eggs further enhance its dispersal potential. Genetic similarity with recently detected Mexican populations( 5 ) suggests strong regional connectivity, although the direction of spread remains unclear. Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.Current socio-environmental conditions in Haiti, including population displacement, informal settlements, inadequate water infrastructure, and unmanaged waste, favour the proliferation of container-breeding mosquitoes and may provide favourable conditions for the establishment of Ae. vittatus. Psorophora ferox was designated as the outgroup.( 17 ) Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses were run for 10 million generations, with trees sampled every 100 generations. Effective sample sizes (ESS) were assessed using Tracer v 1.7.2,( 18 ) with values > 200 considered adequate. Convergence and stationarity were assessed by examining parameter traces, and the first 25% of samples were discarded as burn-in prior to summarising posterior probabilities. The final phylogenetic tree was visualised and edited using FigTree v1.4.4.( 19 ) Network analysis - Analyses at the intraspecific level were performed on datasets that encompassed only Ae. vittatus sequences. The genetic differentiation between specimens belonging to the major phylogroups inferred by the phylogenetic analyses of the combined dataset was assessed for each COI gene using DnaSP v.6.12.03.( 20 ) Haplotype networks were constructed using the median-joining method,( 21 ) which has the ability to deal with missing data as well as to infer ancestral haplotypes. This method also performs well against or outperforms other network approaches.( 22 ) It was implemented using the software PopART v1.7,( 23 ) with epsilon value set to 0 in order to minimise alternative median networks. The resulting networks were visualised and edited in Inkscape v1.2.2 (https://inkscape.org/).
full_text_sections.results: RESULTSDuring the sampling period, Ae. vittatus was detected in eight of the 23 sites (34.7%) across six municipalities in northern Haiti: Cap-Haïtien, Quartier Morin, Milot, Limbé, Trou du Nord, and Terrier Rouge (Table). The species was found alone in three of these sites and co-occurred with Ae. albopictus (three sites) and Ae. aegypti (two sites). Breeding habitats included diverse peridomestic and public environments across urban, peri-urban, and rural settings, such as water storage containers, groundwater accumulations, poultry waterers, wastewater channels, puddles, and tree root cavities. These habitats were generally devoid of vegetation and varied in water volume and organic content. Eight additional mosquito species were recorded, including Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Culex quinquefasciatus, Culex garciai, Culex interrogator, Culex nigripalpus, Psorophora confinnis and Psorophora pygmaea. diagnostic characters for the principal life stages for Ae. vittatus are summarised as follows (Fig. 2).Fig. 2: Aedes vittatus: morphological characteristics of the larval stage. (A) Detail of abdominal segments VIII-X (the long anal papillae are missing); (B) head showing single setae 5-C and 6-C (arrows); (C) mentum; (D) comb VIII with eight spines; (E) detail of the pecten teeth with two or three denticles; (F) atypical pecten with the rare presence of two teeth (instead of one, arrows) inserted distal to the 1-S setae. Female - Head with a dark proboscis with a median scattering of pale yellowish scales. Thorax: scutum with acrostichal setae; three pairs of distinct, small, white spots of narrow scales on the anterior two-thirds of the scutum; scutellum with broad white scales on all three lobes; lower mesepimeral setae present. Legs: tibia with a median white ring, tarsomeres III-1-4 with large basal white bands, tarsomere III-5 entirely white. Abdomen: tergite I with a large median white spot. Male genitalia - Gonocoxite elongated, without basal and apical lobes. The gonostyle has a very characteristic shape, strongly enlarged and globose at its tip, with a long, strongly curved apical spine located at the base of the globose part. The claspette is large, with a narrow base, and distinctly swollen from its middle. Larva (Fig. 2) - Head: setae 5-C single or sometimes double, 6-C single. Abdomen: setae 6-I-IV usually with two long branches; pecten with 19-25 very closely spaced spines, with 3-4 basal denticles; only the most distal spine (rarely two) more widely spaced and implanted beyond seta 1-S; comb of eight (6-10) scales in a single irregular row; saddle incomplete without marginal spicules; 1-X single, 2-X with 5 branches; four precratal setae; anal papillae long, about four times as long as saddle, slender and tapered. Molecular identification - Morphological identification was confirmed with COI-based DNA barcoding. The Ae. vittatus specimens (Haiti_06, Haiti_07, Haiti_08, Haiti_09) clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico).( 3 , 5 (24-27) In the haplotype network, they share closely related haplotypes separated by only a small number of mutations, suggesting a high level of genetic similarity within this group, particularly with Mexican populations( 5 ) (Fig. 3). This Caribbean/American cluster appeared distinct from African haplotypes and from most Asian haplotypes, which form separate groups within the network. The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction. The COI-based DNA barcoding confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Cx. garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study. Sequences of Ae. vittatus were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers PZ344144, PZ344145, PZ344146 and PZ344147. Sequences of Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, Cx. garciai, Cx. interrogator, Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ps. pygmaea have been deposited under accession numbers PZ878903, PZ878904, PZ878905, PZ878906, PZ878907, PZ878908, PZ878909, PZ878910, PZ878911.Fig. 3:haplotype network and phylogenetic tree resulting from the analysis of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I barcoding region (COI) dataset. The haplotype network reconstruction considers missing data and gap. Values between parentheses on nodes indicate the inferred number of mutation steps between haplotypes or ancestral haplotypes (symbolised by a black node). The phylogenetic tree corresponds to the results of a Bayesian inference analysis (see text for details).
full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONSpecies identification was confirmed morphologically and by COI-based DNA barcoding. Haitian Ae. vittatus specimens clustered with Caribbean and American haplotypes (Cuba, Jamaica, Dominican Republic, and Mexico) and were clearly distinct from African and most Asian lineages (Fig. 3). This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Detection of Ae. vittatus in one-third of the sampled habitats and half of the surveyed communes, despite limited sampling, indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.Its absence from earlier surveys in 2013,( 6 ) combined with its detection in the Dominican Republic in 2019,( 3 ) is consistent with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Passive transport via water holding containers and other goods may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown. Passive transport via water-holding goods is a well-documented pathway for mosquito invasions, and the species’ desiccation-resistant eggs further enhance its dispersal potential. Genetic similarity with recently detected Mexican populations( 5 ) suggests strong regional connectivity, although the direction of spread remains unclear. Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.Current socio-environmental conditions in Haiti, including population displacement, informal settlements, inadequate water infrastructure, and unmanaged waste, favour the proliferation of container-breeding mosquitoes and may provide favourable conditions for the establishment of Ae. vittatus. The species exhibits high ecological plasticity, colonising a wide range of artificial and natural habitats. Its tolerance to desiccation, salinity, and high temperatures further enhances its invasion potential.( 28 ) Co-occurrence with Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus raises questions about interspecific interactions and future ecological dynamics in urban environments. Notably, we also reported Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator from Haiti for the first time. Morphological identification of Cx. interrogator was supported by molecular results, showing high sequence identity but lower query coverage, likely reflecting partial sequences or trimming.From a public health perspective, Ae. vittatus is competent for multiple arboviruses, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever.( 29 , 30 ) Its establishment adds complexity to Haiti’s epidemiologic context, which already includes endemic dengue, recurrent chikungunya outbreaks, and ongoing malaria and filariasis transmission. Notably, ecological niche models suggest that Ae. vittatus could find year-round suitable conditions across coastal regions of the Gulf of Mexico and extend into the southern Atlantic states of the United States, as well as large areas of Mexico and Central America.( 31 ) This potential geographic suitability highlights the possibility of further spread into North America, Central and South America and underscores the need for strengthened surveillance and preparedness beyond the Caribbean.Our findings provide the first confirmed record of Ae. vittatus in Haiti and demonstrate its presence in multiple locations. Further surveillance is needed to determine its distribution, extent of establishment, ecological interactions, and potential contribution to arbovirus transmission in the region and beyond.
full_text_sections.other: REVIEWER #1The abstract adequately summarizes the study and highlights the first detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti. This finding fills an important geographical gap and has clear relevance for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas. The manuscript should avoid strong conclusions, as these interpretations are based on limited sampling and a single mitochondrial marker. Inconsistencies in dates and sites / localities should also be corrected. References are generally relevant and updated, but their formatting should be standardized. AUTHORS’ RESPONSE TO THE REVIEWERSDear Prof. Ricardo Lourenço-de-Oliveira and Maria Clara Carvalho:We are pleased to submit the letter of response to the referees for the manuscript entitled “Aedes vittatus in Haiti: continued expansion across the Caribbean and implications for the Americas” for consideration in Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz, on behalf of my co-authors. Here are our point-by-point responses. The comments are in bold and our responses are in regular text in blue. We have added the modifications to a track changes version of the manuscript in red.Reviewer comments:The abstract adequately summarizes the study and highlights the first detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti. This finding fills an important geographical gap and has clear relevance for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas.We sincerely thank you for your positive and constructive and positive comments. We are pleased that you find the study relevant and that the detection of Aedes vittatus in Haiti fills an important geographical gap for mosquito surveillance in the Caribbean and the Americas.The manuscript should avoid strong conclusions, as these interpretations are based on limited sampling and a single mitochondrial marker.We agree and we have moderated the strength of our conclusions throughout the manuscript, particularly in the Abstract and Discussion, to better reflect the limitations of our study, including the relatively limited sampling effort and the use of a single mitochondrial marker (COI). We now explicitly acknowledge these limitations and clarify that our interpretations regarding establishment, regional expansion and spread should be considered with caution.In the abstract, we changed for: “We report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Aedes (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico.” (lines 31-34). Also in the main conclusion of the abstract: “Given its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed.” (lines 35-36).In the results, we substitute the sentence: “The results support a common Asian-rather than African or European origin with regional spread in the Caribbean.”, with “The observed pattern is consistent with the Caribbean/American lineage being genetically distinct from African and most Asian haplotypes, although the limited number of specimens and the use of a single mitochondrial marker preclude firm conclusions about the geographic origin or pathways of introduction.” (lines 172-176).In the conclusion, we substitute: “This pattern supports a shared regional origin and spread within the Caribbean rather than multiple independent introductions from the Old World.”, for “This pattern is consistent with a shared regional genetic background within the Caribbean/American group, although more molecular markers, more populations and specimens are needed to confirm this hypothesis.” (lines 182-184). Also, ”.. indicates that the species is present at multiple localities in northern Haiti. However, given the limited sampling effort, further surveys are needed to assess its wider distribution and establish the extent of its establishment.” (lines 185-188).Also, we changed “...is compatible with a relatively recent arrival on Hispaniola. However, the available data do not allow us to determine the timing or pathway of introduction. Human-mediated transport may have contributed to its spread, but the relative importance of each introduction pathway remains unknown” (lines 190-193).Importantly, we added the sentence: “Additional sampling across Haiti and the use of nuclear and/or genomic markers will be necessary to clarify the distribution, population structure and introduction pathways of the species.” (lines 197-199).Also: “and may provide favorable conditions for the establishment” (line 202), and also: “This potential geographic suitability highlights the possibility of further spread into North America, Central and South America and underscores the value for strengthened surveillance and preparedness beyond the Caribbean.” (lines 215-217).And, finally: “Our findings provide the first confirmed record of Aedes vittatus in Haiti and demonstrate its presence in multiple locations. Further surveillance is needed to determine its distribution, extent of establishment,...” (lines 218-220).Inconsistencies in dates and sites / localities should also be corrected.We have carefully checked and corrected inconsistencies in dates and sampling locations to ensure accuracy and coherence across the manuscript (e.g., sampling period until 31 October 2025 but identifications of Ae. vittatus between 7 and 24 of October). Also the number of localities and municipalities listed in Table I).We have revised in the abstract “Larval surveys were done across 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and North-East departments of Haiti” (Lines 28-29).In Results: “During the sampling period, Ae. vittatus was detected in 8 of 23 sites (34.7%) across..” (lines 137-138).We added also more molecular identifications of other mosquito species, two species that are reported for the first time in Haiti.In the abstract: “Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator in Haiti.”In results: “The COI sequencing confirmed the identification of Ps. pygmaea, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus and Cx. interrogator, with the latter showing high similarity to GenBank reference sequences (99.67% identity; MT999299.1). For Culex garciai, no reference sequences are currently available in GenBank; therefore, we generated the first COI sequences for this species in this study.“(lines 178-182).We have also added some clarifications, regarding the molecular work. In material: “...as one of the five samples did not amplify,..” (line107).In the discussion: “Notably, we also reported Cx. garciai and Cx. interrogator from Haiti for the first time. Morphological identification of Cx. interrogator was supported by molecular results, showing high sequence identity but lower query coverage, likely reflecting partial sequences or trimming. (lines 215-218).References are generally relevant and updated, but their formatting should be standardized.We have carefully reviewed and standardized the formatting of all references according to the journal guidelines. The reference list has been thoroughly checked for consistency in authors’ names, journal abbreviations, publication details, page ranges, and DOI formatting. All changes made to the references are indicated in red in the revised manuscript.We believe these revisions have improved the clarity and rigor of the manuscript, and we thank you again for your helpful feedback.Sincerely,David Roiz, in behalf of the authors REVIEWER #1No comments.
