full_text: AbstractBACKGROUNDLa Crosse encephalitis (LACE), caused by La Crosse virus (LACV), is the leading cause of reported cases of pediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States. However, mosquito-borne disease control capacity in Western North Carolina (WNC), where LACE is endemic, is poorly known.METHODSWe administered an electronic survey to communicable disease nurses (CDNs), environmental health specialists (EHS), and health directors in 10 WNC health departments with the highest reported incidence of LACE. The survey evaluated mosquito-borne disease knowledge and surveillance and control capacity based on respondent public health roles.RESULTSResponses were received from all surveyed health departments. A total of 47 public health professionals (16 CDNs, 23 EHS, and 8 health directors) completed the survey, resulting in a 36.7% response rate. One (10%) department was rated as “fully capable” based on national mosquito surveillance and control standards. Respondents identified gaps in knowledge of case definitions, serology interpretation, environmental and behavioral risk factors, and vector control capacity. Although most participants recognized the importance of preventing and controlling mosquito-borne disease, assessments of response capabilities varied by respondent job role.LIMITATIONSThis study was limited by sample size, moderate response rate, timing of the assessment, and reliance on self-reported data. Variability in job roles may have influenced how questions were interpreted.CONCLUSIONSThis study serves as a foundational assessment of mosquito-borne disease control capacity among health departments in WNC, where LACE remains a public health concern. Our findings highlight the need for improved preparedness through education and resources, and the findings also support a regional approach to strengthen prevention, detection, and response efforts.Keywords: La Crosse, encephalitis, mosquito, surveillance, vector-borne disease, Michael Ratliff, Sarah Brill Thach, Amy Lanou, Carl Williams, Brian Byrd MethodsThis study employed a cross-sectional survey to assess knowledge of vector-borne diseases and control capacity in 10 county-based health departments in WNC (Figure 1). These counties had the highest cumulative incidence of La Crosse encephalitis between 2000 and 2020.7 The primary data collection tool was an electronic survey developed using SurveyMonkey© software (San Mateo, CA). The survey contained 80 total items, including a combination of core questions administered to all participants and role-specific questions tailored to health directors, environmental health specialists, or communicable disease nurses. No individual respondent completed more than 32 questions. The full survey instrument is available from the corresponding author upon request.Figure 1.A) Map of the Study Area: Participating Western North Carolina Counties with the Highest Cumulative Incidence of Neuroinvasive La Crosse Virus Disease, 2000–2020; B) Respondents’ Ratings of Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne Disease CasesFigure note. Preparedness was assessed on a 7-point scale: 1 = extremely prepared and 7 = extremely unprepared. Respondents (N = 46) included local county health directors (HD, n = 8), communicable disease nurses (CDN, n = 16) and environmental health specialists (EHS, n = 22).A map of the state of turkey AI-generated content may be incorrect.The survey assessed vector-borne disease knowledge, perceptions of public health relevance, and existing mosquito surveillance and control capacity. Survey content assessing control capacity was structured around core and supplemental competencies recognized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and adapted from the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) framework for mosquito control programs.5 Because LACV is the most common mosquito-borne pathogen causing human disease in WNC, the scope of the survey was primarily focused on LACV and mosquito-borne disease response instead of other vector-borne diseases.The Office of Human Research Ethics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill determined that this study did not meet the federal definition of human subjects research [45 CFR 46.102(e) or (l); 21 CFR 56.102(c), (e), or (l)] and therefore did not require Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval.Participants included health department directors, communicable disease nurses (CDNs), and registered environmental health specialists or interns (EHS). These specific job roles were selected as they have clearly defined roles as part of the public health response to “arboviral encephalitis/meningitis” as described in the local health department investigation steps within the North Carolina Communicable Disease Manual.22 Potential respondents were identified through a review of health department websites, the North Carolina State Board of Environmental Health Specialist Examiners registry, and professional contacts. The survey was distributed via email to 128 verified email addresses (10 health department directors, 18 CDNs, and 100 EHS). The survey remained open for 4 weeks (February 2024–March 2024), during which two reminder emails and follow-up phone calls were used to encourage participation.Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and contingency tables to compare vector-borne disease preparedness across roles. Basic data analyses (e.g., descriptive and summary statistics) were performed within the SurveyMonkey© website directly or exported to a .csv file for analyses using R/RStudio.23 Confidence intervals were calculated using the exact binomial method. Significance was defined a priori as P < .05 for all statistical tests. For paired ranking data, a global Friedman test was conducted first. When the Friedman test was statistically significant, pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed. Data visualizations and graphs were created using ggplot2 in R/RStudio.24 ResultsResponse RatesThe survey was distributed via email to 128 public health staff across 10 WNC local health departments. Of these, 62 individuals initiated the survey, and 60 individuals acknowledged the consent statement and identified their professional role as either a health director, environmental health specialist (EHS), or communicable disease nurse (CDN). Within individual counties, the number of respondents initiating the survey ranged from 2 to 12, (median: 6; mean: 6.7). A total of 47 participants completed the survey in full, resulting in an overall response rate of 36.7%. Public health personnel from all 10 health departments completed the survey, including 8 health directors, 23 EHS personnel, and 16 CDNs (the CDNs include 2 respondents that identified as public health nurses with communicable disease reporting or investigation responsibilities). Overall survey completion rates for specific job roles varied (80% of health directors, 23% of EHS, and 84.2% of CDNs); because individuals were allowed to skip questions during the survey, the responses to any single question may not equal the total number of participants.Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne DiseasesRespondents ranked their health department’s level of preparedness to respond to mosquito-borne disease cases, where 1 = extremely prepared, 2 = very prepared, 3 = somewhat prepared, 4 = unsure, 5 = somewhat unprepared, 6 = very unprepared, and 7 = extremely unprepared. Overall (N = 46), the median response was 3 (somewhat prepared) (mean: 3.63; range 2–7) (Figure 1). Although health directors responded more favorably (median: 2.5; mean: 2.9; range 2–5) and EHS personnel responded less favorably (median: 4; mean: 4.3; range 2–7), these differences were not statistically significant.Perceived Relative Importance of Mosquito-Borne DiseasesRespondents ranked selected mosquito-borne diseases in order of importance (public health relevance) for their respective counties (Figure 2). The choices included the following endemic and travel-related mosquito-borne diseases: eastern equine encephalitis, chikungunya virus disease, La Crosse encephalitis, malaria, St. Louis encephalitis, West Nile encephalitis, and Zika virus disease; the default order choice in the survey was alphabetical. La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) was overall ranked as the most important mosquito-borne disease of public health relevance (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction, P < .01). Other endemic arboviral diseases, EEE and West Nile encephalitis, were ranked second and third, respectively, in terms of public health importance. This trend was consistent when evaluated by professional job category; however, pairwise comparisons were not significantly different for LACE and EEE (P > .05) for health directors, CDNs, or EHS. Pairwise comparisons suggest that LACE was ranked higher than the remaining mosquito-borne diseases by CDNs and EHS personnel; the small sample size for health directors limits statistical inference.Figure 2.Ranked Importance of Selected Mosquito-Borne DiseasesFigure note. Respondent rankings (1 = most important, 7 = least important), of seven travel-related or endemic mosquito-borne diseases in order of public health relevance. Rankings are presented collectively (A) and by personnel job type (B–D). Ranked choices included eastern equine encephalitis (EEE), chikungunya virus disease (CVD), La Crosse encephalitis (LACE), malaria, St. Louis encephalitis (SLE), West Nile encephalitis (WNE), and Zika virus disease (ZVD).A diagram of a health care worker AI-generated content may be incorrect.Mosquito Surveillance and Control CapacityHealth department directors and EHS personnel reported their respective health department’s mosquito surveillance and control capacities (Table 1) in the context of a comprehensive evidence-based mosquito control program using standards developed by NACCHO and the CDC. The 5 core capacities developed by NACCHO include 1) routine surveillance, standardized trapping, and identifications; 2) treatment decisions using surveillance data; 3) larviciding, adulticiding, or both; 4) routine vector control; and 5) pesticide resistance testing. The percentage of health departments reporting existing capacity for the individual core standards ranged from 10% to 40%, with one county reporting existing capacity for all 5 core standards. The most common standard (i.e., treatment decisions using surveillance data) existed in 40% of the counties; 20% of counties reported routine surveillance or routine vector control. A single county reported pesticide resistance testing. Health departments reporting existing capacity for the individual supplemental standards ranged from 10% to 50%. The most common supplemental capacity (community outreach and education activities) was reported in 50% of the counties. A single health director reported “in house” personnel with a pesticide applicator’s license. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractBACKGROUNDLa Crosse encephalitis (LACE), caused by La Crosse virus (LACV), is the leading cause of reported cases of pediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States. However, mosquito-borne disease control capacity in Western North Carolina (WNC), where LACE is endemic, is poorly known.METHODSWe administered an electronic survey to communicable disease nurses (CDNs), environmental health specialists (EHS), and health directors in 10 WNC health departments with the highest reported incidence of LACE. The survey evaluated mosquito-borne disease knowledge and surveillance and control capacity based on respondent public health roles.RESULTSResponses were received from all surveyed health departments. A total of 47 public health professionals (16 CDNs, 23 EHS, and 8 health directors) completed the survey, resulting in a 36.7% response rate. One (10%) department was rated as “fully capable” based on national mosquito surveillance and control standards. Respondents identified gaps in knowledge of case definitions, serology interpretation, environmental and behavioral risk factors, and vector control capacity. Although most participants recognized the importance of preventing and controlling mosquito-borne disease, assessments of response capabilities varied by respondent job role.LIMITATIONSThis study was limited by sample size, moderate response rate, timing of the assessment, and reliance on self-reported data. Variability in job roles may have influenced how questions were interpreted.CONCLUSIONSThis study serves as a foundational assessment of mosquito-borne disease control capacity among health departments in WNC, where LACE remains a public health concern. Our findings highlight the need for improved preparedness through education and resources, and the findings also support a regional approach to strengthen prevention, detection, and response efforts.Keywords: La Crosse, encephalitis, mosquito, surveillance, vector-borne disease, Michael Ratliff, Sarah Brill Thach, Amy Lanou, Carl Williams, Brian Byrd
full_text_sections.methods: MethodsThis study employed a cross-sectional survey to assess knowledge of vector-borne diseases and control capacity in 10 county-based health departments in WNC (Figure 1). These counties had the highest cumulative incidence of La Crosse encephalitis between 2000 and 2020.7 The primary data collection tool was an electronic survey developed using SurveyMonkey© software (San Mateo, CA). The survey contained 80 total items, including a combination of core questions administered to all participants and role-specific questions tailored to health directors, environmental health specialists, or communicable disease nurses. No individual respondent completed more than 32 questions. The full survey instrument is available from the corresponding author upon request.Figure 1.A) Map of the Study Area: Participating Western North Carolina Counties with the Highest Cumulative Incidence of Neuroinvasive La Crosse Virus Disease, 2000–2020; B) Respondents’ Ratings of Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne Disease CasesFigure note. Preparedness was assessed on a 7-point scale: 1 = extremely prepared and 7 = extremely unprepared. Respondents (N = 46) included local county health directors (HD, n = 8), communicable disease nurses (CDN, n = 16) and environmental health specialists (EHS, n = 22).A map of the state of turkey AI-generated content may be incorrect.The survey assessed vector-borne disease knowledge, perceptions of public health relevance, and existing mosquito surveillance and control capacity. Survey content assessing control capacity was structured around core and supplemental competencies recognized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and adapted from the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) framework for mosquito control programs.5 Because LACV is the most common mosquito-borne pathogen causing human disease in WNC, the scope of the survey was primarily focused on LACV and mosquito-borne disease response instead of other vector-borne diseases.The Office of Human Research Ethics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill determined that this study did not meet the federal definition of human subjects research [45 CFR 46.102(e) or (l); 21 CFR 56.102(c), (e), or (l)] and therefore did not require Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval.Participants included health department directors, communicable disease nurses (CDNs), and registered environmental health specialists or interns (EHS). These specific job roles were selected as they have clearly defined roles as part of the public health response to “arboviral encephalitis/meningitis” as described in the local health department investigation steps within the North Carolina Communicable Disease Manual.22 Potential respondents were identified through a review of health department websites, the North Carolina State Board of Environmental Health Specialist Examiners registry, and professional contacts. The survey was distributed via email to 128 verified email addresses (10 health department directors, 18 CDNs, and 100 EHS). The survey remained open for 4 weeks (February 2024–March 2024), during which two reminder emails and follow-up phone calls were used to encourage participation.Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and contingency tables to compare vector-borne disease preparedness across roles. Basic data analyses (e.g., descriptive and summary statistics) were performed within the SurveyMonkey© website directly or exported to a .csv file for analyses using R/RStudio.23 Confidence intervals were calculated using the exact binomial method. Significance was defined a priori as P < .05 for all statistical tests. For paired ranking data, a global Friedman test was conducted first. When the Friedman test was statistically significant, pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed. Data visualizations and graphs were created using ggplot2 in R/RStudio.24

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis assessment clearly demonstrates that, despite recognizing La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) as the most important mosquito-borne disease in WNC, local health department personnel encounter challenges in preparedness, interpretation of diagnostic laboratory results, and resource availability. These findings underscore an urgent need for targeted investments in workforce training, surveillance infrastructure, and sustainable funding to support effective vector-borne disease response broadly. Surveillance and control capacities were notably limited across the region, and only one county met all 5 NACCHO-defined core and supplemental standards. Key capacities such as routine entomologic surveillance were reported by only a few health departments (Table 1). Knowledge of LACE-specific risk factors also varied, although CDN personnel generally demonstrated a stronger understanding of environmental and behavioral risk factors than EHS personnel; however, both groups exhibited gaps in identifying key behavioral risk factors and protective environmental factors. Most CDN respondents demonstrated difficulty accurately identifying La Crosse virus (LACV) as the likely cause of a case study (Appendix A), while 14.3% selected the correct agent despite appropriate clinical and laboratory evidence. The most common response (“the child’s disease was most likely caused by California encephalitis virus”) may demonstrate uncertainty about the members of the California serogroup of viruses. Additionally, 53.3% of CDN respondents recognized that the case met the laboratory criteria for an arboviral disease, indicating potential gaps in diagnostic interpretation.Our assessment also revealed meaningful barriers to improving local vector-borne disease response. Most health directors cited limited personnel capacity as the primary constraint, emphasizing the need for sustained funding to support capacity building. State and federal financial support was rare, and health departments reported limited awareness of existing external resources. The one county that had all 5 core and supplemental mosquito control and surveillance capabilities was also the only county reporting active state funding (AA908 contracts). While most EHS respondents recognized vector-borne disease prevention as a professional responsibility and expressed interest in participating, many felt unqualified or too overburdened to provide such services. Overall, the health department personnel expressed strong interest in increased training opportunities. Respondents favored short (1-day) regional offerings focused on practical skills such as mosquito identification, laboratory result interpretation, and disease trends. These findings highlight a regional need for increased investment in personnel, training, and infrastructure to strengthen preparedness and response capacity for LACV and other mosquito-borne pathogens.LimitationsThis study was limited by a small sample size (N = 47), a moderate response rate (36.7%), and reliance on self-reported data. Variation in job roles may have affected how questions were interpreted. However, participation from all 10 WNC counties with the highest incidence of LACE disease and statistically significant findings for key risk factors and roles support the study’s robustness. Also, the low number of health directors (n = 8) limits the robustness of the study statistically, and thus their role-specific responses should be contextualized as such.The primary goal of this study was to evaluate LACV prevention, detection, and response capacity in North Carolina county health departments. Other public health agencies, namely the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Public Health & Human Services agency and the North Carolina Public Health Preparedness and Response branch (North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services) were not included in this survey. Future efforts to develop a regional approach to LACV prevention, detection, and response should include these important partners. The survey was developed using CDC and NACCHO vector control capacity guidance with additional questions developed by state and regional vector-borne disease subject matter experts. The instrument was designed as an applied public health capacity assessment rather than a psychometric scale. As such, formal scale validation methods were not conducted. The survey included both role-specific response items and structural indicators to evaluate operational realities across health departments.This study was conducted in 2024, nearly a year after the World Health Organization announced the end of the COVID-19 epidemic as a public health emergency of international concern.27 The impacts of COVID-19 on the public and environmental health workforce clearly limited vector-borne disease preparedness and response, as many personnel had to shift priorities to support the pandemic response. These shifts contributed to underdiagnosis, underreporting, and reduced data availability in 2020 and 2021, which likely continues to affect funding, staffing, and institutional prioritization of vector-borne diseases in local health departments.28 The results of our study should thus be contextualized with the potential lingering impacts of COVID-19 in addition to other shifting public health priorities and chronic public health workforce challenges.3 Furthermore, the survey was conducted in February and March of 2024, which is outside the typical time when mosquito activity is common in WNC. Finally, while the assessment presented here emphasizes LACV, the survey instrument assessed vector-borne disease capacity more broadly, and respondents may have interpreted some items in the context of general mosquito-borne disease preparedness rather than LACV specifically.ConclusionGoing forward, the information gained from our survey can be used to prioritize training interventions to improve LACE case prevention, detection, and response capacity for WNC. Training sessions, including the use of case studies, to help improve CDN knowledge and application of case definitions for La Crosse encephalitis (and other vector-borne diseases) should be developed. Given that LACE is clearly recognized as a regional public health issue and that individual counties report very few cases each year, it may be more effective to use a regional approach to training and vector control that combines personnel, equipment, and other resources for case investigations and response. By leveraging coordinated approaches like region-specific training opportunities (e.g., tabletop exercises simulating local mosquito-borne disease outbreaks; mosquito surveillance and control workshops; virtual competency-based trainings for arboviral laboratory test interpretation), WNC can more effectively build the workforce capacity, surveillance systems, and resource-sharing networks needed to reduce the burden of LACE and other vector-borne diseases.Disclosure of InterestsThe authors have no relevant conflicts of interest relating to this study.CorrespondenceAddress correspondence to Dr. Brian Byrd, Western Carolina University, 3971 Little Savannah Road, Cullowhee, NC 28723 (bdbyrd@wcu.edu).

full_text_sections.other: IntroductionIn recent decades, vector-borne infectious disease incidence has tripled in the United States.1,2 Despite this increase, many regions across the United States lack adequate public health infrastructure, mosquito surveillance and control capacity, and invasive vector detection capabilities.3–5 In North Carolina, the primary causes of endemic mosquito-borne disease are La Crosse, eastern equine encephalitis (EEE), and West Nile viruses. In most years, La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) accounts for the largest burden of endemic mosquito-borne disease in the state.6,7 Notably, LACE disproportionately impacts children, with a median case age of 9 years.7 During the past two decades, persistent spatial clusters of LACE have been identified in Western North Carolina (WNC) counties.8La Crosse virus (LACV) is an arbovirus in the genus Orthobunyavirus and a member of California serogroup (CSG) of viruses. The CSG contains 18 viruses, including species such as Jamestown Canyon virus that overlaps geographically and is antigenically similar, resulting in cross-reactivity for some diagnostic methods.9,10 The disease ecology of LACV is complex. The virus is primarily transmitted by the eastern tree hole mosquito (Aedes triseriatus), although two invasive mosquito species (Aedes albopictus and Aedes japonicus) are likely secondary vectors.11 Horizontal transmission includes virus-amplifying hosts such as chipmunks and squirrels (family Sciuridae).12 Humans are “dead end” hosts as they do not appear to have detectable viremias that are able to infect host-feeding mosquitoes. Importantly, LACV can be vertically transmitted from a female mosquito to her offspring via transovarial infection, which likely leads to the spatial persistence of the virus over decades.13,14From a national perspective, LACE is rare.2 However, in areas of Appalachia where the disease is endemic, the relative risk of disease in high-risk clusters can be 23 to 70 times higher than non-endemic counties.15 From 2003–2021, the risk of LACE was approximately 44 to 53 times higher in WNC high-risk clusters than in non-endemic counties, clearly demonstrating the regional importance of this disease. full_text: IntroductionHomeless individuals are a highly vulnerable population with complex medical and social needs. Emergency departments (EDs) often serve as the primary point of contact for healthcare for homeless persons in India, yet systematic data on their profile and outcomes from tertiary care settings remain limited.MethodologyA prospective observational study was conducted in the emergency medicine department of a tertiary care centre in North India from July 2022 to December 2023 (18-month duration). All homeless patients aged over 18 years presenting to the emergency department and meeting inclusion criteria were enrolled. Sociodemographic data, clinical presentation, investigations, consultations and ED outcomes were recorded using a structured pro forma, and data were analysed using SPSS v23.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY).ResultsForty-eight homeless patients were enrolled in the study. The majority were men (93.8%), adults aged 31-60 years (52.1%) and from Uttarakhand (85.4%). Most patients (75%) were staying alone, and 81.2% were uninsured. The most common mode of arrival was ambulance (85.4%), with 66.7% referred from another healthcare facility. The most common presenting complaints were abdominal symptoms (22.9%), dyspnoea (18.8%) and trauma (16.7%). Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was the most common diagnosis (12.5%), followed by head injury (10.4%) and decompensated chronic liver disease (8.3%). Two-thirds of the patients (66.7%) were triaged to the red area. ED in-hospital mortality was 18.8%. The median ED length of stay was two days. Fourteen patients had ED revisits during the study period.ConclusionsHomeless patients presenting to the ED are predominantly men and uninsured and arrive in critical condition via ambulance. They carry a high burden of chronic disease, present late in the course of illness and have substantially high in-ED mortality. Integrated care models, policy-level expansion of health coverage and dedicated ED protocols for homeless individuals are urgently needed in India. Materials and methodsStudy design and settingA single-centre, prospective observational study was conducted at the Department of Emergency Medicine of All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Rishikesh, a tertiary care academic hospital located in Rishikesh, Uttarakhand, India. The study period extended from July 2022 to December 2023 (18 months total, with 15 months of data collection, one month for follow-up and two months for data analysis and report writing).ParticipantsInclusion CriteriaAll homeless patients aged >18 years who presented to the ED during the study period and were willing to participate in the study were included.Exclusion CriteriaPatients who declined to participate in the study were excluded.Operational Definition of HomelessnessAccording to the Census of India, an individual is considered homeless if they reside in a shelter or a place not meant for human habitation, are exiting an institution where they temporarily resided or stay on pavements, roadsides, railway platforms, staircases, temples, streets, pipes or other open spaces [2].For this study, homelessness was verified at enrolment through direct interviews and assessments of the participant's current living situations. Participants were considered eligible if they reported that they did not have access to a regular, fixed residential dwelling and were living on the streets, pavements and railway/bus stations; under flyovers; in temporary/open spaces; or in other locations not constituting a conventional residence.Informed written consent was obtained from all eligible patients prior to enrolment. For patients who were unable to consent (e.g., altered sensorium), deferred consent was obtained from the treating team.Sample sizeAll eligible patients meeting inclusion criteria were included in the study. Based on a previous census of the ED, approximately two homeless patients visited the ED each month. Over a 15-month data collection period, the expected sample size was approximately 30 patients; however, all eligible homeless patients who visited the ED were enrolled, yielding a final sample size of 48.Data collectionA structured data collection pro forma was used to record sociodemographic variables, substance use history, the mode of transport to the ED, the type of referral, clinical data (including presenting complaints, triage area, primary survey findings {airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, ABCDE}, clinical examination findings, provisional diagnosis and investigations performed), interdepartmental consultations, total expenditure in the ED, the season of presentation and ED disposition.OutcomesThe primary outcome is the description of the sociodemographic and clinical profile of homeless patients. Secondary outcomes are (1) ED disposition (discharged, admitted to ward, admitted to ICU, died in ED, LAMA or absconded), (2) ED length of stay, (3) in-ED mortality and (4) ED revisits during the study period.Statistical analysisData were entered in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA) and analysed using SPSS version 23.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Continuous variables were tested for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test; normally distributed variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and non-normally distributed variables as median (interquartile range, IQR). This study was exploratory in design, and no prior hypothesis was tested.EthicsThe study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of AIIMS Rishikesh with letter number AIIMS/IEC/22/453 on 20/10/2022. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Data confidentiality was maintained throughout. No conflict of interest exists. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis prospective observational study is one of the first from India to systematically characterise the sociodemographic and clinical profile of 48 homeless patients presenting to a tertiary care emergency department over 18 months. The principal findings are descriptive: the cohort was overwhelmingly male, uninsured and locally resident; was presented predominantly by ambulance and in critical condition; and experienced substantial in-ED mortality. Subgroup comparisons were exploratory, and no association survived correction for multiple testing; they are reported to inform future hypothesis-driven work rather than to support inference.The predominance of male patients (45, 93.8%) is consistent with global literature. Tadros et al. [19] reported 72.3% men, and Burak et al. [20] and Little and Watson [21] reported comparable male predominance. The low representation of women likely reflects gender differences in stigma and vulnerability that affect both the visibility and the reporting of homeless women, rather than a true absence of need; women experiencing homelessness may preferentially seek shelter-based or informal care.Most patients (25, 52.1%) were in the 31-60-year age group, with 13 (27.1%) elderly (>60 years). Age group was not associated with in-ED mortality (exact p = 0.790), alcohol use (exact p = 0.668) or insurance status (exact p = 0.791), with Cramér's V of 0.12 for each, indicating negligible association. These null results should be attributed to limited power as much as to a true absence of effect: With nine deaths and 11 alcohol users across three age strata, the study can exclude only very large effects, and larger multi-centre studies are needed. Smoking prevalence did differ by age group, rising from 2/10 (20.0%) among young adults to 11/25 (44.0%) among adults and 10/13 (76.9%) among elderly patients (Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact p = 0.029; Cramér's V = 0.40). This was the only association of appreciable magnitude in the cohort and is consistent with cumulative lifetime exposure during prolonged street residence, although it does not survive correction for multiple comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.129) and cross-sectional data cannot separate a cohort effect from differential survival.The substantial proportion of elderly patients carries clinical implications, as older homeless individuals bear a higher burden of chronic disease and worse outcomes. This aligns with Brown and Steinman's finding that older homeless patients have more severe medical presentations [6]. In our cohort, in-ED mortality was numerically higher in older groups (1/10, 10.0%, in young adults; 5/25, 20.0%, in adults; and 3/13, 23.1%, in the elderly), but this gradient was not statistically significant (exact p = 0.790; Cramér's V = 0.12) and is compatible with chance at this sample size. It is reported as a descriptive observation rather than as evidence of an age-mortality relationship.Thirty-two patients (66.7%) were triaged to the red (immediate/emergency) area, indicating that homeless patients present critically ill. This high acuity is consistent with barriers to earlier ambulatory care that have been described in homeless populations, although our single-centre descriptive design cannot establish the timing or causality of presentation.The ambulance utilisation rate of 41/48 (85.4%) far exceeds the 51% reported by Pearson et al. in the USA, suggesting that homeless patients in this setting reach the ED largely passively, transported by others rather than self-presenting [10]. That 32 patients (66.7%) were referred from another healthcare facility rather than presenting directly further suggests that a substantial proportion of patients are transferred after initial contact elsewhere. This observation is compatible with capacity constraints at primary and secondary levels, but our data cannot quantify those constraints or attribute causality.Abdominal symptoms (11, 22.9%) were the most common presenting complaint, followed by dyspnoea (nine, 18.8%) and trauma (eight, 16.7%). Unlike Western studies, in which substance-related and psychiatric presentations predominate, our cohort showed a higher burden of medical illness, COPD, chronic liver disease and infectious disease, reflecting disease epidemiology and environmental exposures particular to the Indian homeless population. Psychiatry consultation was nonetheless sought in eight patients (16.7%), so psychiatric morbidity is present but was not the leading reason for attendance.The in-ED mortality rate of 9/48 (18.8%) is notably high and reflects the severity of illness at presentation. A global systematic review by Vohra et al. documented high adverse outcomes among homeless ED patients [16]; our rate sits at the upper end of reported ranges, likely reflecting the combination of late presentation, high disease burden and resource constraints. That four patients (8.3%) were brought dead further underscores the critical nature of these presentations.Among subgroup comparisons, in-ED mortality was lower among smokers (1/23, 4.3%) than non-smokers (8/25, 32.0%; Fisher's exact OR = 0.10; 95% CI, 0.002-0.87; p = 0.024). This must not be read as a protective effect of smoking, and three considerations argue against any causal interpretation. First, the estimate rests on a single death among 23 smokers, and its confidence interval spans more than two orders of magnitude. Second, it does not survive correction for multiplicity across the nine post hoc comparisons reported in Table 3 (Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.129). Third, at least two noncausal mechanisms could generate it: confounding by presentation severity, if non-smokers presented with more acute illness, a greater proportion brought dead or in advanced organ failure, than the older, chronic-disease-burdened smoking subgroup, and collider stratification, since both smoking status and survival to ED registration depend on the pathway by which a homeless individual reaches hospital. We regard this finding as an artefact of sparse data and report it for completeness rather than as a result.No alcohol user died in the emergency department (0/11) compared with 9/37 (24.3%) of nonusers. Because one cell is zero, the conditional maximum-likelihood odds ratio is 0 with an exact 95% confidence interval of 0-1.58. This analysis is uninformative rather than negative: It has essentially no power to exclude an effect in either direction, and it should not be presented as a parallel to, or corroboration of, the smoking finding.Thirty-nine patients (81.2%) were uninsured, and only nine (18.8%) were covered under Ayushman Bharat, a figure that likely underrepresents true eligibility in this population given the documentation requirements for enrolment. Uninsured status did not differ across age groups (exact p = 0.791). This is consistent with literature documenting that the absence of insurance drives delayed healthcare-seeking and adverse outcomes among homeless populations and identifies scheme enrolment at the point of ED contact as a tractable intervention.The median ED length of stay, excluding patients brought dead, was two days (IQR, 2-3; mean, 2.77 days; SD, 2.01), substantially longer than the 2.6-7.5 hours reported by Pearson et al. [10]. This difference is of an order that reflects a structural rather than a clinical distinction: prolonged stay here represents boarding driven by the practical impossibility of discharging a homeless patient without destination, caretaker or follow-up arrangement, compounded by medical complexity. Mean expenditure was INR 3,923 (SD: 2,716) per patient, borne entirely by the hospital or the Ayushman Bharat scheme, highlighting the financial burden carried by the public health system.Fourteen of the 39 patients who survived the index visit (35.9%, 95% CI: 21.2%-52.8%) had at least one ED revisit during the study period, and four (10.3%) returned three times. Restricting the denominator to patients actually at r…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsHomeless patients presenting to the ED at AIIMS Rishikesh are predominantly men, middle-aged and uninsured and arrive critically ill by ambulance, usually referred from other facilities. They carry a high burden of chronic disease, including COPD, chronic liver disease and trauma and frequently present with advanced or critical illness. The in-ED mortality rate was 18.8%, with a notable proportion brought dead. ED length of stay was longer than general populations, and revisit rates were high.These findings underscore the need for targeted, integrated care strategies within the emergency department, including systematic social assessment at triage, linkage with government welfare schemes and structured post-discharge planning. This study provides foundational data for future multi-centre research and evidence-based policymaking for homeless health in India.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionFood, clothing and shelter are three basic human needs. While many individuals struggle to meet the first two, permanent residence often remains beyond reach for a significant proportion of the population [1]. Homelessness is a growing global phenomenon with diverse definitions across countries. The definition of homelessness according to the Census of India 2011 is 'an individual who resides in a shelter or place not meant for human habitation and who is exiting an institution where he or she temporarily resided and stays on pavements, roadsides, railway platforms, staircases, temples, streets, pipes or other open spaces' [2].India is home to approximately 0.45 million homeless families, comprising a total homeless population of 1.773 million individuals, with the highest burden in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra [3]. In search of shelter and food, a homeless person attends the emergency department (ED), and due to their inability to reach the primary health centre, homeless patients have high rates of ED utilisation [4,5].Due to difficulty accessing outpatient facilities, homeless persons are often dropped at the ED by EMS personnel, autorickshaw drivers or members of the public. They frequently present without money, identification or a caretaker. In some cases, individuals deliberately seek the ED during extreme weather conditions in search of shelter, food and basic safety.Previous studies have shown that homeless patients frequently use emergency departments and have distinct demographic and clinical characteristics. Older homeless adults are more likely to have alcohol abuse and arrive by ambulance, while homeless patients overall have higher rates of ED revisits and hospital readmissions, particularly after discharge to shelters or the streets. Compared with non-homeless patients, they are often younger but have a greater likelihood of hospitalisation despite similar healthcare costs and lengths of stay. These findings emphasise the necessity of targeted interventions to improve the continuity of care and reduce recurrent emergency department utilisation [6-9].Previous studies consistently demonstrate that homeless patients have higher rates of emergency department utilisation, ambulance use, substance abuse and mental health disorders than non-homeless individuals. They also experience longer ED stays and increased 30-day revisits and hospital readmissions, particularly among those with mental illness. Homeless individuals are more likely to have infectious diseases, alcohol and drug dependence, social isolation and injury-related presentations, especially involving the lower limbs. These findings emphasise the necessity of integrated medical, psychiatric and social interventions to improve outcomes in this vulnerable population [10-14].Studies consistently show that homeless patients are more likely to arrive at the emergency department by ambulance, be uninsured and present with substance abuse, alcohol-related problems and injuries. They have significantly higher rates of emergency department revisits and 30-day hospital readmissions than non-homeless individuals. Despite lower hospital admission rates, the emergency department remains a critical point of access for healthcare among the homeless population, pointing out the need for targeted interventions and improved continuity of care [15-19].The primary outcome of the study is the description of the sociodemographic and clinical profile of homeless patients.Secondary outcomes of the study are (1) ED disposition (discharged, admitted to ward, admitted to ICU, died in ED, left against medical advice {LAMA} or absconded), (2) ED length of stay, (3) in-ED mortality and (4) ED revisits during the study period.

full_text: Conclusion: implications for GHD and PHDBoth cases show PHD as the practical, relationship-based complement to GHD. The railway programme was preventive and corridor-based, focusing on sustained risk management within commercial infrastructure. The flood response was reactive and geographically broader in addressing disrupted diagnostic capacity. It relied on trust and coordination developed through earlier programmes. Routine cooperation thus helped create “diplomatic infrastructure” that became rapidly repurposed during emergencies.Three implications follow. First, implementation is a distinct diplomatic site: negotiation continues as agreements are interpreted, adapted and operationalized. Second, non-state actors are boundary-spanning intermediaries among health authorities, infrastructure operators, diplomatic institutions and communities. Their value lies not only in delivering resources but also in translating priorities and building local ownership of problems [10]. Third, evaluations should extend beyond immediate outputs to include relationships, trust and coordination capacities.PHD should not be conflated with mere communication or programme coordination. It becomes necessary when actors must reconcile different interests, mandates, expertise and control over scarce resources. Negotiations may concern infrastructure access, responsibilities, intervention adaptation and local knowledge. Implementation is thus far from being a technical stage following agreement, but instead a setting where commitments are interpreted, adapted or resisted.GHD and PHD should remain conceptually distinct but practically complementary. HSR conjoins health objectives with national strategy and international relations, while the GX–China–Laos Railway experience shows how these ambitions become practice through shared problem-solving.This complementarity requires equity and accountability. NGO–enterprise partnerships work best when roles are clear, financing supports continuity and activities strengthen public institutions. Equitable involvement of local authorities and communities in decisions and implementation promotes ownership and responsiveness. PHD should thus be understood as ethical, accountable diplomacy that strengthens public health resilience. Introduction: from high-level commitments to local implementationHealth diplomacy, the mobilization of health issues to influence foreign policy and interstate relations, is increasingly important: public health problems frequently intersect with geopolitical competition, economic integration and infrastructural development. Infectious diseases move through transport networks and across borders, while the authority and resources needed to address them are distributed among differing stakeholders. This pattern raises a practical question: how can political commitments become effective, locally legitimate interventions when no institution has sufficient capacity to act alone?Health diplomacy has traditionally been examined through global health diplomacy (“GHD”), which concerns the negotiation of health interests through foreign policy, international relations and global governance [1, 2]. This literature explains how states establish agreements, mobilize resources and incorporate health into strategic agendas. However, health diplomacy increasingly depends on sub-state and non-state actors working in hospitals, communities, transport systems and emergencies. Public health diplomacy (“PHD”) offers a lens for examining the practical negotiations through which public health capacity and resilience are built [3].China’s Belt and Road Initiative (“BRI”), a global infrastructure and connectivity programme, is a case in point. Within the BRI, an initiative known as the Health Silk Road (“HSR”) seeks to strengthen global health cooperation, improve healthcare infrastructure and expand China’s influence in international health governance. Transport corridors facilitate trade but also create pathways for disease transmission, requiring cooperation among health authorities, infrastructure operators and communities. The HSR thus illustrates how infrastructure, mobility and health security are intertwined [4, 5]. Its outcomes, however, depend on specific epidemiological risks and institutional contexts.This commentary examines these socio-political dynamics through GX Foundation’s work along the China–Laos Railway and its later flood response in northern Laos against the backdrop of the HSR. Established in Hong Kong [6] in 2018, GX provides international medical and humanitarian assistance through partnerships that emphasize “people-to-people connectivity” [7]. Its boundary-spanning position demonstrates how non-state actors connect diplomatic commitments with operational expertise. We conclude that GHD secures high-level commitments, while PHD makes them workable and durable. Although conceptually distinct, they are practically complementary. Preventing dengue along a transnational railway corridorThe China–Laos Railway is a 1,035-km BRI corridor connecting Kunming and Vientiane through dengue-endemic areas. While advancing economic integration, it creates a shared epidemiological space in which mosquitoes, infected travellers and disease risks cross national boundaries. Managing this risk requires translating national commitments into coordinated practices across stations and communities.Since 2020, GX has worked under Lao national and provincial health authorities with the Laos–China Railway Company, railway personnel and local stakeholders to embed dengue prevention in railway operations through a “Health Emergency and Disaster Risk Management” approach [8].The initiative illustrates PHD as the cross-border mobilization of non-state and sub-state actors. Formal China–Laos engagement provided legitimacy and communication but left open how prevention would operate at individual stations. GX and the railway company filled this implementation gap by determining where equipment should be installed, who would maintain it, how staff would participate and how messages would be disseminated. The company provided infrastructural access, operational knowledge and logistics; Chinese and Lao personnel adapted interventions to station layouts and exposure patterns; and passengers and communities participated through risk communication and preventive activities.Implementation required negotiation rather than simple equipment delivery. Sites were selected according to passenger volume, existing coverage and exposure to cross-border movements. Measures were adapted to station layouts, staff routines and electricity availability. Monitoring, for example, showed that posters were useful for staff who saw them repeatedly but less so for transient passengers.By July 2024, 871 mosquito-killing lamps had been deployed across all 29 stations — 511 in China and 360 in Laos—in waiting halls, ticketing areas, washrooms, platforms, offices and staff accommodation. Monitoring at six locations, together with 60 interviews and 1,243 staff survey responses, informed maintenance and adaptation [8]. High satisfaction and preventive behaviours showed participation beyond equipment coverage. No dengue infections were reported among railway staff during the following 12 months, although this observational result cannot establish causation. Strong acceptance of the programme also contributed to the partnership’s two-year renewal in 2025 [9]. Repurposing diplomatic infrastructure during an emergencyThe programme’s relationships proved valuable during the September 2024 response to Typhoon Yagi. GX’s capacity to act in northern Laos arose not from a linear expansion of dengue-control activities but from existing, overlapping forms of health cooperation.After severe flooding in Luang Namtha, assessments by GX and local health partners identified increased post-flood dengue risk. Flooding also damaged Namtha District Hospital’s laboratory facilities, weakening local diagnosis and referral. Under provincial and national health authorities, GX launched the four-month Project X, supplying vector-control materials and laboratory equipment to restore diagnostic and disease-control capacity [8].Rather than creating an emergency partnership from scratch, Project X mobilized existing relationships. Authorities set priorities and retained oversight; hospital personnel identified the support required to resume testing and referrals; and GX mobilized supplies, diagnostic equipment and implementation support through Chinese and Lao networks. Local health workers and communities extended surveillance and prevention beyond the hospital, expanding diagnostic coverage from approximately 20–78 villages [8].GX acted as a boundary-spanning intermediary connecting authorities, hospitals and communities with transport, logistics and other stakeholders under the legitimacy provided by authorities. Health facilities identified clinical needs, while local partners contributed contextual knowledge. Relationships formed through vector control and transport operations became what we call “diplomatic infrastructure”, producing immediate outputs and latent emergency-response capacity. Effective implementation depended both on the use of the railway corridor to deliver assistance and also on the resilience of the networks surrounding it. The railway programme was preventive and corridor-based, focusing on sustained risk management within commercial infrastructure. The flood response was reactive and geographically broader in addressing disrupted diagnostic capacity. It relied on trust and coordination developed through earlier programmes. Routine cooperation thus helped create “diplomatic infrastructure” that became rapidly repurposed during emergencies.Three implications follow. First, implementation is a distinct diplomatic site: negotiation continues as agreements are interpreted, adapted and operationalized. Second, non-state actors are boundary-spanning intermediaries among health authorities, infrastructure operators, diplomatic institutions and communities. Their value lies not only in delivering resources but also in translating priorities and building local ownership of problems [10]. Third, evaluations should extend beyond immediate outputs to include relationships, trust and coordination capacities.PHD should not be conflated with mere communication or programme coordination. It becomes necessary when actors must reconcile different interests, mandates, expertise and control over scarce resources. Negotiations may concern infrastructure access, responsibilities, intervention adaptation and local knowledge. Implementation is thus far from being a technical stage following agreement, but instead a setting where commitments are interpreted, adapted or resisted.GHD and PHD should remain conceptually distinct but practically complementary. HSR conjoins health objectives with national strategy and international relations, while the GX–China–Laos Railway experience shows how these ambitions become practice through shared problem-solving.This complementarity requires equity and accountability. NGO–enterprise partnerships work best when roles are clear, financing supports continuity and activities strengthen public institutions. Equitable involvement of local authorities and communities in decisions and implementation promotes ownership and responsiveness. PHD should thus be understood as ethical, accountable diplomacy that strengthens public health resilience.
full_text_sections.other: Introduction: from high-level commitments to local implementationHealth diplomacy, the mobilization of health issues to influence foreign policy and interstate relations, is increasingly important: public health problems frequently intersect with geopolitical competition, economic integration and infrastructural development. Infectious diseases move through transport networks and across borders, while the authority and resources needed to address them are distributed among differing stakeholders. This pattern raises a practical question: how can political commitments become effective, locally legitimate interventions when no institution has sufficient capacity to act alone?Health diplomacy has traditionally been examined through global health diplomacy (“GHD”), which concerns the negotiation of health interests through foreign policy, international relations and global governance [1, 2]. This literature explains how states establish agreements, mobilize resources and incorporate health into strategic agendas. However, health diplomacy increasingly depends on sub-state and non-state actors working in hospitals, communities, transport systems and emergencies. Public health diplomacy (“PHD”) offers a lens for examining the practical negotiations through which public health capacity and resilience are built [3].China’s Belt and Road Initiative (“BRI”), a global infrastructure and connectivity programme, is a case in point. Within the BRI, an initiative known as the Health Silk Road (“HSR”) seeks to strengthen global health cooperation, improve healthcare infrastructure and expand China’s influence in international health governance. Transport corridors facilitate trade but also create pathways for disease transmission, requiring cooperation among health authorities, infrastructure operators and communities. The HSR thus illustrates how infrastructure, mobility and health security are intertwined [4, 5]. Its outcomes, however, depend on specific epidemiological risks and institutional contexts.This commentary examines these socio-political dynamics through GX Foundation’s work along the China–Laos Railway and its later flood response in northern Laos against the backdrop of the HSR. Established in Hong Kong [6] in 2018, GX provides international medical and humanitarian assistance through partnerships that emphasize “people-to-people connectivity” [7]. Its boundary-spanning position demonstrates how non-state actors connect diplomatic commitments with operational expertise. We conclude that GHD secures high-level commitments, while PHD makes them workable and durable. Although conceptually distinct, they are practically complementary. Preventing dengue along a transnational railway corridorThe China–Laos Railway is a 1,035-km BRI corridor connecting Kunming and Vientiane through dengue-endemic areas. While advancing economic integration, it creates a shared epidemiological space in which mosquitoes, infected travellers and disease risks cross national boundaries. Managing this risk requires translating national commitments into coordinated practices across stations and communities.Since 2020, GX has worked under Lao national and provincial health authorities with the Laos–China Railway Company, railway personnel and local stakeholders to embed dengue prevention in railway operations through a “Health Emergency and Disaster Risk Management” approach [8].The initiative illustrates PHD as the cross-border mobilization of non-state and sub-state actors. Formal China–Laos engagement provided legitimacy and communication but left open how prevention would operate at individual stations. GX and the railway company filled this implementation gap by determining where equipment should be installed, who would maintain it, how staff would participate and how messages would be disseminated. The company provided infrastructural access, operational knowledge and logistics; Chinese and Lao personnel adapted interventions to station layouts and exposure patterns; and passengers and communities participated through risk communication and preventive activities.Implementation required negotiation rather than simple equipment delivery. Sites were selected according to passenger volume, existing coverage and exposure to cross-border movements. Measures were adapted to station layouts, staff routines and electricity availability. Monitoring, for example, showed that posters were useful for staff who saw them repeatedly but less so for transient passengers.By July 2024, 871 mosquito-killing lamps had been deployed across all 29 stations — 511 in China and 360 in Laos—in waiting halls, ticketing areas, washrooms, platforms, offices and staff accommodation. Monitoring at six locations, together with 60 interviews and 1,243 staff survey responses, informed maintenance and adaptation [8]. High satisfaction and preventive behaviours showed participation beyond equipment coverage. No dengue infections were reported among railway staff during the following 12 months, although this observational result cannot establish causation. Strong acceptance of the programme also contributed to the partnership’s two-year renewal in 2025 [9]. Repurposing diplomatic infrastructure during an emergencyThe programme’s relationships proved valuable during the September 2024 response to Typhoon Yagi. GX’s capacity to act in northern Laos arose not from a linear expansion of dengue-control activities but from existing, overlapping forms of health cooperation.After severe flooding in Luang Namtha, assessments by GX and local health partners identified increased post-flood dengue risk. Flooding also damaged Namtha District Hospital’s laboratory facilities, weakening local diagnosis and referral. Under provincial and national health authorities, GX launched the four-month Project X, supplying vector-control materials and laboratory equipment to restore diagnostic and disease-control capacity [8].Rather than creating an emergency partnership from scratch, Project X mobilized existing relationships. Authorities set priorities and retained oversight; hospital personnel identified the support required to resume testing and referrals; and GX mobilized supplies, diagnostic equipment and implementation support through Chinese and Lao networks. Local health workers and communities extended surveillance and prevention beyond the hospital, expanding diagnostic coverage from approximately 20–78 villages [8].GX acted as a boundary-spanning intermediary connecting authorities, hospitals and communities with transport, logistics and other stakeholders under the legitimacy provided by authorities. Health facilities identified clinical needs, while local partners contributed contextual knowledge. Relationships formed through vector control and transport operations became what we call “diplomatic infrastructure”, producing immediate outputs and latent emergency-response capacity. Effective implementation depended both on the use of the railway corridor to deliver assistance and also on the resilience of the networks surrounding it.
